Artificial intelligence is getting a permission slip in Florida’s public school classrooms.Under rules approved Wednesday by the State Board of Education, parents will have to opt in before public and charter school students interact directly with AI instructional tools. Students whose families decline must receive a comparable alternative without AI.WATCH BELOW: Florida adopts classroom AI rules Public school districts and charter schools have until July 1, 2027, to adopt and implement the required policies. Central Florida Public Media.Gov. Ron DeSantis promoted the requirements during a Thursday appearance in Melbourne, saying technology should supplement classroom instruction.“We are not going to be displacing a classroom teacher with machines,” DeSantis said. “We're going to continue to value the human experience in education, and not sacrifice that at the altar of technology.”The rules require schools to notify parents when an AI instructional tool is approved, including which tool students would use, the courses involved and how students would interact with it. Tools used with children in pre-kindergarten through fifth grade face additional review for age and developmental appropriateness.The requirements also prohibit instructional chatbots designed to simulate friendship or emotional relationships with students, undisclosed psychological profiling and vendors selling student data.The board also approved rules for Florida College System institutions. Their policies must prohibit students from using AI on graded assignments or tests unless an instructor explicitly authorizes it.Education Commissioner Henry Mack said the concern is whether students are developing their own understanding when they turn to AI for answers.“So if a course is designed to cultivate critical thinking, we do not want AI doing that on behalf of the learner,” Mack said.Florida Education Association Vice President Carole Gauronskas has expressed support for the policies overall while questioning how much additional work implementation could create for school districts.Gauronskas urged the board to seek more input as schools prepare.“We encourage this board to convene a panel of experts, including parents, guardians, and come up with more guidance and guardrails just to make sure that that human touch is there,” she said.Teachers and administrators will also need training on AI’s risks, limitations, safety and compliance requirements. Many districts already have AI policies but will need to align them with the new statewide requirements.Asked Thursday about support for schools, including rural districts, Mack said the Department of Education would organize work groups, coordinate with superintendents and provide resources to help carry out the rules.

Lucie Police say they used a dead man's own phone to text his alleged drug dealer and arrange a buy, an investigation that led to a search warrant, thousands in cash, guns and drugs found at the dealer's home. According to the arrest affidavit, officers responded to an apartment at 700 SE Collins Lane on September 13th for an overdose. They found 34-year-old Miqueias Oliveira Silva dead, with a bloody syringe and a bag of cocaine next to him. The affidavit says rigor mortis suggested Silva had been dead for about 24 hours. It’s destroying the community. It’s destroying the members of the community, said Magalys Koch, a substance abuse expert at Hibiscus Counseling. A neighbor who called 911 told police he last saw Silva getting out of the passenger side of a black SUV before going inside, according to the affidavit. Investigators say they went through Silva's phone and found months of text exchanges with a contact saved under the name Danilo Jaramillo, going back to August 17th. The affidavit says the messages followed a pattern, with Silva asking if Jaramillo was "available" and Jaramillo confirming before the two met up. Police say they used Silva's phone to text Jaramillo and arrange another deal. Jaramillo responded he could be there within the hour. Investigators say they followed Jaramillo's black Kia Telluride to Silva's apartment complex, then pulled him over. A K9 alerted to narcotics inside the vehicle. Investigators say they found a bag of fentanyl on the passenger seat, along with a large amount of cash. According to a separate affidavit, investigators searched the master bedroom. Jaramillo's wife, Selina Jaramillo, was home with their children during the search. According to the affidavit, she told investigators she didn't know he was involved in drugs and said she'd last seen him with narcotics about eight months earlier. She said one of the firearms was hers, but that the rest, along with the drugs and cash, belonged to her husband. While state data points to a steady decline in overdose deaths since 2021, Koch says that addiction is still a rampant cycle. We're moving away from being in touch with who we are. A Fort Pierce man was arrested after a raid Friday by the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office and U.S. Marshals Service found a massive amount of illicit drugs, including fentanyl and cocaine, worth several million dollars. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office Special Investigations Division, with assistance from the SWAT Team and the U.S. Marshals Service, executed a narcotics-related search warrant at a residence in the 3100 block of S. 24th Street in Fort Pierce. The subject of the investigation, Tony Saunders, 48, was taken into custody. Saunders, a three-time convicted felon who is on federal probation, also had two active warrants related to the sale and delivery of controlled substances. Afterward, Saunders faced additional charges of trafficking in fentanyl, trafficking in cocaine, trafficking in MDPV, manufacturing cocaine, tampering with evidence and possession of marijuana with intent to sell. https://www.facebook.com/stluciesheriff/posts/pfbid0j4igLYhtX4QpfPCZhHkYeREcfiqd9eehsAoAcjVwDWTipnXHZNWyrJLe6gbwukcvl The search resulted in the seizure of approximately 4.5 kilograms of fentanyl, 303 grams of cocaine, 97 grams of marijuana laced with MDPV, and 60 oxycodone pills totaling approximately 6.2 grams, the sheriff's office said. The street value of 4.5 kilograms of fentanyl can range from $150,000 to nearly $1.8 million, depending heavily on its purity, geographic location, and whether it is sold as wholesale powder or broken down into counterfeit pills, according to U.S. Customs and Border Protection. The estimated street value of 303 grams of cocaine in the U.S. ranges between roughly $18,180 and $60,600. Detectives also seized assorted ammunition, drug paraphernalia and materials consistent with the preparation and distribution of narcotics. A single kilogram of fentanyl has the potential to kill 500,000 people, making 4.5 kilograms a lethal volume capable of millions of fatal doses, according to the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration. “4.5 kilos of fentanyl are 4.5 kilos that will not reach our streets," Sheriff Richard Del Tro said. "Fentanyl is a deadly poison, and those who traffic in it are putting lives at risk for profit. I commend our detectives, SWAT Team, and the U.S. Marshals Service for their commitment to this mission. We will continue to pursue those who traffic dangerous narcotics and do everything within our authority to make St. Lucie County the safest county in Florida.” Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

The Martin County Commission approved a zoning compromise for land in Hobe Sound, but the 3-2 vote has left some residents and at least one commissioner with lingering concerns about what could be built there. Commissioners voted to rezone a property along Southeast Powerline Avenue to limited-industrial, stepping back from a general industrial designation that drew pushback from nearby residents. The property has long been slated for some form of industrial use, but the county said the existing zoning was outdated and due for an update. WATCH: Hobe Sound zoning compromise raises data center concerns Residents who spoke at the Tuesday commission meeting said their primary concern was protecting the character of the community. Steve Addison said he has lived in the area since 1969. “Our biggest concern was preserving our quality of life. We don’t have a lot of industry and a lot of noise,” Addison said. Other residents echoed concerns about the scope of the original rezoning proposal. “I understand that Martin County has to plan for the future but I also believe that growth needs to be compatible with the community that already exists,” Kim Call, a resident, said. “We’re concerned about the permanence of a GI classification which we believe is too broad and too open-ended,” Patrick McDonough, a Hobe Sound resident and Eaglewood Community HOA president, said. After hearing from residents, the property owner offered to accept the less-intensive classification. “To cooperate and show if that’s what the neighbors feel is more appropriate and that would be a better use then we are willing to accept the light industrial,” Bob Reins, a land-use attorney with Gunster law firm, said. Despite the compromise, Commissioner Blake Capps voted against the rezoning, citing concerns about the potential for a data center on the site. “Who knows where this is really going in the future and to approve a zoning for this property that allows a data center. I’m not into that,” Capps said. The county said there are no plans for a data center at the site. Any proposal exceeding 100,000 square feet would require board approval. In speaking with residents, WPTV’S Cassandra Garcia learned not everyone was happy with the outcome. However, residents like Addison felt it was the right move. “I don’t want to see over development, but I also don’t want to be that guy that doesn’t understand land-use and doesn’t understand property rights,” Addison said. “I feel like it was a win win for the both of us.” This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office announced more than 50 arrests following a multi-agency, multi-day operation targeting human trafficking and illegal sexual activity in the county. Operation Late Checkout ran from Sept. 13 in Indian River County. The operation netted over 60 contacts, more than 50 arrests, and three ICE detainers, Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a press conference on Thursday. Flowers announced the results alongside a representative from the Florida Department of Law Enforcement. “Agencies involved in the operation included the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office, Florida Department of Law Enforcement, St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office, Seminole County Sheriff’s Office, Altamonte Springs Police Department, Vero Beach Police Department, Homeland Security Investigations, Florida Office of Statewide Prosecutor and the U.S. Attorney’s Office,” Flowers said. The operation’s targeted goal was stopping human trafficking in the Indian River County area, the sheriff’s office said. During the operation, several victims were identified, and investigators said ongoing investigations are underway. Flowers said there are no specific arrests on human trafficking charges at this time. One case involved a man who traveled to Indian River County to meet a minor. Flowers said the arrest was the result of the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force working across agencies to apprehend individuals attempting to lure children online. “Our team did a great job of getting him off the street,” Flowers said. Undercover teams were deployed in a variety of capacities during the operation, the sheriff’s office said. Victims’ advocates trained to work with trafficking victims were also on hand to speak with women involved in prostitution to determine whether they were being trafficked. “We have many ongoing investigations as a result of this,” Flowers said. Flowers called the operation unprecedented for Indian River County. “We’ve never had an investigation like this, to my knowledge, in Indian River County with this many agencies involved, with this many arrests in one shot,” he said. FDLE Assistant Special Agent in Charge Alfonso Williams said Operation Late Checkout was initiated by FDLE in coordination with the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office and is the first operation of this magnitude conducted in the county. “This operation shows that within our communities there are dangerous individuals committing heinous crimes who think they can get away with it,” Williams said. Williams said the operation focused on identifying human trafficking victims, reducing the demand for prostitution, and apprehending individuals seeking sexual contact with minors. “Our work is far from done,” Williams said. “This operation requires a lot of resources and time. We cannot do this work alone, and our success depends on the great partnership and collaboration that you see today.” FDLE said it houses the Florida Trafficking Hotline. Anyone who suspects someone is a victim of trafficking can contact the hotline at 1-855-352-7233. READ OPERATION LATE CHECKOUT BELOW:

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis has signed a death warrant for 77-year-old William Reaves Jr., the man convicted of murdering Indian River County Sheriff’s Deputy Richard Raczkoski in 1986. The execution is scheduled for Tuesday, Oct. Reaves was convicted of murdereing Raczkoski on Sept. 23, 1986, after a confrontation at a convenience store. Deputy Raczkoski had responded to a 911 call at the store when he encountered Reaves. During a conversation between the two, a gun fell from Reaves’s shorts. Deputy Raczkoski placed his knee on the weapon. Reaves then pushed the deputy away, grabbed the gun and pointed it at Deputy Raczkoski’s face. As Deputy Raczkoski attempted to draw his own weapon, Reaves said, “I wouldn’t do that if I were you.” The deputy backed away, turned, and ran. Reaves fired seven rounds, striking Deputy Raczkoski four times. Reaves was tried in the 19th Judicial Circuit in Indian River County. On direct appeal, the Florida Supreme Court reversed the initial conviction and remanded the case for a new trial. On remand, Reaves was again convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death on March 6, 1992, in Vero Beach. The Florida Supreme Court affirmed the conviction and death sentence on April 7, 1994. The United States Supreme Court denied Reaves’s petition for a writ of certiorari on Nov. Reaves pursued numerous postconviction challenges in both state and federal courts over the following decades. District Court for the Southern District of Florida granted Reaves’s federal petition for a writ of habeas corpus. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit overturned that ruling and ordered that the petition be denied. Additional postconviction motions and petitions were subsequently denied, and those denials were affirmed on appeal. Executive clemency was also considered and denied. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, in his letter recommending the warrant, wrote that “the record is legally sufficient to support the issuance of a death warrant,” and confirmed that “there are no stays of execution issued by any court of competent jurisdiction in this cause.” The execution is scheduled to take place at Florida State Prison in Raiford. If carried out as scheduled, it will come 40 years after the murder of Deputy Raczkoski.

Some Greenacres residents are reaching out to WPTV with concerns about traffic and safety around Manatee Elementary School, saying parents dropping off and picking up students outside nearby neighborhoods are creating problems on local roads.One message sent to WPTV through Instagram alleged traffic congestion, damage to grass and safety to children.WATCH BELOW: School traffic chaos angers residents near this school"This morning I noticed if there is no space to park on the side, they make a quick stop on the road to drop off their kids. This is causing the traffic to back up blocking the exit to the residents of Spinnaker Bay Dr. I have seen the police presence but parents are ignoring it" said the message.That tip led WPTV to Manatee Elementary School and the nearby Lake Charleston community.A mother named Michelle, who was picking up two of her children from school, said she understands why residents are frustrated."This is a pain in the butt if I lived in Lake Charleston," Michelle said. "It's a nightmare, it's a chaos of kids with a bunch of people loading right here and then some walking down here you never know what are crossing."Michelle said there are not enough places to park, but she chooses to park at a nearby approved county park and walk to the school because it takes about half as long as waiting in the traditional pick-up and drop-off line.She said the drop off look took her as long as two and a half hours, parking and walking took 15 minutes. To see whether the concerns matched what residents were reporting, WPTV photographer Johann Hoffend visited the area during morning drop-off hours.He observed cars and trucks pulled over along the roadway, including vehicles parked directly in front of signs stating "No Parking" and signs warning that drop-offs in travel lanes are prohibited.When WPTV returned during afternoon dismissal, a similar scene unfolded despite multiple no parking signs throughout Charleston Shores Blvd."I park in the grass right there, see the white car that's mine," said Scott Ross while picking up one of his students.Ross said he while he is using the park-and-walk method, he isn't a fan of it and has considered using the school's pick-up line instead, but agrees with Michelle that the line is too long."Almost better to put your kid on a bus, bus takes them right to our house," Ross said.The School District of Palm Beach County said safety must come before convenience."The District urges families and students to prioritize safety over convenience during drop-off and pick-up," the district said in a statement. "We support any and all improvements to improve local traffic flow, and our jurisdiction remains on School District property."The district also shared reminders sent to Manatee Elementary families, instructing parents to use the school's designated parent drop-off and pick-up loop off Hypoluxo Road. Families with students who walk or bike are encouraged to use the county park parking lot next door to campus and access the school's east-side biker and walker entrance.The district also warned families not to use the nearby Public Storage facility as a parking or drop-off location."Please refrain from using the Public Storage facility (behind the Winn Dixie plaza) as a parking space or drop off location in the morning," the message states. "This has become a safety concern due to the volume of cars, unsupervised children, along with customers arriving and departing from the facility."Lake Charleston representatives have also voiced concerns.According to a message shared by the district:"We have had numerous complaints from our residents that many parents who walk their children to your school park their vehicles on the streets of our community. We would like to ask you to send a notice home with the students that we are asking PBSO to start ticketing and subsequently towing cars that are parked in Spinnaker Bay, The Reefs and The Islands. This is causing safety issue for the community and your students."The message also reminds drivers that vehicles should not park along Charleston Shores Boulevard, where signs prohibit parking.Ross said he believes the school itself is not the problem."I think this school is wonderful, it's just this method is awful," he said.After WPTV shared residents' concerns with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office, deputies increased enforcement efforts in the area.PBSO said school traffic safety deputies regularly patrol the area but are responsible for multiple schools and cannot be present every day. Following reports about Manatee Elementary, additional patrols and enforcement efforts began Wednesday.According to PBSO, deputies issued only three warnings and three citations related to school traffic concerns between August and September of this school year before the additional enforcement effort.Last school year, deputies issued 336 warnings and 89 citations in the area.Of the 339 total warnings issued during those periods, 159 were for improper stopping violations.After the increased enforcement effort Wednesday, deputies issued 14 citations and 13 warnings in a single day, nearly five times the number issued during the entire school year.When asked what her solution would be, Michelle answered simply:"Extra parking."Representatives from Lake Charleston told WPTV they have asked PBSO to begin ticketing and towing vehicles that park in residential areas around the school.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A 42-year-old travel MRI technician was arrested after Port St. Lucie police said a patient reported she was sexually assaulted while undergoing an MRI at HCA Florida St. Gabriel Cruz was arrested in Brevard County on the evening of Sept. 16 on a charge of sexual battery involving a physically helpless or incapacitated victim, a first-degree felony, police said. Wasana Chesler is a former patient of St. Lucie Hospital and couldn't believe the news. That's very horrible," Chesler said. "That's very sad." The investigation began Sept. 14 after hospital staff reported that a 64-year-old female patient said she had been sexually assaulted during an MRI the day before at the hospital, 1800 SE Tiffany Ave. Police said the woman had been admitted for medical treatment and was given medication before the MRI that left her significantly drowsy. Detectives identified Cruz as the technician assigned to the procedure. With the hospital’s assistance, investigators obtained video that police said showed Cruz leaving the MRI room after the patient and disposing of materials. See also: Amazon closes Port St. Lucie warehouse for major renovation, hundreds impacted by layoffs Those materials were recovered and tested, returning presumptive positive results for male semen, according to police. Cruz had worked at the hospital as a travel MRI technician since Aug. 24 and was hired through a third-party agency, police said. Monica Defoster said she's been to St. Lucie Hospital many times including on Thursday while visiting her husband. She calls the allegations disturbing. They should have more than one person in the MRI room," Defoster said. "You go to the hospital and don't expect something like that." The investigation remains active. Lucie Hospital has cooperated with investigators, police said. Lucie Hospital provided CBS12 News with the following statement: We do not tolerate behavior that jeopardizes the safety or security of our patients. When this serious allegation was reported to us, we contacted law enforcement and ended the individual’s assignment. We have assisted law enforcement throughout its investigation and remain focused on supporting our patient. A hospital spokesman told CBS12 no other complaints have been reported since Cruz stared working there late last month. Cruz's employer could not be reached for comment. He remains behind bars in Brevard County.

Health officials have issued a blue-green algae health alert for an area of Lake Okeechobee after water samples detected harmful toxins. The Florida Department of Health in Martin County said the alert covers the Lake Okeechobee NES135 area and was issued in response to samples collected Sept. The area is located on the north shore of the lake at J&S Fish Camp in Martin County. Residents and visitors should use caution in and around the lake, officials said. People should not drink, swim, wade, use personal watercraft or otherwise come into contact with water where a visible algae bloom is present. Health officials also advised people to keep pets and livestock away from affected water. Anyone who comes into contact with algae, discolored water or water with an unpleasant odor should wash their skin and clothing with soap and water, according to the department. Officials said contaminated water should not be used for cooking or washing dishes because boiling does not remove algae toxins. Blue-green algae are bacteria commonly found in Florida freshwater. Blooms can discolor water and create floating mats, scum, foam or paint-like material on the surface, sometimes with an unpleasant odor. The blooms can produce toxins that may harm people, pets and aquatic life. Children, older adults and people with weakened immune systems may be at risk even at low toxin concentrations and should avoid exposure, health officials said. RELATED: 'Influence campaign': Okeechobee County leaders want to change Lake O's narrative Officials said it is safe to eat fillets from healthy freshwater fish caught in lakes experiencing blooms if the fillets are rinsed with tap or bottled water, the guts are discarded and the fish is thoroughly cooked. People should not eat shellfish from waters with algae blooms. The Florida Department of Environmental Protection monitors reported blooms and collects samples for analysis. The public can report an algae bloom online at ReportAlgalBloom.com or call 1-855-305-3903 . Anyone who develops symptoms after exposure to a harmful algae bloom can call the Florida Poison Information Center at 800-222-1222 . Pet owners who believe an animal became ill after exposure should contact a veterinarian. For health questions about blue-green algae, call DOH-Martin at 772-221-4090 .

Lucie Police say they used a dead man's own phone to text his alleged drug dealer and arrange a buy, an investigation that led to a search warrant, thousands in cash, guns and drugs found at the dealer's home. According to the arrest affidavit, officers responded to an apartment at 700 SE Collins Lane on September 13th for an overdose. They found 34-year-old Miqueias Oliveira Silva dead, with a bloody syringe and a bag of cocaine next to him. The affidavit says rigor mortis suggested Silva had been dead for about 24 hours. It’s destroying the community. It’s destroying the members of the community, said Magalys Koch, a substance abuse expert at Hibiscus Counseling. A neighbor who called 911 told police he last saw Silva getting out of the passenger side of a black SUV before going inside, according to the affidavit. Investigators say they went through Silva's phone and found months of text exchanges with a contact saved under the name Danilo Jaramillo, going back to August 17th. The affidavit says the messages followed a pattern, with Silva asking if Jaramillo was "available" and Jaramillo confirming before the two met up. Police say they used Silva's phone to text Jaramillo and arrange another deal. Jaramillo responded he could be there within the hour. Investigators say they followed Jaramillo's black Kia Telluride to Silva's apartment complex, then pulled him over. A K9 alerted to narcotics inside the vehicle. Investigators say they found a bag of fentanyl on the passenger seat, along with a large amount of cash. See also: Vero Beach animal hospital manager accused of reclaiming cats, abandoning them outside Detectives then obtained a search warrant for Jaramillo's home on SW Longfellow Road. According to a separate affidavit, investigators searched the master bedroom. They found three firearms a Smith & Wesson .40 caliber handgun, a Ruger LC9 and an AR-15 along with ammunition, digital scales, a written ledger, cocaine, marijuana and $17,715 in cash. Jaramillo's wife, Selina Jaramillo, was home with their children during the search. According to the affidavit, she told investigators she didn't know he was involved in drugs and said she'd last seen him with narcotics about eight months earlier. She said one of the firearms was hers, but that the rest, along with the drugs and cash, belonged to her husband. The affidavit says Jaramillo told police anything illegal in the home belonged to him, then asked for a lawyer before answering further questions. Because Jaramillo is a convicted felon, investigators charged him with three counts of possessing a firearm or ammunition as a felon. Police say body cameras were active throughout the search and the footage was submitted into evidence. Jaramillo, 43, faces multiple felony drug charges, including fentanyl trafficking, along with three felony weapons counts and a misdemeanor paraphernalia charge. The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office announced more than 50 arrests following a multi-agency, multi-day operation targeting human trafficking and illegal sexual activity in the county. Operation Late Checkout ran from Sept. 13 in Indian River County. The operation netted over 60 contacts, more than 50 arrests, and three ICE detainers, Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a press conference on Thursday. Flowers announced the results alongside a representative from the Florida Department of Law Enforcement. “Agencies involved in the operation included the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office, Florida Department of Law Enforcement, St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office, Seminole County Sheriff’s Office, Altamonte Springs Police Department, Vero Beach Police Department, Homeland Security Investigations, Florida Office of Statewide Prosecutor and the U.S. Attorney’s Office,” Flowers said. The operation’s targeted goal was stopping human trafficking in the Indian River County area, the sheriff’s office said. During the operation, several victims were identified, and investigators said ongoing investigations are underway. Flowers said there are no specific arrests on human trafficking charges at this time. One case involved a man who traveled to Indian River County to meet a minor. Flowers said the arrest was the result of the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force working across agencies to apprehend individuals attempting to lure children online. “Our team did a great job of getting him off the street,” Flowers said. Undercover teams were deployed in a variety of capacities during the operation, the sheriff’s office said. Victims’ advocates trained to work with trafficking victims were also on hand to speak with women involved in prostitution to determine whether they were being trafficked. “We have many ongoing investigations as a result of this,” Flowers said. Flowers called the operation unprecedented for Indian River County. “We’ve never had an investigation like this, to my knowledge, in Indian River County with this many agencies involved, with this many arrests in one shot,” he said. FDLE Assistant Special Agent in Charge Alfonso Williams said Operation Late Checkout was initiated by FDLE in coordination with the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office and is the first operation of this magnitude conducted in the county. “This operation shows that within our communities there are dangerous individuals committing heinous crimes who think they can get away with it,” Williams said. Williams said the operation focused on identifying human trafficking victims, reducing the demand for prostitution, and apprehending individuals seeking sexual contact with minors. “Our work is far from done,” Williams said. “This operation requires a lot of resources and time. We cannot do this work alone, and our success depends on the great partnership and collaboration that you see today.” FDLE said it houses the Florida Trafficking Hotline. A Vero Beach animal hospital manager was arrested after investigators said she reclaimed two cats from the Humane Society of Vero Beach and Indian River County, then abandoned them outdoors without care. Deanna Rae Wesley, 43, was arrested Sept. 15 on an active warrant charging her with two counts of animal abandonment, both first-degree misdemeanors, according to Indian River County court records. Animal Control investigators said Wesley, who works at Dr. Dan’s Animal Hospital , picked up two white-and-brown tabby cats from the Humane Society on Sept. Wesley reportedly told staff the cats were being returned to a caregiver, but she would not identify that person, the affidavit said. The next day, Animal Control received a complaint about a white-and-brown tabby cat crying at a resident’s front door. Investigators said the cat was taken to Animal Control, where its microchip and Humane Society staff confirmed it was one of the cats Wesley had picked up. An investigator said Wesley initially denied it was the same cat but acknowledged the matching microchip number. According to the affidavit, she declined to explain how the cat ended up loose at the home. The resident told investigators that a woman matching Wesley’s description, wearing a Dr. Dan’s T-shirt, spoke with her mother and warned her to watch out for Animal Control in the area. The woman allegedly called the cats colony cats, the affidavit said. Both cats were described as extremely friendly, with debris on their faces and chins. Investigators said the cats were not capable of surviving outdoors on their own and that no one was known to be caring for them. The warrant alleges Wesley abandoned the cats on a public street without providing care, food, protection or shelter. A judge set bond at $250 per count, for a total of $500.

Health officials have issued a blue-green algae health alert for an area of Lake Okeechobee after water samples detected harmful toxins. The Florida Department of Health in Martin County said the alert covers the Lake Okeechobee NES135 area and was issued in response to samples collected Sept. The area is located on the north shore of the lake at J&S Fish Camp in Martin County. Residents and visitors should use caution in and around the lake, officials said. People should not drink, swim, wade, use personal watercraft or otherwise come into contact with water where a visible algae bloom is present. Health officials also advised people to keep pets and livestock away from affected water. Anyone who comes into contact with algae, discolored water or water with an unpleasant odor should wash their skin and clothing with soap and water, according to the department. Officials said contaminated water should not be used for cooking or washing dishes because boiling does not remove algae toxins. Blue-green algae are bacteria commonly found in Florida freshwater. Blooms can discolor water and create floating mats, scum, foam or paint-like material on the surface, sometimes with an unpleasant odor. The blooms can produce toxins that may harm people, pets and aquatic life. Children, older adults and people with weakened immune systems may be at risk even at low toxin concentrations and should avoid exposure, health officials said. RELATED: 'Influence campaign': Okeechobee County leaders want to change Lake O's narrative Officials said it is safe to eat fillets from healthy freshwater fish caught in lakes experiencing blooms if the fillets are rinsed with tap or bottled water, the guts are discarded and the fish is thoroughly cooked. People should not eat shellfish from waters with algae blooms. The Florida Department of Environmental Protection monitors reported blooms and collects samples for analysis. The public can report an algae bloom online at ReportAlgalBloom.com or call 1-855-305-3903 . Anyone who develops symptoms after exposure to a harmful algae bloom can call the Florida Poison Information Center at 800-222-1222 . Pet owners who believe an animal became ill after exposure should contact a veterinarian. For health questions about blue-green algae, call DOH-Martin at 772-221-4090 .

Martin County High School received another threat through the state's FortifyFL reporting system, the third bomb threat involving our campus this week, the school district said Friday afternoon. "I recognize that you have heard from me repeatedly this week regarding safety-related disruptions on our campus," Principal Lori Vogel said in a message to families. The latest threat referenced two specific buildings, requiring students and staff to be evacuated while law enforcement conducted a thorough search. Students and staff were relocated to other areas of campus during the response. On Monday, students and staff were evacuated after a bomb threat prompted a response from the Martin County Sheriff's Office. Eight days ago, students and staff were evacuated in the afternoon after a bomb threat was received via email, according to school officials. In a message sent to families, school officials said all buildings were being evacuated at the direction of law enforcement while authorities investigate the threat. Vogel noted the seriousness of the threats. "Every threat must be taken seriously," the principal said. "Each report generates a significant law enforcement response, disrupts instruction, displaces students and staff, and creates understandable concern throughout our school community. Unlike many situations that may require an emergency response, the behavior prompting these repeated disruptions is entirely avoidable. We need our families as partners in addressing this behavior. Please speak directly with your children about the seriousness and far-reaching impact of making or participating in a false threat." The message added: "What a student may view as a joke or a temporary way to avoid class can have widespread consequences for an entire campus and community. FortifyFL is an important safety resource. Information about submitting a report is available on our school's and the School District's websites. "However, FortifyFL must never be used to submit information that someone knows to be false," the message said. "The District has zero tolerance for anyone who knowingly misuses the platform or participates in making a false threat. The principal concluded: "We appreciate your partnership in reinforcing that false threats are neither harmless nor funny. They place an unacceptable burden on students, employees, families, law enforcement and the broader community—and they must stop.Thank you for your immediate attention to this serious matter and for partnering with us to maintain a safe, orderly learning environment for every student and staff member at Martin County High School. Three cities in the United States were selected as sites for the 2027 women's volleyball World Cup, the new name for the world championships, the sport's international governing body announced Thursday.The 32-nation tournament will be played in North America for the first time Aug. 5.Pool play and round-of-16 matches will be played in Omaha, Nebraska, at the CHI Health Center Arena, and in Orlando, Florida, at the Kia Center. The Honda Center in Anaheim, California, will host the quarterfinals, semifinals and final and then serve as the host venue for the men's and women's indoor volleyball competition for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.Host cities in Canada will be announced later.In March, FIVB announced the rebranding of the men's and women's world championships. The men's World Cup will be played in Poland. The tournament, previously played once every four years, will now be played every two years.The tournament is an Olympic qualifier, with the top three national teams not yet qualified for the 2028 Games earning spots.Sports and entertainment network ION will provide 17 days of coverage, including 19 live matches and 10 hours of studio show coverage. The network also will stream 45 matches.Italy defeated Turkey in five sets to win the 2025 championship in Bangkok, Thailand.

In opening the Buffalo Bills' new stadium, rookie coach Joe Brady was more interested in seeing his team put on a clinic rather than a show.Turns out, Brady got to see both in a 41-31 victory over the Detroit Lions on Thursday night in the Bills' first regular-season game at Highmark Stadium.Fireworks. And a win.“The atmosphere was incredible,” Brady said. “It was the game Buffalo deserved.”The 41 points were the third-most by a team in its regular-season stadium debut, behind only Dallas, which scored 44 in its first game at Texas Stadium in 1971, and Miami scoring 42 in its first outing at Joe Robbie Stadium in 1987.Josh Allen accounted for five touchdowns, including the first one, by scoring on a 1-yard run six minutes in. A sell-out crowd arrived early, and about 1,000 fans still lingered long after the final horn in cheering on Allen and left tackle Dion Dawkins as they were being interviewed at the Prime TV booth along the sideline.Among those on hand was former Bills quarterback-turned-broadcaster Ryan Fitzpatrick. He opened the day by throwing passes across the international border — from one boat to another on the Niagara River — to former Bills receiver Stevie Johnson.And the Bills honored their cross-border fanbase by having both the U.S. and Canadian anthems performed with both countries’ flags displayed on the field.The Toronto musical group Barenaked Ladies was greeted by a loud cheer before singing “O, Canada.” They were followed by Hawaiian-born actress and singer Auli’i Cravalho performing “The Star-Spangled Banner.” U.S. pop group OneRepublic also performed at halftime, while set up on a platform in the stands at the north end of the field.RELATED STORY | Chicago Bears could merge 2 sites for potential stadium in northwest Indiana“It was crazy. I don’t really get starstruck, but there was a few times I looked up like, this is crazy,” defensive tackle Deone Walker said.The festivities began with an elaborate light show with fans wearing bracelets that blinked, followed by a fireworks display as the Bills offensive starters were introduced, with Allen greeted by a roar and chants of “M-V-P! M-V-P!”And the Bills even rolled out a new green grass carpet by choosing to resod the entire field ahead of schedule following their preseason finale against Pittsburgh on Aug. They did so after the original turf, which had been laid down in October, showed signs of wear and tear, and with large divots having to be replaced during two preseason games and two practices.Bills players indicated after practicing in the stadium on Tuesday that the grass felt firmer, and noticed a larger infill of sand. That was evident in pregame warmups when clumps of sand came up when players made hard cuts on the field.During the opening drive, an on-field official was spotted having to tamp down a clump of grass that came up at the 30.Otherwise, there were few other noticeable issues.“I thought it held up extremely well tonight,” Allen said.The only other apparent hiccup occurred when the teams lined up prematurely for the opening kickoff, and then stayed in formation for several minutes during a commercial break.The field was painted for the first time, with the word “BILLS” in large white block letters featured prominently in both end zones over red-painted grass. The team’s charging Buffalo logo was also added at midfield.The new stadium has a capacity of just over 60,000, about 12,000 less than the old facility, which now lies in rubble across the street.RELATED STORY | Lakers ownership drama: Jeanie Buss challenges siblings’ sale planWhat’s different is the layout, with the new facility’s seating structure built more vertically in placing viewers more on top of the action. The new building also features a canopy, which helps project crowd noise directly onto the field.“It was great. Everything was awesome,” edge rusher Greg Rousseau said, before crediting the team’s owner Terry Pegula. “Shout out Pegula for an amazing stadium.”

Two men were arrested after a road rage incident escalated into a shooting near SW California Boulevard and SW Brevity Terrace on Sept. 17, 2026, at approximately 6:30 p.m., according to the Port St. Investigators determined the incident began as a misunderstanding between two drivers. One driver believed he was being followed after changing lanes and merging from SW Crosstown Parkway, where the vehicles had crossed paths, and one driver thought the other had cut him off. However, police said the investigation revealed there was no intentional following. One of the drivers, identified as 57-year-old Tylon Kukielka, was traveling with his girlfriend to her home after visiting a local restaurant. The other driver, identified as 41-year-old Dean Plotts, happened to be traveling in the same direction and onto the same streets. As the vehicles continued, the situation escalated into a physical confrontation near SW Brevity Terrace. During the altercation, Kukielka fired a handgun, striking Plotts twice. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputy who was in the area traveling on SW California Boulevard observed the incident and detained Kukielka. Plotts sustained gunshot wounds to his left wrist and legs and was transported to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital for treatment. Kukielka was also transported for medical evaluation. Detectives responded to the scene and collected evidence, including shell casings, surveillance video, dash cam footage, and other physical evidence. Based on the evidence collected, witness information, video footage, and statements obtained during the investigation, detectives determined there was probable cause to charge Kukielka with attempted homicide – murder, dangerous depraved without premeditation, a first-degree felony under Florida Statute 782.04(2). Detectives also determined there was probable cause to charge Plotts with burglary with assault or battery, a felony under Florida Statute 810.02(2)(a). Both men were taken into custody in connection with the investigation, which remains ongoing. All defendants are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty in a court of law. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis has signed a death warrant for 77-year-old William Reaves Jr., the man convicted of murdering Indian River County Sheriff's Deputy Richard Raczkoski in 1986. The execution is scheduled for Tuesday, Oct. 20, at 6 p.m.Reaves was convicted of murdereing Raczkoski on Sept. 23, 1986, after a confrontation at a convenience store.Deputy Raczkoski had responded to a 911 call at the store when he encountered Reaves. During a conversation between the two, a gun fell from Reaves's shorts. Deputy Raczkoski placed his knee on the weapon. Reaves then pushed the deputy away, grabbed the gun and pointed it at Deputy Raczkoski's face.As Deputy Raczkoski attempted to draw his own weapon, Reaves said, "I wouldn't do that if I were you." The deputy backed away, turned, and ran. Reaves fired seven rounds, striking Deputy Raczkoski four times.Reaves was tried in the 19th Judicial Circuit in Indian River County. On direct appeal, the Florida Supreme Court reversed the initial conviction and remanded the case for a new trial. On remand, Reaves was again convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death on March 6, 1992, in Vero Beach.The Florida Supreme Court affirmed the conviction and death sentence on April 7, 1994. The United States Supreme Court denied Reaves's petition for a writ of certiorari on Nov. 7, 1994.Reaves pursued numerous postconviction challenges in both state and federal courts over the following decades.In 2015, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida granted Reaves's federal petition for a writ of habeas corpus. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit overturned that ruling and ordered that the petition be denied.Additional postconviction motions and petitions were subsequently denied, and those denials were affirmed on appeal. Executive clemency was also considered and denied.Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, in his letter recommending the warrant, wrote that "the record is legally sufficient to support the issuance of a death warrant," and confirmed that "there are no stays of execution issued by any court of competent jurisdiction in this cause."The execution is scheduled to take place at Florida State Prison in Raiford. If carried out as scheduled, it will come 40 years after the murder of Deputy Raczkoski.

But then conversely, if it’s a less popular event, you can wait until the last minute and hope that some tickets open up," she said.Bodge recommends shopping secondhand for team gear."If I go to Goodwill or Salvation Army or a thrift store, I see lots of team merch, and it’s very deeply discounted," she said.RELATED STORY | Streamers, mergers driving up price of watching sports, lawmakers sayFor newer jerseys, shirts, and sweatshirts, waiting for end-of-season sales or checking discount stores like TJ Maxx and Marshalls can also help cut costs.Being a sports fan in 2026 does come with a price."It’s an amenity, and if we want to watch it, we got to pay for it," said sports fan Elizabeth Cromer. Twenty-five years after the September 11 attacks, Frank Frangella still carries the memories of what he witnessed at Ground Zero. The Martin County School District's Director of Safety & Security was a New York City Police Department officer when terrorists struck the World Trade Center on Sept. 11, 2001.WATCH BELOW:"It's always there and there are always little things that remind you of what happened," Frangella said from his office, surrounded by photos, statues and a book of memories honoring those lost in the attacks.Frangella was asleep after working the midnight shift when his wife woke him with news that would change his life forever."I was actually asleep when the first plane hit and my wife woke me up and she goes – a plane just hit the World Trade Center," Frangella recalled. "There was a big hole in that building and I knew right away what that was, so I just started dressing."The weather that morning remains etched in his memory. "The one thing I remember from that day, soon as I walked out of the house – it was the most beautiful day in the world. There wasn't a cloud in the sky, and I'm thinking to myself driving to where I was going – how can this happen on such a beautiful day."Initially assigned to help intake victims at a Staten Island triage area, Frangella waited for hours as no injured survivors arrived. "It was like what's happening, you know. We're not getting any information."With communication systems failing, Frangella and fellow officers decided to take a boat directly to Ground Zero. What they found defied comprehension."By that time, both buildings were down. And I mean - it looked like a war zone," he said. "It was literally a pile, and it was huge."The scale of destruction was unlike anything Frangella had ever seen. "You figure two of the largest buildings in Manhattan, you didn't see a desk. Nothing that resembled an office building," he said. "Everything was pulverized."SPECIAL COVERAGE: Remembering 9/11What began as a rescue mission quickly became a recovery operation, according to Frangella. "Everybody that was down there was doing it because they wanted to save lives, and then we found out pretty quickly on that there was no lives to save, and it was a recovery mission more than anything else."Despite their efforts, Frangella's team did not find any survivors.The emotional toll of those days followed Frangella home to his family. "A few weeks later, I remember sitting home and it all hit. I just started crying and I don't even know why I was crying," he said.The dust-covered uniforms from Ground Zero created an unexpected memorial in the Frangella household. "We had a washing machine in the basement that she was washing all my clothing with and how many souls were in that wash. So, it was almost like a shrine in my house. We never used it again after 9/11 because it was like – it just felt wrong to use it."Today, Frangella applies his experience from that tragic day to his role protecting Martin County's school children. He often shares his story with students, creating powerful moments of connection."This little girl about this big walks over to me and she says -- can I hug you? When that little girl came over, there wasn't a dry eye in the house. I mean everybody started crying and she just said… thank you. It was the most amazing thing in the world," Frangella said.Despite his role in the response efforts, Frangella has never visited the 9/11 Memorial and Museum. "I was there when it happened. I don't need to relive it again," he said.As the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks approaches, first responders like Frangella continue processing their experiences while serving their communities in new ways. His transition from protecting New York City to safeguarding Martin County schools demonstrates how the impact of that day continues to shape public service careers across the country.Twenty-five years later, Frangella honors not just his own experience, but that of every person who responded that day. "There are thousands upon thousands of stories. This is just mine," he said. "Everybody says that time heals all, and I know for me and everybody who was down there -- we're still waiting."To hear more stories be sure to watch Echoes of September: A 9/11 Special on Friday, Sept. on WPTVThis story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Vero Beach Regional Airport is adding a new long-term parking lot — but with the newest upgrade, free parking is going away.Vero Beach City Council approved the construction of a new long-term parking lot that will expand capacity from 80 spaces to over 500.WATCH BELOW: Free parking is going away at Vero Beach airportBrandon Dambeck, interim airport director, said the expansion is driven by new flights coming to the airport."We have to meet the parking demand," Dambeck said.Dambeck said the current parking situation is not keeping up."It looks a little disorganized, especially in the grass parking area. So that's one thing this parking will really solve," Dambeck said.When asked why the airport is introducing paid parking, Dambeck said the airport operates without taxpayer dollars and must use the funds to cover the costs of any upgrades to the airport.We first told you about some of the upgrades, including new covered walkways and baggage claim, and a new patio."The airport is responsible for maintaining its self-sustainability, meaning we don't take any taxpayer dollars," said Dambeck. "We have to make sure that our charges will help to to maintain the operations that happen at the airport."The lot will be built and paid for by Envision Parking Partners. The airport will be responsible for maintaining it. John Mostoller with Envision said travelers will be able to pay through a prepaid option using license plate readers or at the lot gate."There's a lot of opportunities to make the experience seamless," Mostoller said.The new lot will also add cameras and lighting for security. Mostoller said convenience will remain a priority."No parking spot will be more than two to four minutes from the terminal," Mostoller said.Some travelers said they will miss the free parking."That sucks. I mean, that's — it's a nice plus to be able to park, especially if it was already free," traveler Reana Tejada said.Sydney Banak, who was able to park for free during her visit, said she understands the reasoning behind the change."Free parking is nice," Sydney said. "But maybe they need to expand the airport or provide more services, so I do understand where they're coming from with that." Construction is expected to begin in March and be completed by next summer.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. The Martin County Commission approved a zoning compromise for land in Hobe Sound, but the 3-2 vote has left some residents and at least one commissioner with lingering concerns about what could be built there.Commissioners voted to rezone a property along Southeast Powerline Avenue to limited-industrial, stepping back from a general industrial designation that drew pushback from nearby residents. The property has long been slated for some form of industrial use, but the county said the existing zoning was outdated and due for an update.WATCH: Hobe Sound zoning compromise raises data center concernsResidents who spoke at the Tuesday commission meeting said their primary concern was protecting the character of the community.Steve Addison said he has lived in the area since 1969."Our biggest concern was preserving our quality of life. We don't have a lot of industry and a lot of noise," Addison said.Other residents echoed concerns about the scope of the original rezoning proposal."I understand that Martin County has to plan for the future but I also believe that growth needs to be compatible with the community that already exists," Kim Call, a resident, said."We're concerned about the permanence of a GI classification which we believe is too broad and too open-ended," Patrick McDonough, a Hobe Sound resident and Eaglewood Community HOA president, said.After hearing from residents, the property owner offered to accept the less-intensive classification."To cooperate and show if that's what the neighbors feel is more appropriate and that would be a better use then we are willing to accept the light industrial," Bob Reins, a land-use attorney with Gunster law firm, said.Despite the compromise, Commissioner Blake Capps voted against the rezoning, citing concerns about the potential for a data center on the site."Who knows where this is really going in the future and to approve a zoning for this property that allows a data center. I'm not into that," Capps said.The county said there are no plans for a data center at the site. Any proposal exceeding 100,000 square feet would require board approval.In speaking with residents, WPTV'S Cassandra Garcia learned not everyone was happy with the outcome. However, residents like Addison felt it was the right move."I don't want to see over development, but I also don't want to be that guy that doesn't understand land-use and doesn't understand property rights," Addison said. "I feel like it was a win win for the both of us."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. New footage of rare Florida panthers is a promising sign that the endangered species might be getting more of a foothold.The video, captured by a trail camera, shows a mother and three young cubs at a nature reserve in Fort Myers. That's further north of where the endangered cats are usually seen in the state.Experts say it's a positive sign that they're expanding their breeding range, which could help the panther population recover. Florida has spent decades trying to protect its panthers, primarily from encounters with cars and from a shrinking natural habitat, which has been reduced by about 95% from its original expanse.RELATED STORY | World's most endangered tigers born in Greece as zoos build a safety netFlorida panthers are an isolated population of the North American cougar, a species of large, solitary wild cats that range mostly in western North America and most of South America. There are thought to be some 200 individuals living in southern Florida.

A more unsettled weather pattern is setting up across the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches for the middle and latter part of the week, bringing elevated chances for showers and thunderstorms, breezy northeast winds and a growing risk of rougher conditions at the beaches. An upper-level low approaching Florida from the western Atlantic is the feature behind the change. In simple terms, it will add energy higher in the atmosphere while pulling in deep tropical moisture at lower levels. That combination should make it easier for showers and storms to develop not just during the typical afternoon window, but at times earlier or later in the day as well. Wednesday will feature a mix of sun and clouds, with scattered showers and thunderstorms becoming more likely through the afternoon and evening. High temperatures will still reach the upper 80s to around 90 degrees, so it will remain warm and humid despite the increase in clouds and rain chances. Heat indices look to be a few degrees below the triple digits to near 100 degrees, a few degrees cooler than recently. A few storms could produce frequent lightning, brief heavy downpours and gusty winds. The storm coverage is expected to increase further Thursday and Friday as the upper-level low moves closer to the peninsula. Rain chances are elevated across both the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches, with numerous showers and thunderstorms possible at times. This does not mean the entire area will see nonstop rain or a complete washout, but outdoor plans could face interruptions, especially during the afternoon and evening. The main concern will be pockets of heavy rain. Storms may move slowly at times or repeatedly affect the same locations, raising the risk for localized street flooding and ponding water in poor-drainage areas. The severe-weather threat appears low overall, but isolated stronger storms could still bring gusty winds and plenty of cloud-to-ground lightning. Breezy easterly to northeasterly winds will also become more noticeable, particularly near the coast. Those winds may offer only limited relief from the humidity while creating choppier conditions along the Atlantic waters. For boaters, a Small Craft Advisory is in effect from this afternoon through late tonight for the entire Treasure Coast and Palm Beach coastal waters. Northeast to east winds are expected to increase to 15 to 20 knots, while seas build to 4 to 6 feet, occasionally reaching 8 feet offshore. Conditions in the Intracoastal Waterway will also become choppy in exposed areas. Beachgoers should use extra caution as the onshore flow increases. The National Weather Service has posted a Rip Current Statement for Atlantic beaches. Increasing onshore wind and building surf can create dangerous currents that pull swimmers away from shore, even when the weather appears calm between showers. By the weekend, the upper-level low should begin shifting west, allowing the weather pattern to gradually return toward more typical scattered afternoon storms.

The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office announced more than 50 arrests following a multi-agency, multi-day operation targeting human trafficking and illegal sexual activity in the county. Operation Late Checkout ran from Sept. 13 in Indian River County. The operation netted over 60 contacts, more than 50 arrests, and three ICE detainers, Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a press conference on Thursday. Flowers announced the results alongside a representative from the Florida Department of Law Enforcement. “Agencies involved in the operation included the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office, Florida Department of Law Enforcement, St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office, Seminole County Sheriff’s Office, Altamonte Springs Police Department, Vero Beach Police Department, Homeland Security Investigations, Florida Office of Statewide Prosecutor and the U.S. Attorney’s Office,” Flowers said. The operation’s targeted goal was stopping human trafficking in the Indian River County area, the sheriff’s office said. During the operation, several victims were identified, and investigators said ongoing investigations are underway. Flowers said there are no specific arrests on human trafficking charges at this time. One case involved a man who traveled to Indian River County to meet a minor. Flowers said the arrest was the result of the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force working across agencies to apprehend individuals attempting to lure children online. “Our team did a great job of getting him off the street,” Flowers said. Undercover teams were deployed in a variety of capacities during the operation, the sheriff’s office said. Victims’ advocates trained to work with trafficking victims were also on hand to speak with women involved in prostitution to determine whether they were being trafficked. “We have many ongoing investigations as a result of this,” Flowers said. Flowers called the operation unprecedented for Indian River County. “We’ve never had an investigation like this, to my knowledge, in Indian River County with this many agencies involved, with this many arrests in one shot,” he said. FDLE Assistant Special Agent in Charge Alfonso Williams said Operation Late Checkout was initiated by FDLE in coordination with the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office and is the first operation of this magnitude conducted in the county. “This operation shows that within our communities there are dangerous individuals committing heinous crimes who think they can get away with it,” Williams said. Williams said the operation focused on identifying human trafficking victims, reducing the demand for prostitution, and apprehending individuals seeking sexual contact with minors. “Our work is far from done,” Williams said. “This operation requires a lot of resources and time. We cannot do this work alone, and our success depends on the great partnership and collaboration that you see today.” FDLE said it houses the Florida Trafficking Hotline. Anyone who suspects someone is a victim of trafficking can contact the hotline at 1-855-352-7233. READ OPERATION LATE CHECKOUT BELOW:

Widespread flooding swamped parts of western Palm Beach County on Thursday, inundating a local wildlife sanctuary in Royal Palm Beach and leaving residents questioning the local drainage authority’s response after nearly nine inches of rain saturated the area.The Palm Beach Wildlife Conservation group is facing what its owner estimates to be tens of thousands of dollars in damages. Meanwhile, neighboring homeowners reported their properties were flooding from an overflowing canal, and their calls to the Indian Trail Improvement District went unanswered.The district cited an "unusually high volume of calls" and said crews were working to manage the water levels.WATCH: Flooding damages wildlife sanctuary‘A major setback’ for wildlife GroupAt the Palm Beach Wildlife Conservation group in Royal Palm Beach, part-owner Mario Lequerique was moving tortoises and other exotic animals to higher ground. The facility, established four years ago, is being rebranded to offer animal interactions for children with autism, and was covered in floodwater."This should be about three feet over the water, and now it’s about a foot under the water," Lequerique told WPTV, pointing to a submerged section of his property.He said the flooding has ruined essential equipment, including pumps and refrigerators."We’ve had mishap with a lot of tools, pumps, some equipment, refrigeration," Lequerique said. "I would put it between $20-30 thousand dollars."The cleanup is expected to take weeks, posing a significant challenge to the group's planned grand opening. "Right now, this is gonna be a major setback," he added.Residents frustrated by flooding, lack of responseNearby, the Duprey family watched as water from an overflowing canal crept into their yard."The canal overflowed and the canal is coming right into our yard and there’s nothing we can do about it," said Debby Duprey.Her husband, Rick Duprey, expressed frustration after his calls to the Indian Trail Improvement District were not returned."You call them and you call them and you call them and at least they could’ve returned the call, and they didn’t even do that," he said. "I keep telling them, it's overflowing, my house is going to flood."Improvement district cites intense rainfallIn a statement to WPTV, the Indian Trail Improvement District acknowledged the flooding and residents' concerns. The agency reported that nearly nine inches of rain fell in 24 hours, a significant amount in a short period.Read the full state below: “Prior to and throughout the storm, the District maintained its canal system to provide available capacity for stormwater. However, during periods of intense rainfall, water can enter the drainage system faster than it can be moved through and discharged. Even after the rain subsides, the system requires time to move that volume of water through swales, canals and ultimately out of the community. District crews have been working throughout the day monitoring canals and water levels, operating pumps, checking drainage conditions and responding to areas experiencing flooding. We are continuing that work as water moves through the system.We also understand the frustration regarding the delay in returning the organization's call. The District office received an unusually high volume of calls related to today's storm and flooding conditions. Staff responded as quickly as possible, and contact was made later in the day. We recognize that when someone is dealing with flooding, waiting for a response can be frustrating, and we appreciate their patience during an exceptionally busy response period.The District will continue monitoring conditions and working to move water through the system as safely and efficiently as possible.”This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A diver’s search for lobster off Fort Pierce beach last month led to the discovery of a suspected World War II-era torpedo, prompting a controlled detonation by the U.S. Luke Neiman, who was diving with his father and a friend just south of the jetty, described where he was when he made the discovery. "So, I was like right around about right there where that big condo is right there just past that," Neiman said. He explained how he realized the object was unusual. "I couldn't really make out what it was, but I just knew it wasn't a reef, and I was kind of inspecting it, looking at it," Neiman said. "I'm like, this just looks different, you know, and then before I knew it, I'm like, this is a torpedo, because I could make out the end of it and it had a cone nose." Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates Neiman returned to the boat, told his father to mark the spot, and contacted the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC). The FWC then alerted the U.S. Lucie County Sheriff's Office bomb squad, and the U.S. On Tuesday afternoon, Navy Explosive Ordnance Disposal personnel conducted a controlled underwater detonation at the site. Officials confirmed the operation in a statement, saying, "Navy Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) personnel conducted a routine underwater ordnance disposal operation Sept. 15, 2026, in the waters off St. Lucie County." The Navy identified the object as a suspected World War II-era munition. Amazon has laid off roughly 300 workers at its Port St. Lucie fulfillment center as the facility prepares to shut down for renovations, with more employees transferred to other Amazon sites. Since the company filed a WARN notice in July listing 494 affected workers, Amazon says more than 200 additional employees have transferred to other facilities. Workers who aren't transferring will begin receiving paid severance this month. Amazon filed the notice July 15 with Florida's State Trade and Rapid Response Coordinator and sent a copy to Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin, as required under the federal Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act. The filing states operations will shut down at Amazon's PBI3 facility, 7600 LTC Pkwy, effective Thursday, September 17. Roughly 494 employees will be separated from the company, with separations effective September 17 and December 17. Amazon told affected workers about the closure around June 18, according to the filing. The job cuts are expected to be permanent, the notice states. Affected employees aren't represented by a union and don't have seniority-based "bumping rights" to displace other workers. Amazon says it will pay employees through their separation date, provided they don't resign early, and will share benefits and severance information separately. The vast majority of the affected positions 466 of the 494 are "FC Associate I" roles, the facility's entry-level warehouse position. The rest include operations managers, HR staff, a safety specialist, an IT support associate and other roles, according to a list attached to the filing. Local economic development officials say that reduced number didn't happen by accident. Lucie Economic Development Council says the facility typically employs between 850 and 1,000 workers depending on the season. In the four months before Amazon filed the WARN notice, CareerSource Research Coast and the EDC held weekly job fairs and helped place many affected workers with other area employers, including Costco, Cheney Brothers and ImportMex, which the EDC says brought the number of employees ultimately listed in the WARN filing down to 494. Amazon describes the closure differently than the legal notice does. In a statement shortly after the notice, company spokesperson Amber Plunkett said, "The Treasure Coast is a great place to live and work, and we're proud of our partnerships across St. These investments and improvements reflect our long-term confidence in the region." On the Port St. Lucie facility specifically, Plunkett said, "We're always evaluating our network to make sure it fits our business needs and to improve the experience for our employees, customers, partners, and drivers. As part of that effort, we occasionally convert existing facilities to a new type of facility which is what we plan to do here later this year. When these renovations are done, Port St. Lucie will be home to a new fulfilment center that will create long-term benefits for our customers, employees, and the community for many years to come." On what happens to the facility's workers, Plunkett said, "Our goal is to keep all of our employees based at this facility with Amazon. Our HR team will work with everyone to offer transfers to another location that fits their preferences we have 30 facilities across South Florida. For those who prefer not to transfer, we'll be providing transition support. When this facility reopens in mid-to-late 2028, it will employ approximately 1,000 people, and everyone from the site will have the option to return at that time." Amazon says the project represents a $200 million investment in the South Florida region. The company says operations will shift to other nearby facilities during the closure and that customers won't be affected. Amazon also said it's working to transfer roughly 850 employees to nearby locations a figure that doesn't match the roughly 494 workers listed as affected in the WARN filing. It's not clear from the materials Amazon provided how the two numbers relate. Employees have the option to transfer to two nearby facilities specifically, or to any of the company's roughly 30 sites across South Florida, and Amazon says it's offering relocation bonuses to employees who transfer more than 50 miles from Port St. All employees affected by this closure will be eligible for rehire once the Port St. Lucie facility reopens, according to Amazon. Lucie County Commissioner Cathy Townsend called the closure part of a bigger strain on businesses in the county. It's devastating," Townsend said. Townsend said the impact will ripple beyond the workers who lost their jobs. "They rent, they eat in restaurants, their children go to daycare, they go to our schools," Townsend said. "And so it's going to ripple down. It is going to hurt the economy here in Saint Lucie County. And I have concerns for those families. And jobs are not plentiful right here in this county." Townsend credited the EDC's job-placement efforts with softening the blow, but said the layoffs point to a broader pattern of job insecurity in the county. She said local leaders should focus on attracting small businesses that are more likely to stay rooted in the community rather than larger corporations. "They're the fabric of what makes up our community," Townsend said. "And they live here, and they pay taxes here. And we need to do what we have to do to make them successful, not be worried about the big box stores, because these are things that can happen."

Florida Panthers fans have plenty to be excited about ahead of training camp on Thursday, with the Tkachuk brothers suiting up together for the first time and captain Aleksander Barkov returning from a season-ending ACL injury.Both Matthew and Brady Tkachuk are now Panthers, following a blockbuster trade this offseason that brought Brady to Florida from the Ottawa Senators, where he served as captain.WATCH BELOW: Tkachuk brothers talk 'brotherly love' ahead of training campMatthew said the moment still feels surreal."Oh my God, I never thought this was going to be possible. So we've been enjoying every second since," Matthew said. How often do people get to play in the NHL with their brother?"Brady echoed that sentiment."It still doesn't feel real. You know, living a dream here," Brady said. It's been a great experience so far."The brothers have always competed against each other, making the opportunity to play on the same team even more meaningful. Brady said being on the same ice will be a new experience."That's going to be a special feeling,” Brady said.Brady also said playing under head coach Paul Maurice is an added benefit."Whatever the coach and team think is best for my role and to fit in, because at the end of the day it's all about winning," Brady said.Leading the team is Barkov. The Panthers captain missed all of last season after suffering an ACL injury on the first day of training camp in 2025. He said he is feeling like himself heading into camp."Like going into this camp that starts tomorrow. I feel totally normal," Barkov said.Barkov spoke about his mindset and message to the team."You have to come to the rink and try to bring your best out of you and that's all we can ask for" Barkov said.Training camp is shorter this year. The Panthers will play four preseason games, with restrictions on how much ice time veteran players can receive.
