Head coach Paul Maurice said he is not holding back and that training camp will be hard.The Panthers open preseason play Sunday against the defending Stanley Cup-champion Carolina Hurricanes.

The Oxbridge Academy Thunderwolves received their state championship rings this week, celebrating their Division 2A softball title from earlier this year. The team was honored during a halftime ring ceremony at a home football game. The rings feature diamonds and school colors.🥎 WATCH: Standout players Riley Lyons and Aubrey Vital recount the win with WPTV's Eleanor Sheahan Senior pitcher Aubrey Vital said the rings look pretty cool.“I love it, they are so amazing, so nice,” Lyons said.The championship would not have been possible without standout players Riley Lyons and Aubrey Vital. The two formed a key unit as pitcher and catcher throughout the season, working together on the field."She's telling me what's working, what's not working in between innings. We have a lefty batter, we have a different approach than with the righty,” Lyons said.That communication proved critical against Cornerstone Charter Academy in the state championship game."There are a lot of bigger hitters like towards the end of the lineup. So we know in the beginning we need to get our outs. We need to pound the zone quick so we don't have anybody on base when we face the bigger hitters," Lyons said.The Thunderwolves were tied 1-1 heading into the seventh inning. Lyons stepped up to bat with runners on first and second."I was just thinking, barrel through the zone," Lyons said.Her RBI hit sparked a four-run seventh inning, and Oxbridge Academy went on to win the state championship 5-1."That was a really fun one. I remember being on base and the whole dugout, like, erupting after that hit," Lyons said.The road to the championship was built on preparation and trust in their coaches."They didn't really put a lot of pressure on us when we got to our last games because throughout the whole season, we knew our goal was to make it to states. We knew our path from the beginning and how it would take a lot of hard work to get there, but we all knew we had a really good team,” Lyons said.She said the Thunderwolves leaned in to each other.“I think we all knew our role going into our last couple games and just all our hard work was there for a reason," Lyons said.Vital notes how proud she is not only of herself, but her teammates and what this win means for the program."I'm really proud we did it together, because Oxbridge had never gotten one of those before. So just accomplishing that made me feel really happy and proud," Vital said.Lyons added that the rings serve as a reminder of everything the team put in."Like, know that all of our hard work really paid off at the end," Lyons said.With the next season expected to begin in January, Vital is already looking ahead."I'm really excited for this season too because we have a lot of newer girls. So I'm really excited to see how we can all probably win again," Vital said.Lyons said her softball journey began at a young age, though it was not always a straight path to the championship."If we go all the way back to the beginning, I played T-ball with my little sister when I was around, like, 7 years old and then I was on a team called the Green Machines out of Palm Beach Gardens,” Lyons said.Lyons said she took a break from the sport a couple of times growing up, but eventually after COVID she reached out to Coach Ed and began playing again.“That's when I started catching for the first time, and I played in one rec league and I did pretty good. After that, I kind of reached out to Coach Ed, and I started playing travel ball with him, and the rest is history," Lyons said.Lyons said she is still with softball. While she has her senior year season still ahead of her, Lyons is already prepared for the next step with a verbal offer in-hand to play in college.

The Senate has cleared a major procedural hurdle on the bipartisan "Protect College Sports Act," a measure supporters say would create guardrails for the new era of pay-to-play college athletics.The legislation comes as fans, athletes, and institutions have grown increasingly frustrated that college sports conversations have shifted away from players, and games to money, lawsuits, and the transfer portal.The bill would establish compensation rules for name, image, and likeness payments to players, set athlete eligibility at 5 years with generally one transfer allowed, and create protections for scholarships, women's, and Olympic sports programs.Senator Ted Cruz (R-TX), a co-sponsor of the bill, asked his colleagues, "Do we want college sports to have clear, national, enforceable rules, or do we want another decade of lawsuits, conflicting state laws, bidding wars, roster chaos and uncertainty?"RELATED STORY | 79% of prediction-market users have lost money, and many borrow to keep betting, survey findsThe measure would also provide the NCAA with immunity from federal antitrust lawsuits when enforcing its rules. Something critics argue would limit athletes' bargaining power and earning potential.Senator Chris Murphy (D-CT) says, "It basically sets up two different systems, two sets of rules, one for the adults that run and profit from the billion dollar college sports industry, and a different system, a different set of rules for the student athletes."Most opponents of the bill agree changes are needed but say the current measure falls short of the goal line.If the bill passes the Senate and House, President Trump has indicated he will sign it.

Friday night football in Palm Beach County is special.With 30 teams over the years claiming state championships, the history is rich, and Forest Hill High School wants in on it.WATCH BELOW: Forest Hill looks to build winning culture with young roster"If anyone is from West Palm, they know that if Forest Hill was on the schedule, they could go ahead and check a W," head coach Evan Williams, a Forest Hill alum, said.So, as you'd expect, he doesn't like that his school was overlooked for many years, so as a second-year head coach, he's bringing new life into his team."The biggest thing is leading by example. Lucie County staff found at least 14 license plate reader cameras installed on county rights-of-way without a permit, and the county says it does not know who owns them. Staff shared the finding with commissioners Tuesday night in an update on the board's Sept. 1 decision to remove automated license plate readers from county-controlled property. The number of unpermitted cameras has climbed quickly. A county agenda report signed Sept. 10 said field checks had turned up three cameras at unpermitted locations. By Tuesday, staff said the count had reached at least 14, and the search is not finished. County commissioner James Clasby says the issue isn't as much about the cameras as who's receiving the data. Not knowing who they belong to, I think, is another issue. Perhaps that goes about the entirety of Flock camera reform, Clasby said. "There's the potential for non-law enforcement to have cameras out there, and I'm not okay with that. Because the county has no permit on file for those cameras, staff said it cannot identify an applicant to contact. Instead, the county is posting removal notices directly on the devices. "It's like a bright red notice that says you have 30 days to remove this. And we will also bag the cameras so they're not operable," said interim county administrator Mayte Santamaria. Staff said the county has not yet gone through its entire right-of-way and more unauthorized cameras may still be found. Staff is also double-checking some traffic signals that interact with state right-of-way, which could add a handful more. The agenda report says staff is comparing crowdsourced data from various sources against known locations to find unknown or unauthorized installations. See also: Florida boaters rescued after capsized vessel leaves them stranded in tree The unpermitted cameras are in addition to 52 devices the county previously authorized within its rights-of-way. Staff said all 52 had received revocation notices as of Monday, giving their owners 30 days to remove them. According to the report, county permit records indicate most of the authorized devices were installed on behalf of law enforcement agencies. The county shared its inventory with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, the Fort Pierce Police Department and the Port St. Lucie Police Department ahead of the notices. The report says that step was meant both to give the agencies advance notice and to let them review the data for accuracy. Staff also told commissioners there are no active applications for new devices under review. Commissioners voted 3-2 on Sept. 1 to stop issuing permits for Flock cameras and other automated license plate readers on county-owned or county-controlled property. The vote went beyond a state order that applies only to state highways. Commissioner James Clasby made the motion, which he said was about protecting residents' privacy. Commissioners Clasby, Lee and Lowry voted yes, and Chair Jamie Fowler and Commissioner Cathy Townsend voted no. The board's direction does not apply to license plate readers mounted in law enforcement vehicles or cameras on private property.

Lucie Police Department arrested Gabriel Cruz, a 42-year-old MRI technician, on charges of felony sexual battery after a 64-year-old female patient reported being assaulted during an MRI procedure at HCA Florida St. 14, 2026, detectives responded to the hospital, located at 1800 SE Tiffany Ave., after staff reported that the patient disclosed she was sexually assaulted while undergoing an MRI the previous day. Detectives learned the victim had been admitted for medical treatment and was administered medication that caused her to become significantly drowsy prior to the procedure. Cruz was identified as the MRI technician assigned to the procedure. Video evidence obtained with the hospital’s assistance showed Cruz exiting the MRI room after the victim and disposing of materials that were later secured by law enforcement. Testing of the materials returned presumptive positive results for the presence of male semen. Detectives confirmed Cruz had been working at the hospital as a travel MRI technician since Aug. 24, 2026, and was hired through a third-party agency. Following the review of evidence, detectives determined there was probable cause to charge Cruz with sexual battery, a first-degree felony under Florida Statute 794.011(4)(b), involving a victim who was physically helpless or incapacitated. Cruz was arrested in Brevard County on the evening of Sept. 16, 2026, in connection with the investigation. The investigation remains active and ongoing. Lucie Hospital has cooperated fully with law enforcement throughout the investigation. In a statement, the hospital said, “We do not tolerate behavior that jeopardizes the safety or security of our patients. When this serious allegation was reported to us, we contacted law enforcement and ended the individual’s assignment. We have assisted law enforcement throughout its investigation and remain focused on supporting our patient.” The Port St. Lucie Police Department reminded the community to report incidents of sexual assault immediately to law enforcement or trusted resources, emphasizing that such reports can ensure victims receive support and allow law enforcement to investigate. Defendants are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty in a court of law. Lucie Police say they used a dead man's own phone to text his alleged drug dealer and arrange a buy, an investigation that led to a search warrant, thousands in cash, guns and drugs found at the dealer's home. According to the arrest affidavit, officers responded to an apartment at 700 SE Collins Lane on September 13th for an overdose. They found 34-year-old Miqueias Oliveira Silva dead, with a bloody syringe and a bag of cocaine next to him. The affidavit says rigor mortis suggested Silva had been dead for about 24 hours. It’s destroying the community. It’s destroying the members of the community, said Magalys Koch, a substance abuse expert at Hibiscus Counseling. A neighbor who called 911 told police he last saw Silva getting out of the passenger side of a black SUV before going inside, according to the affidavit. Investigators say they went through Silva's phone and found months of text exchanges with a contact saved under the name Danilo Jaramillo, going back to August 17th. The affidavit says the messages followed a pattern, with Silva asking if Jaramillo was "available" and Jaramillo confirming before the two met up. Police say they used Silva's phone to text Jaramillo and arrange another deal. Jaramillo responded he could be there within the hour. Investigators say they followed Jaramillo's black Kia Telluride to Silva's apartment complex, then pulled him over. A K9 alerted to narcotics inside the vehicle. Investigators say they found a bag of fentanyl on the passenger seat, along with a large amount of cash. See also: Vero Beach animal hospital manager accused of reclaiming cats, abandoning them outside Detectives then obtained a search warrant for Jaramillo's home on SW Longfellow Road. According to a separate affidavit, investigators searched the master bedroom. They found three firearms a Smith & Wesson .40 caliber handgun, a Ruger LC9 and an AR-15 along with ammunition, digital scales, a written ledger, cocaine, marijuana and $17,715 in cash. Jaramillo's wife, Selina Jaramillo, was home with their children during the search. According to the affidavit, she told investigators she didn't know he was involved in drugs and said she'd last seen him with narcotics about eight months earlier. She said one of the firearms was hers, but that the rest, along with the drugs and cash, belonged to her husband. The affidavit says Jaramillo told police anything illegal in the home belonged to him, then asked for a lawyer before answering further questions. Because Jaramillo is a convicted felon, investigators charged him with three counts of possessing a firearm or ammunition as a felon. Police say body cameras were active throughout the search and the footage was submitted into evidence. Jaramillo, 43, faces multiple felony drug charges, including fentanyl trafficking, along with three felony weapons counts and a misdemeanor paraphernalia charge. He was booked into the St. Koch says oftentimes the pain is felt not just by the victims and dealers, but by the people around them. Many parents or family members feel guilty, like they didn't do enough or they couldn't. They say, "What could have been done differently?" So, they actually carry the guilt, Koch said. While state data points to a steady decline in overdose deaths since 2021, Koch says that addiction is still a rampant cycle. We're moving away from being in touch with who we are. We don't want to have any pain. We don't want to be bored. We want to be entertained. So these drugs come in, and who can compete with cocaine? CBS12 News has reached out to Port St. Lucie Police for comment and is working to confirm additional details.

The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office announced more than 50 arrests following a multi-agency, multi-day operation targeting human trafficking and illegal sexual activity in the county. Operation Late Checkout ran from Sept. 13 in Indian River County. The operation netted over 60 contacts, more than 50 arrests, and three ICE detainers, Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a press conference on Thursday. Flowers announced the results alongside a representative from the Florida Department of Law Enforcement. “Agencies involved in the operation included the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office, Florida Department of Law Enforcement, St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office, Seminole County Sheriff’s Office, Altamonte Springs Police Department, Vero Beach Police Department, Homeland Security Investigations, Florida Office of Statewide Prosecutor and the U.S. Attorney’s Office,” Flowers said. The operation’s targeted goal was stopping human trafficking in the Indian River County area, the sheriff’s office said. During the operation, several victims were identified, and investigators said ongoing investigations are underway. Flowers said there are no specific arrests on human trafficking charges at this time. One case involved a man who traveled to Indian River County to meet a minor. Flowers said the arrest was the result of the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force working across agencies to apprehend individuals attempting to lure children online. “Our team did a great job of getting him off the street,” Flowers said. Undercover teams were deployed in a variety of capacities during the operation, the sheriff’s office said. Victims’ advocates trained to work with trafficking victims were also on hand to speak with women involved in prostitution to determine whether they were being trafficked. “We have many ongoing investigations as a result of this,” Flowers said. Flowers called the operation unprecedented for Indian River County. “We’ve never had an investigation like this, to my knowledge, in Indian River County with this many agencies involved, with this many arrests in one shot,” he said. FDLE Assistant Special Agent in Charge Alfonso Williams said Operation Late Checkout was initiated by FDLE in coordination with the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office and is the first operation of this magnitude conducted in the county. “This operation shows that within our communities there are dangerous individuals committing heinous crimes who think they can get away with it,” Williams said. Williams said the operation focused on identifying human trafficking victims, reducing the demand for prostitution, and apprehending individuals seeking sexual contact with minors. “Our work is far from done,” Williams said. “This operation requires a lot of resources and time. We cannot do this work alone, and our success depends on the great partnership and collaboration that you see today.” FDLE said it houses the Florida Trafficking Hotline. A proposal to rezone 200 acres near Interstate 95 and Midway Road in Fort Pierce for a data center and commercial development has prompted mixed reactions from residents and led the city’s planning board to delay a decision pending further research. The property, currently zoned for a mixed-use development called "Willow Lakes," would be partially rezoned under the proposal. About 174 acres would be designated for light industrial use, limited to data center operations, while the remaining 26 acres along Midway Road would be rezoned for general commercial use, potentially allowing for a hotel, gas station, restaurants or retail businesses. The applicant, Willow Lakes LLC, emphasized the site’s access to significant electrical infrastructure, including Florida Power Light transmission lines and a nearby substation. A large man-made lake on the property could also serve as a water source for the data center’s cooling system. During the meeting, the planning board made two motions. The first requested the planning department to conduct further research on the data center proposal and report back. The second motion called for the city to discuss the item at the next commission meeting. As a result, the board did not decide whether a data center qualifies as a permitted use within the light industrial zoning category, prompting the applicant to table the rezoning application. "Therefore, there is no point in us moving forward with rezoning to light industrial," said W. Lee Dobbins, the attorney representing Willow Lakes LLC. "We would need to wait until that decision is over and make a decision at that time based upon what they changed the code to say." Residents expressed a range of opinions about the proposal. "We're not OK with them building a data center right next to our homes," said resident Sarah Quinette. "An area like that, if we keep it as agricultural land, it has a great impact in the form of pollinating insects that will return season after season." Felix Rodriguez, another resident, shared a different perspective. "I think it's pretty cool personally, just because it brings in more jobs, construction, that trade. All the freight just brings in more business," he said. Shirley McHellon voiced her opposition to the project. "I think they need to stop. They're taking away the trees, the woods and the animals ... they're just killing the animals," she said. Before the data center can move forward with approval, the city must first decide whether to approve the rezoning request. Further research is required before the planning board revisits the proposal. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

Florida's Amendment 3 is a proposed property tax measure on the ballot this November.If approved, it will reshape local government funding and property taxes starting Jan. It requires 60% voter approval to pass.WPTV is hosting a Property Tax Town Hall on Oct. It will be held at the Public Safety Conference Center at Palm Beach State College's Lake Worth Campus. It is located at 4200 Congress Ave. in Lake Worth.We will be holding a Let's Hear It community event from 3 p.m. The town hall will then take place from 7 p.m. to 9 p.m.WPTV reporter Matt Sczesny will host the event, taking your questions and concerns, while also talking with experts about this amendment referendum.If you would like to attend, please fill out the form below:What Amendment 3 would doThe Legislature approved Amendment 3 during a June special session called by Gov. Ron DeSantis.For people who establish permanent Florida residency by Dec. 31, the proposal would increase the non-school homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028. School district property taxes would remain unaffected. Florida Tax Watch estimates the losses to local governments in the next five years will be $48 billion.The measure would also reduce the assessment-growth cap for non-homestead property from 10% to 5%, establish a waiting period for newer residents and place constitutional language around how cities and counties spend property-tax revenue.

Lucie Police say they used a dead man's own phone to text his alleged drug dealer and arrange a buy, an investigation that led to a search warrant, thousands in cash, guns and drugs found at the dealer's home. According to the arrest affidavit, officers responded to an apartment at 700 SE Collins Lane on September 13th for an overdose. They found 34-year-old Miqueias Oliveira Silva dead, with a bloody syringe and a bag of cocaine next to him. The affidavit says rigor mortis suggested Silva had been dead for about 24 hours. A neighbor who called 911 told police he last saw Silva getting out of the passenger side of a black SUV before going inside, according to the affidavit. Investigators say they went through Silva's phone and found months of text exchanges with a contact saved under the name Danilo Jaramillo, going back to August 17th. The affidavit says the messages followed a pattern, with Silva asking if Jaramillo was "available" and Jaramillo confirming before the two met up. Police say they used Silva's phone to text Jaramillo and arrange another deal. Jaramillo responded he could be there within the hour. Investigators say they followed Jaramillo's black Kia Telluride to Silva's apartment complex, then pulled him over. A K9 alerted to narcotics inside the vehicle. Investigators say they found a bag of fentanyl on the passenger seat, along with a large amount of cash. See also: Vero Beach animal hospital manager accused of reclaiming cats, abandoning them outside Detectives then obtained a search warrant for Jaramillo's home on SW Longfellow Road. According to a separate affidavit, investigators searched the master bedroom. They found three firearms a Smith & Wesson .40 caliber handgun, a Ruger LC9 and an AR-15 along with ammunition, digital scales, a written ledger, cocaine, marijuana and $17,715 in cash. Jaramillo's wife, Selina Jaramillo, was home with their children during the search. According to the affidavit, she told investigators she didn't know he was involved in drugs and said she'd last seen him with narcotics about eight months earlier. She said one of the firearms was hers, but that the rest, along with the drugs and cash, belonged to her husband. The affidavit says Jaramillo told police anything illegal in the home belonged to him, then asked for a lawyer before answering further questions. Because Jaramillo is a convicted felon, investigators charged him with three counts of possessing a firearm or ammunition as a felon. Police say body cameras were active throughout the search and the footage was submitted into evidence. Jaramillo, 43, faces multiple felony drug charges, including fentanyl trafficking, along with three felony weapons counts and a misdemeanor paraphernalia charge. He was booked into the St. CBS12 News has reached out to Port St. Lucie Police for comment and is working to confirm additional details.

WPTV's Let's Hear It team is in Okeechobee County on Thursday, connecting with residents and local leaders at the Okeechobee County Library, 206 SW 16th St., until 6:30 p.m.The monthly meet-up is designed to give community members a chance to share the stories and issues that matter most to them — whether that's a problem that needs answers or a community concern that deserves attention.One common theme heard throughout the day, so far, is that Okeechobee is a close-knit community where local leaders and residents work together.Okeechobee County Fire Rescue Deputy Fire Chief Justin Hazellief told WPTV's Brooke Chau his department makes it a mission to build relationships across the community."It's not county versus city. We are Okeechobee together and it's something that we're very proud of," he said. "I've known the mayor my whole life and, I'm proud to say that and he's a wealth of knowledge and history for Okeechobee, as well as a vision for the future."Hazellief also addressed hurricane preparedness, warning that "hurricane fatigue" can set in when storms don't directly impact the area, causing residents to let their guard down during storm season.WATCH: Okeechobee County Fire Rescue Deputy Fire Chief Justin Hazellief emphasizes hurricane preparedness"We look at the tropics daily," Hazellief said. "We want to make sure that that our residents are still staying prepared. They still have their go-bags ready. They still have an evacuation plan ready."Okeechobee County Mayor Dowling Watford Jr. also spoke with WPTV reporter Brooke Chau and said growth is a threat to the community, but the city council and county commission are focused on keeping development controlled to preserve local lifestyle."With private enterprise and private property rights, not an awful lot you can do about some developments," he said. "Thank goodness our city council and our county commission, they try to focus on planned growth and controlled growth."One woman raised concerns about Flock cameras during today's event after the state ordered law enforcement to stop using them.Laurie Bergman told WPTV she is concerned about how the cameras were being used. "I'm not a criminal, that's my beef, I am not a criminal," she said. "They've gotten on there and found out where their ex-girlfriends are going, where their ex-wives are going. You don't need to know where I'm going. That's my problem."WPTV plans to follow up on her concerns and take them to the county.Can't make it to the library in person? The Let's Hear It team still wants to hear from you. Reach them anytime by emailing LetsHearIt@wptv.com.We want to be your voice and help you find solutions.While we hold our monthly Let's Hear It meet-ups, we know many are not able to attend, but we still want to hear from you and start taking action to get you answers. You can e-mail us at LetsHearIt@wptv.com.

By: Samantha Roesler Posted and last updated DELRAY BEACH, Fla. — A jackknifed semi blocked Interstate 95 southbound in Delray Beach late Thursday morning, causing major traffic delays. The crash occurred at the Atlantic Avenue exit at around 10:20 a.m. with injuries, according to the Florida Highway Patrol's (FHP) website. Cars were passing on the shoulder just after noon, when units were able to pull the semi-truck to the side of the highway. WPTV has reached out to FHP for more details on the crash. No word on what caused the semi to jackknife but FHP is investigating the accident.

A Palm Beach County sheriff's deputy is recovering from injuries after a violent struggle with a suspect who tried to steal her patrol car and wrestle away her firearm outside a South Palm Beach fire station Thursday morning.WATCH BELOW: Deputy 'saved her own life' by fatally shooting suspect after attackThe confrontation began around 7:35 a.m. when Rex Magann, 32, walked to the fire station and called dispatch, saying he had taken his mother's car and needed help because "she wouldn't help me," according to Palm Beach County Sheriff Ric Bradshaw.When the female deputy arrived to assist what appeared to be someone in distress, the situation quickly escalated. Magann approached her and demanded her patrol car, saying, "I need a car, I'm taking your car.""She says, 'You're not taking my car,'" Bradshaw said during a press briefing. "At that point, he lunges at her to grab her gun, and then they get into a very violent confrontation."Magann, described as about 5-foot-11 and 250 pounds, overpowered the deputy, knocking her to the ground where she hit her head. The violent struggle continued as both fought for control of her weapon.WATCH THE FULL PRESS CONFERENCE BELOW:"He's on top of her; they're still wrestling for the gun," Bradshaw said. "He finally starts beating her in the face and in the chest to see if he can knock her unconscious."The deputy was ultimately able to access her firearm and fatally shoot Magann in the chest.The deputy was taken to JFK Medical Center, where she was treated for facial injuries and evaluated for a possible concussion. Her injuries are not considered life-threatening. Bradshaw said Magann's next-of-kin has been notified. "This could have gone very, very bad for this female deputy. She literally was fighting for her life," Bradshaw emphasized. This guy was intent on getting that gun."Magann had an extensive criminal history, including multiple arrests for battery on emergency personnel, burglary, assault on law enforcement officers, and fleeing from felonies. He had been involuntarily committed under the Baker Act three times in the past three years and was currently on probation for battery on a law enforcement officer.

Lucie parent is calling for changes to a school bus stop near Paar Drive and Winslow Street, saying students are forced to walk along portions of the road where there is no sidewalk.Belinda Green said she became concerned about the safety of students using the specific bus stop and shared a video on TikTok showing the area.WATCH: Port St. Lucie parent raises safety concerns over bus stop“This is an easy resolve, make two stops,” Green said.She tells WPTV her biggest concern is the limited space available for students walking along Paar Drive.“That's the white line for the car... that shouldn't be for a human being,” Green said.Green suggests splitting the stops in the area so students have less distance to walk along the roadway. Instead of having students use only the bus stop at Paar Drive and Winslow Street, she would like to see an additional bus stop at Paar Drive and Jarmer Road. She says that could help prevent students from having to walk along a narrow stretch of roadway and cross the street after the bus has already left.“One little slip up — and we are looking at a tragedy unfolding,” Green said.WPTV reached out to St. Lucie Public Schools about Green's concerns.The district said its transportation department reviewed all routes and bus stops in the area and determined the existing stops are appropriate for student use.But after WPTV brought Green's concerns to the district, the school district made a change to one route nearby.Officials said a route change nearby was made to reduce the need for students to cross the road, while students who do need to cross should do so under the direction of the bus driver and with the bus's safety control devices.Green said she believes addressing potential safety concerns now is better than waiting for a serious incident.“I'd rather we find a resolution now than one day we have hashtags or there's a GoFundMe for some child or parent's funeral fund,” Green said.

The Indian River County Sheriff's Office announced more than 50 arrests following a multi-agency, multi-day operation targeting human trafficking and illegal sexual activity in the county.WATCH BELOW: Indian River County Sheriff's Office reveals results of multi-agency operationOperation Late Checkout ran from Sept. 13 in Indian River County. The operation netted over 60 contacts, more than 50 arrests, and three ICE detainers, Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a press conference on Thursday.Flowers announced the results alongside a representative from the Florida Department of Law Enforcement."Agencies involved in the operation included the Indian River County Sheriff's Office, Florida Department of Law Enforcement, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Seminole County Sheriff's Office, Altamonte Springs Police Department, Vero Beach Police Department, Homeland Security Investigations, Florida Office of Statewide Prosecutor and the U.S. Attorney's Office," Flowers said.The operation's targeted goal was stopping human trafficking in the Indian River County area, the sheriff's office said.During the operation, several victims were identified, and investigators said ongoing investigations are underway. Flowers said there are no specific arrests on human trafficking charges at this time.One case involved a man who traveled to Indian River County to meet a minor. Flowers said the arrest was the result of the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force working across agencies to apprehend individuals attempting to lure children online."Our team did a great job of getting him off the street," Flowers said.Undercover teams were deployed in a variety of capacities during the operation, the sheriff's office said. Victims' advocates trained to work with trafficking victims were also on hand to speak with women involved in prostitution to determine whether they were being trafficked."We have many ongoing investigations as a result of this," Flowers said.Flowers called the operation unprecedented for Indian River County."We've never had an investigation like this, to my knowledge, in Indian River County with this many agencies involved, with this many arrests in one shot," he said.FDLE Assistant Special Agent in Charge Alfonso Williams said Operation Late Checkout was initiated by FDLE in coordination with the Indian River County Sheriff's Office and is the first operation of this magnitude conducted in the county."This operation shows that within our communities there are dangerous individuals committing heinous crimes who think they can get away with it," Williams said.Williams said the operation focused on identifying human trafficking victims, reducing the demand for prostitution, and apprehending individuals seeking sexual contact with minors."Our work is far from done," Williams said. "This operation requires a lot of resources and time. We cannot do this work alone, and our success depends on the great partnership and collaboration that you see today."FDLE said it houses the Florida Trafficking Hotline. Anyone who suspects someone is a victim of trafficking can contact the hotline at 1-855-352-7233.READ OPERATION LATE CHECKOUT BELOW:

A 42-year-old travel MRI technician was arrested after Port St. Lucie police said a patient reported she was sexually assaulted while undergoing an MRI at HCA Florida St. Gabriel Cruz was arrested in Brevard County on the evening of Sept. 16 on a charge of sexual battery involving a physically helpless or incapacitated victim, a first-degree felony, police said. The investigation began Sept. 14 after hospital staff reported that a 64-year-old female patient said she had been sexually assaulted during an MRI the day before at the hospital, 1800 SE Tiffany Ave. Police said the woman had been admitted for medical treatment and was given medication before the MRI that left her significantly drowsy. Detectives identified Cruz as the technician assigned to the procedure. With the hospital’s assistance, investigators obtained video that police said showed Cruz leaving the MRI room after the patient and disposing of materials. See also: Amazon closes Port St. Lucie warehouse for major renovation, hundreds impacted by layoffs Those materials were recovered and tested, returning presumptive positive results for male semen, according to police. Cruz had worked at the hospital as a travel MRI technician since Aug. 24 and was hired through a third-party agency, police said. The investigation remains active. Lucie Hospital has cooperated with investigators, police said. Lucie Hospital provided CBS12 News with the following statement: We do not tolerate behavior that jeopardizes the safety or security of our patients. When this serious allegation was reported to us, we contacted law enforcement and ended the individual’s assignment. We have assisted law enforcement throughout its investigation and remain focused on supporting our patient.

Amazon has laid off roughly 300 workers at its Port St. Lucie fulfillment center as the facility prepares to shut down for renovations, with more employees transferred to other Amazon sites. Since the company filed a WARN notice in July listing 494 affected workers, Amazon says more than 200 additional employees have transferred to other facilities. Workers who aren't transferring will begin receiving paid severance this month. Amazon filed the notice July 15 with Florida's State Trade and Rapid Response Coordinator and sent a copy to Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin, as required under the federal Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act. The filing states operations will shut down at Amazon's PBI3 facility, 7600 LTC Pkwy, effective Thursday, September 17. Roughly 494 employees will be separated from the company, with separations effective September 17 and December 17. Amazon told affected workers about the closure around June 18, according to the filing. The job cuts are expected to be permanent, the notice states. Affected employees aren't represented by a union and don't have seniority-based "bumping rights" to displace other workers. Amazon says it will pay employees through their separation date, provided they don't resign early, and will share benefits and severance information separately. The vast majority of the affected positions 466 of the 494 are "FC Associate I" roles, the facility's entry-level warehouse position. The rest include operations managers, HR staff, a safety specialist, an IT support associate and other roles, according to a list attached to the filing. Local economic development officials say that reduced number didn't happen by accident. Lucie Economic Development Council says the facility typically employs between 850 and 1,000 workers depending on the season. In the four months before Amazon filed the WARN notice, CareerSource Research Coast and the EDC held weekly job fairs and helped place many affected workers with other area employers, including Costco, Cheney Brothers and ImportMex, which the EDC says brought the number of employees ultimately listed in the WARN filing down to 494. Amazon describes the closure differently than the legal notice does. In a statement shortly after the notice, company spokesperson Amber Plunkett said, "The Treasure Coast is a great place to live and work, and we're proud of our partnerships across St. These investments and improvements reflect our long-term confidence in the region." On the Port St. Lucie facility specifically, Plunkett said, "We're always evaluating our network to make sure it fits our business needs and to improve the experience for our employees, customers, partners, and drivers. As part of that effort, we occasionally convert existing facilities to a new type of facility which is what we plan to do here later this year. When these renovations are done, Port St. Lucie will be home to a new fulfilment center that will create long-term benefits for our customers, employees, and the community for many years to come." On what happens to the facility's workers, Plunkett said, "Our goal is to keep all of our employees based at this facility with Amazon. Our HR team will work with everyone to offer transfers to another location that fits their preferences we have 30 facilities across South Florida. For those who prefer not to transfer, we'll be providing transition support. When this facility reopens in mid-to-late 2028, it will employ approximately 1,000 people, and everyone from the site will have the option to return at that time." Amazon says the project represents a $200 million investment in the South Florida region. The company says operations will shift to other nearby facilities during the closure and that customers won't be affected. Amazon also said it's working to transfer roughly 850 employees to nearby locations a figure that doesn't match the roughly 494 workers listed as affected in the WARN filing. It's not clear from the materials Amazon provided how the two numbers relate. Employees have the option to transfer to two nearby facilities specifically, or to any of the company's roughly 30 sites across South Florida, and Amazon says it's offering relocation bonuses to employees who transfer more than 50 miles from Port St. All employees affected by this closure will be eligible for rehire once the Port St. Lucie facility reopens, according to Amazon. Lucie County Commissioner Cathy Townsend called the closure part of a bigger strain on businesses in the county. It's devastating," Townsend said. Townsend said the impact will ripple beyond the workers who lost their jobs. "They rent, they eat in restaurants, their children go to daycare, they go to our schools," Townsend said. "And so it's going to ripple down. It is going to hurt the economy here in Saint Lucie County. And I have concerns for those families. And jobs are not plentiful right here in this county." Townsend credited the EDC's job-placement efforts with softening the blow, but said the layoffs point to a broader pattern of job insecurity in the county. She said local leaders should focus on attracting small businesses that are more likely to stay rooted in the community rather than larger corporations. "They're the fabric of what makes up our community," Townsend said. "And they live here, and they pay taxes here. And we need to do what we have to do to make them successful, not be worried about the big box stores, because these are things that can happen."

Fort Pierce city commissioners voted 3-2 Monday to give developers of the Kings Landing development 180 days to find $15 million in funding for the hotel portion of the development. Developers Live Oak and Main Sail say the Marriott hotel portion of the project will now cost around $65 million — $15 million more than previously planned. WATCH BELOW: Developers of Kings Landing given 6 months to fund hotel Earlier this summer, developers asked the city for the funds through a loan or grant, but were denied. Now, Jon Collier with Main Sail said they will look to secure the funds privately. "We can get it done," Collier said. A representative from Live Oak said the development team remains committed. "With millions of dollars invested thus far and an enormous amount of time, we're extremely motivated to see this through to a successful completion," the representative said. The extension comes after developers missed a July 15 deadline to secure the funding for the project. Fort Pierce Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky voted against the extension. "My opinion, based on the legal review of this, is that we need to stop now. Because if we do another amendment, it continues to weaken us and makes it more difficult to get the property back," Dzadovsky said. On Tuesday, WPTV sat down with Commissioner Michael Broderick, who voted for the extension. Broderick said taking back the property — currently owned by Audubon Development — would be costly and lead to litigation. "Everybody's going to be suing everybody. It's like having three fighters in the same ring, and they're all going to come out swinging at each other," Broderick said. Broderick said the city has 30 days to draft a new amendment with developers, after which the six-month countdown will begin. When asked what happens if developers fail to find the money in time, Broderick was direct. "I'm going to kick them to the curb. I'll make the motion to terminate the deal," Broderick said. Jon Nolli, who owns the Funky Cuda and other businesses in Fort Pierce and has a deposit on space in the Kings Landing development for a beer garden and deli, said he is cautiously watching the situation unfold. "If this is really what it takes and they can find the money to be able to do this, great. Then we can get moving forward," Nolli said. Nolli said he is still concerned about further delays. "If this is just another step extending it along, that's going to be pretty tough on everybody," Nolli said. The Florida Panthers opened training camp Thursday, with forward Brady Tkachuk taking the ice for the first time as a Panther. This year, the team looks to bounce back from an injury-plagued season that ended without a playoff berth.Brad Marchand, one of the Panthers' top goal scorers, is missing training camp due to an injury. General Manager Bill Zito said he expects Marchand back sometime in the early regular season, something they will push back if need be. Head coach Paul Maurice said Thursday that Marchand will do rehab for the month of October. RELATED: Latest Panthers news"That may mean he's ready to play right at the end of it; it may mean he needs a short period of time, assuming no setbacks, but we're planning on rehabbing for October," Maurice said. This season, both Tkachuk brothers are on the roster, Aleksander Barkov is back and 50 prospects took the ice for the first day of camp. "I thought that was a great first day. Everyone pushed themselves to the limits and pushed the guys around," Brady Tkachuk said.Tkachuk said coach Paul Maurice made clear that practices would be demanding."Really tough, really challenging, but now the ones that are going to help in the long run. So it was great to grind that out with the group," Tkachuk said.Tkachuk also spoke about his focus beyond the on-ice work."(Off the ice) just getting to know everybody, continuing to build on relationships, and the best part about doing that is when you go through something tough like that skate that you already have that bond you're creating with the guy next to you," Tkachuk said.Training camp is shorter this year, with the team scheduled to play only four preseason games. The Panthers play at home Sunday in their first preseason game against the Carolina Hurricanes.

A Vero Beach animal hospital manager was arrested after investigators said she reclaimed two cats from the Humane Society of Vero Beach and Indian River County, then abandoned them outdoors without care. Deanna Rae Wesley, 43, was arrested Sept. 15 on an active warrant charging her with two counts of animal abandonment, both first-degree misdemeanors, according to Indian River County court records. Animal Control investigators said Wesley, who works at Dr. Dan’s Animal Hospital , picked up two white-and-brown tabby cats from the Humane Society on Sept. Wesley reportedly told staff the cats were being returned to a caregiver, but she would not identify that person, the affidavit said. The next day, Animal Control received a complaint about a white-and-brown tabby cat crying at a resident’s front door. Investigators said the cat was taken to Animal Control, where its microchip and Humane Society staff confirmed it was one of the cats Wesley had picked up. An investigator said Wesley initially denied it was the same cat but acknowledged the matching microchip number. According to the affidavit, she declined to explain how the cat ended up loose at the home. The resident told investigators that a woman matching Wesley’s description, wearing a Dr. Dan’s T-shirt, spoke with her mother and warned her to watch out for Animal Control in the area. The woman allegedly called the cats colony cats, the affidavit said. See also: Amazon closes Port St. Lucie warehouse for major renovation, hundreds impacted by layoffs Animal Control recovered the second cat at the same residence Sept. Both cats were described as extremely friendly, with debris on their faces and chins. Investigators said the cats were not capable of surviving outdoors on their own and that no one was known to be caring for them. The warrant alleges Wesley abandoned the cats on a public street without providing care, food, protection or shelter. A judge set bond at $250 per count, for a total of $500.

The Indian River County Sheriff's Office announced more than 50 arrests following a multi-agency, multi-day operation targeting human trafficking and illegal sexual activity in the county. WATCH BELOW: Indian River County Sheriff's Office reveals results of multi-agency operation Operation Late Checkout ran from Sept. 13 in Indian River County. The operation netted over 60 contacts, more than 50 arrests, and three ICE detainers, Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a press conference on Thursday. Flowers announced the results alongside a representative from the Florida Department of Law Enforcement. "Agencies involved in the operation included the Indian River County Sheriff's Office, Florida Department of Law Enforcement, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Seminole County Sheriff's Office, Altamonte Springs Police Department, Vero Beach Police Department, Homeland Security Investigations, Florida Office of Statewide Prosecutor and the U.S. Attorney's Office," Flowers said. The operation's targeted goal was stopping human trafficking in the Indian River County area, the sheriff's office said. During the operation, several victims were identified, and investigators said ongoing investigations are underway. Flowers said there are no specific arrests on human trafficking charges at this time. One case involved a man who traveled to Indian River County to meet a minor. Flowers said the arrest was the result of the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force working across agencies to apprehend individuals attempting to lure children online. "Our team did a great job of getting him off the street," Flowers said. Undercover teams were deployed in a variety of capacities during the operation, the sheriff's office said. Victims' advocates trained to work with trafficking victims were also on hand to speak with women involved in prostitution to determine whether they were being trafficked. "We have many ongoing investigations as a result of this," Flowers said. Flowers called the operation unprecedented for Indian River County. "We've never had an investigation like this, to my knowledge, in Indian River County with this many agencies involved, with this many arrests in one shot," he said. FDLE Assistant Special Agent in Charge Alfonso Williams said Operation Late Checkout was initiated by FDLE in coordination with the Indian River County Sheriff's Office and is the first operation of this magnitude conducted in the county. "This operation shows that within our communities there are dangerous individuals committing heinous crimes who think they can get away with it," Williams said. Williams said the operation focused on identifying human trafficking victims, reducing the demand for prostitution, and apprehending individuals seeking sexual contact with minors. "Our work is far from done," Williams said. "This operation requires a lot of resources and time. We cannot do this work alone, and our success depends on the great partnership and collaboration that you see today." FDLE said it houses the Florida Trafficking Hotline. Anyone who suspects someone is a victim of trafficking can contact the hotline at 1-855-352-7233. READ OPERATION LATE CHECK OUT BELOW:

A 42-year-old travel MRI technician was arrested after Port St. Lucie police said a patient reported she was sexually assaulted while undergoing an MRI at HCA Florida St. Gabriel Cruz was arrested in Brevard County on the evening of Sept. 16 on a charge of sexual battery involving a physically helpless or incapacitated victim, a first-degree felony, police said. The investigation began Sept. 14 after hospital staff reported that a 64-year-old female patient said she had been sexually assaulted during an MRI the day before at the hospital, 1800 SE Tiffany Ave. Police said the woman had been admitted for medical treatment and was given medication before the MRI that left her significantly drowsy. Detectives identified Cruz as the technician assigned to the procedure. With the hospital’s assistance, investigators obtained video that police said showed Cruz leaving the MRI room after the patient and disposing of materials. See also: Amazon closes Port St. Lucie warehouse for major renovation, hundreds impacted by layoffs Those materials were recovered and tested, returning presumptive positive results for male semen, according to police. Cruz had worked at the hospital as a travel MRI technician since Aug. 24 and was hired through a third-party agency, police said. The investigation remains active. Lucie Hospital has cooperated with investigators, police said.

A Vero Beach animal hospital manager was arrested after investigators said she reclaimed two cats from the Humane Society of Vero Beach and Indian River County, then abandoned them outdoors without care. Deanna Rae Wesley, 43, was arrested Sept. 15 on an active warrant charging her with two counts of animal abandonment, both first-degree misdemeanors, according to Indian River County court records. Animal Control investigators said Wesley, who works at Dr. Dan’s Animal Hospital , picked up two white-and-brown tabby cats from the Humane Society on Sept. Wesley reportedly told staff the cats were being returned to a caregiver, but she would not identify that person, the affidavit said. The next day, Animal Control received a complaint about a white-and-brown tabby cat crying at a resident’s front door. Investigators said the cat was taken to Animal Control, where its microchip and Humane Society staff confirmed it was one of the cats Wesley had picked up. An investigator said Wesley initially denied it was the same cat but acknowledged the matching microchip number. According to the affidavit, she declined to explain how the cat ended up loose at the home. The resident told investigators that a woman matching Wesley’s description, wearing a Dr. Dan’s T-shirt, spoke with her mother and warned her to watch out for Animal Control in the area. The woman allegedly called the cats colony cats, the affidavit said. See also: Amazon closes Port St. Lucie warehouse for major renovation, hundreds impacted by layoffs Animal Control recovered the second cat at the same residence Sept. Both cats were described as extremely friendly, with debris on their faces and chins. Investigators said the cats were not capable of surviving outdoors on their own and that no one was known to be caring for them. The warrant alleges Wesley abandoned the cats on a public street without providing care, food, protection or shelter. A judge set bond at $250 per count, for a total of $500.

The Fort Pierce city commission approved a contract with a body-worn camera manufacturer to provide equipment for its police department. During a meeting on Monday, Sept. 14, commissioners voted unanimously 5-0 to approve a contract with Axon Enterprise, Inc. for body-worn cameras and other technology provided by the company. Fort Pierce Police Department Chief David M. Smith said prior to the commissioners’ vote on Monday that the package with Axon Enterprise was the company's "top tier" offering that included Tasers, also known as stun guns, artificial intelligence technology tools, along with body cameras that translate languages immediately for officers. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 The officer would then speak in their language, and the body camera will relay the officers’ message to the subject in their language. “It will absolutely be a force multiplier for us,” Smith said. The Axon technology will also help officers with redaction of police reports. Redactions are used to prevent personal information, like Social Security numbers, from being made public. The contract is for five years with an optional automatic renewal for another five years. The 10-year contract will cost Fort Pierce $10,139,037.87. The first five years, the city will make annual payments of $999,000. If the option is picked up for the final five years of the contract, the city will pay Axon Enterprise $1,028,807.57 annually. A Lake Worth man is facing charges after deputies say he stole liquor from a Martin County store, then drove recklessly into Palm Beach County before being taken into custody. According to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office, 24-year-old Derwyn Don Edwards entered the Publix liquor store at 8605 SE Federal Highway around 11:24 a.m. 10 and stole multiple bottles of liquor. The retailer provided deputies with a description of Edwards and the vehicle he was driving. A deputy located the vehicle near SE Dominica Terrace and Federal Highway and attempted a traffic stop, but authorities said Edwards failed to stop and continued driving recklessly. See also: Indian River sheriff's sergeant on leave amid Flock camera investigation Because the incident did not meet the agency’s pursuit-policy criteria, the deputy turned off emergency lights and siren and disengaged. Deputies said Edwards nevertheless continued driving dangerously, at times exceeding 80 mph, running red lights and endangering the public before heading south on Interstate 95. MCSO Air 1 then located the vehicle and monitored it from above, guiding deputies as Edwards entered Palm Beach County without a ground pursuit. Authorities said Edwards eventually parked and attempted to hide. Air 1 directed an unmarked unit to his location, and he was taken into custody with assistance from the Florida Highway Patrol. Edwards was charged with reckless fleeing and eluding and petit theft. He is being held at the Martin County Jail.

Lucie parent is calling for changes to a school bus stop near Paar Drive and Winslow Street, saying students are forced to walk along portions of the road where there is no sidewalk. Belinda Green said she became concerned about the safety of students using the specific bus stop and shared a video on TikTok showing the area. Lucie parent raises safety concerns over bus stop “This is an easy resolve, make two stops,” Green said. She tells WPTV her biggest concern is the limited space available for students walking along Paar Drive. “That's the white line for the car... that shouldn't be for a human being,” Green said. Green suggests splitting the stops in the area so students have less distance to walk along the roadway. Instead of having students use only the bus stop at Paar Drive and Winslow Street, she would like to see an additional bus stop at Paar Drive and Jarmer Road. She says that could help prevent students from having to walk along a narrow stretch of roadway and cross the street after the bus has already left. “One little slip up — and we are looking at a tragedy unfolding,” Green said. Lucie Public Schools about Green's concerns. The district said its transportation department reviewed all routes and bus stops in the area and determined the existing stops are appropriate for student use. But after WPTV brought Green's concerns to the district, the school district made a change to one route nearby. Officials said a route change nearby was made to reduce the need for students to cross the road, while students who do need to cross should do so under the direction of the bus driver and with the bus's safety control devices. Green said she believes addressing potential safety concerns now is better than waiting for a serious incident. “I'd rather we find a resolution now than one day we have hashtags or there's a GoFundMe for some child or parent's funeral fund,” Green said.

A diver’s search for lobster off Fort Pierce beach last month led to the discovery of a suspected World War II-era torpedo, prompting a controlled detonation by the U.S. Luke Neiman, who was diving with his father and a friend just south of the jetty, described where he was when he made the discovery. "So, I was like right around about right there where that big condo is right there just past that," Neiman said. He explained how he realized the object was unusual. "I couldn't really make out what it was, but I just knew it wasn't a reef, and I was kind of inspecting it, looking at it," Neiman said. "I'm like, this just looks different, you know, and then before I knew it, I'm like, this is a torpedo, because I could make out the end of it and it had a cone nose." Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates Neiman returned to the boat, told his father to mark the spot, and contacted the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC). The FWC then alerted the U.S. Lucie County Sheriff's Office bomb squad, and the U.S. On Tuesday afternoon, Navy Explosive Ordnance Disposal personnel conducted a controlled underwater detonation at the site. Officials confirmed the operation in a statement, saying, "Navy Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) personnel conducted a routine underwater ordnance disposal operation Sept. 15, 2026, in the waters off St. Lucie County." The Navy identified the object as a suspected World War II-era munition. Reflecting on the discovery, Neiman said, "Yeah, it just really blew my mind literally that I found a torpedo down here right where I catch a bunch of lobster and stuff!" Amazon workers at the Port St. Lucie fulfillment center will be paid for the last time Sept. 17 as the facility begins a two-year renovation, with local leaders working to help the displaced employees transition to new opportunities. Stay up to date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 “Obviously, the greatest impact is on the workers and their families,” said Wicker Perlis, spokesperson for the St. Lucie County Economic Development Council. Since the closure was announced in May, county officials tell WPBF 25 News that many employees have successfully transferred to other Amazon locations or found work with new employers. “We can say at this point that a majority of the employees who were there in May, easily a majority, have found new work by the time the closure took place,” Perlis said. The EDC partnered with CareerSource Research Coast and local businesses to assist workers in finding new jobs. CareerSource organized hiring events and job assistance programs specifically for the displaced Amazon employees, bringing in companies such as Walmart, CVS and Pursuit Aero to connect with workers. Walmart interviewed dozens of employees and hired 25. Import Mex hired 12 workers and is considering others for future openings, while CVS Distribution hired two. Additionally, four reemployment sessions were held, reaching over 100 affected workers with information on job placement services, training programs and other resources. County officials said the timing of new employers and expanding businesses helped create options for many of the people looking for their next paycheck. “There are jobs out there. And we can try and help you, connect you with a good job,” Perlis said. Amazon has announced that the renovated facility is expected to reopen in 2028 with about 1,000 employees. Until then, officials said the focus remains on ensuring those impacted by the temporary closure have a plan for what is next. According to CareerSource Research Coast, the fulfillment center has been closed since Sept. 6, and affected workers are still being paid on time until Sept. 17, when their employment will be officially terminated. The Fort Pierce city commission approved a contract with a body-worn camera manufacturer to provide equipment for its police department. During a meeting on Monday, Sept. 14, commissioners voted unanimously 5-0 to approve a contract with Axon Enterprise, Inc. for body-worn cameras and other technology provided by the company. Fort Pierce Police Department Chief David M. Smith said prior to the commissioners’ vote on Monday that the package with Axon Enterprise was the company's "top tier" offering that included Tasers, also known as stun guns, artificial intelligence technology tools, along with body cameras that translate languages immediately for officers. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 The officer would then speak in their language, and the body camera will relay the officers’ message to the subject in their language. “It will absolutely be a force multiplier for us,” Smith said. The Axon technology will also help officers with redaction of police reports. Redactions are used to prevent personal information, like Social Security numbers, from being made public. The contract is for five years with an optional automatic renewal for another five years. The 10-year contract will cost Fort Pierce $10,139,037.87. The first five years, the city will make annual payments of $999,000. If the option is picked up for the final five years of the contract, the city will pay Axon Enterprise $1,028,807.57 annually. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. In the commission agenda, it was noted that the current Axon body cameras owned by the police department were at the end of their life and needed to be replaced. is in Scottsdale, Arizona.

Lucie County staff are providing updates to commissioners tonight on the removal of automated license plate readers, including Flock cameras, from county-maintained roads after a vote earlier this month. Erick Gill, communications director for St. Lucie County, said letters were sent earlier this week to all permit holders, notifying them of the decision and giving them 30 days to remove the cameras. "Earlier this week, letters went out to all the permit holders, whether some of those were permits were submitted on the behalf of law enforcement agencies, some were directly manufacturers of those cameras. So, they were notified this week and have 30 days to remove those cameras from the St. Lucie County right-of-ways," Gill said. County right-of-ways include the shoulders of highways and roads maintained by the county. Gill said there were about 50 to 55 permits issued for the cameras. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 If permit holders fail to remove the cameras within the 30-day period, county staff will step in to remove them. "I'm sure the permit owners going to want to do that because...I'm sure there's value to these cameras that they don't want damaged, and they did the installations, so we're going to make sure they comply with the 30-day rule, or we'll begin the process of removing them ourselves," Gill said. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. Lucie County residents expressed opposition to the surveillance cameras. "I'm not happy about them. I think they are too intrusive and they might really impede our freedom," said Toria Hoke, a St. Another resident, Herman Felton, shared similar concerns. "I think it's a spy on the city...it's spying on the people, that's what I think it is," Felton said. However, Felton also acknowledged the cameras could be useful in certain situations. "It's good in one area, and it's not so good in another area because people have their privacy...you can't invade on their privacy. Whatever they're doing at their house is their business," he said. County leaders clarified that the removal of the cameras from public roads does not mean they are banned entirely. Cameras can still be installed on private property or non-maintained rights-of-way.

A Lake Worth man is facing charges after deputies say he stole liquor from a Martin County store, then drove recklessly into Palm Beach County before being taken into custody. According to the Martin County Sheriff’s Office, 24-year-old Derwyn Don Edwards entered the Publix liquor store at 8605 SE Federal Highway around 11:24 a.m. 10 and stole multiple bottles of liquor. The retailer provided deputies with a description of Edwards and the vehicle he was driving. A deputy located the vehicle near SE Dominica Terrace and Federal Highway and attempted a traffic stop, but authorities said Edwards failed to stop and continued driving recklessly. See also: Indian River sheriff's sergeant on leave amid Flock camera investigation Because the incident did not meet the agency’s pursuit-policy criteria, the deputy turned off emergency lights and siren and disengaged. Deputies said Edwards nevertheless continued driving dangerously, at times exceeding 80 mph, running red lights and endangering the public before heading south on Interstate 95. MCSO Air 1 then located the vehicle and monitored it from above, guiding deputies as Edwards entered Palm Beach County without a ground pursuit. Authorities said Edwards eventually parked and attempted to hide. Air 1 directed an unmarked unit to his location, and he was taken into custody with assistance from the Florida Highway Patrol. The WTA Finals, the elite season-ending event in women's tennis, will be held in Charlotte, North Carolina, for the next three years in a move that organizers hope will create "the Super Bowl for women's sports."The tournament will be played at the Spectrum Center, home of the NBA's Charlotte Hornets, the WTA and the Charlotte Sports Foundation announced Wednesday.The year's top eight singles players and doubles teams qualify for the event, which is usually held in November."Our ambition is for the WTA Finals to be not only the premier championship in women's tennis, but one of the defining global events in women sports," WTA chair Valerie Camillo said. "We want to create the Super Bowl for women's sports. And not just the competition, but an event that is the annual gathering for women's tennis, women's sports, and women's sport business.""Audiences are growing, investment is growing, female athletes are increasingly at the center of sports and culture around the world. And women's tennis has helped lead and define that progress for more than 50 years. And we believe our biggest championship should reflect the scale of this moment," Camillo added.Camillo called it a "minimum three-year deal. She added, "We'll see what goes on beyond that."The announcement comes at a time of financial difficulty for the WTA after it announced in July that it was opting out of the final year of a three-year hosting arrangement with Saudi Arabia to move this year's Finals to Indian Wells, California.There were concerns about going back to Saudi Arabia due to military conflicts in the Middle East.IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | WTA introduces gene testing for all players on women's tennis tourCamillo noted that "2026 is a year of transition for the WTA" and that "we are doing the normal belt tightening you would expect in any business while also absorbing the unexpected cost of relocating the WTA finals to Indian Wells."What's most important to know is that we have a clear path to deliver consistent, sustainable financial performance in 2027 and beyond," she added.With Indian Wells now set to host only once, Charlotte will become the eighth different venue for the Finals since 2018.The WTA did not announce any prize money figures for the upcoming tournaments, and could struggle to match the record-setting amounts that were on offer in Saudi Arabia.Elena Rybakina collected $5.23 million for winning the 2025 WTA Finals in Riyadh after going 5-0 at the event. The WTA said that was the largest payout in the history of women's sports. Aryna Sabalenka earned $2.7 million as runner-up.Rybakina also beat Sabalenka in Saturday's U.S. Open final and claimed the No. 1 ranking.Coco Gauff won the 2024 finals in Riyadh.The partnership will extend beyond the Finals. The WTA will also relocate its global headquarters from St. Petersburg, Florida, to Charlotte, as part of the deal.And there's a plan to bring a WTA 500 tournament to Charlotte after 2029."The WTA has always owned the WTA finals, but now going forward, we're going to operate it too," Camillo said. "We're taking control of the creation of the revenues and the controlling of the expenses and the delivery of the entire thing."And that allows us to control our own destiny," Camillo added. "Whether it's around what we're doing with our media rights and our production, whether it's related to the WTA finals, whether we're approaching our calendar, we're going to be making bold and aggressive moves for women's tennis that shapes the future that we want rather than reacting."RELATED STORY | Mirra Andreeva, 19, wins French Open to become youngest champion since 1992Camillo replaced retiring chair Steve Simon at the end of last year.She previously oversaw business operations for the Philadelphia Flyers and Wells Fargo Center as the president and CEO of the sports and entertainment division of Comcast Spectacor, and has held senior roles with the Washington Nationals and the NBA.Asked if there was a desire to eventually merge with the ATP Finals — the men's season-ending event — Camillo said "there hasn't been an in-depth conversation about merging" the two tournaments."I think that when we create our ambition, people are going to want to merge with us on this event and many more," she added.The move to the Hornets arena during the NBA season means that the Finals will be condensed from eight to five days.That means the traditional schedule of two singles and two doubles matches per day could become four singles and four doubles matches per day."We are exploring a series of alternate formats," Camillo said.The Spectrum Center has already hosted high-profile tennis exhibition events in recent years."As an organization, our mission is quite simple," Will Pitts, CEO of the Charlotte Sports Foundation, said of the Finals. "It's drive economic impact and add to the quality of life through high-profile sporting events and unique partnerships. And this certainly does that."The move comes as Carolina Panthers owner David Tepper is investing an additional $500 million into ongoing stadium renovations with an eye toward potentially bringing the Super Bowl, NFL draft, 2031 Women's World Cup and other major sporting events to Charlotte.

In the mind of Florida Panthers captain Aleksander Barkov, the difficult part of his comeback is already over.It happened in May, in a far-from-filled Swedish arena, when Barkov suited up for Finland in an exhibition against Switzerland for his first game since shredding his right knee in the Panthers' first training camp practice 7 1/2 months earlier. And on one of his very first shifts, he tumbled to the ice.WATCH BELOW: Panthers ice crew preps Amerant Bank ArenaRELATED: More Florida Panthers newsNothing bad happened.“Very good news,” Barkov said.That was it. That was all it took for Barkov to realize his surgically repaired knee was good, that he could play without fear or concern. A few weeks later, he hoisted the trophy when Finland won the IIHF world championship.And now he's home in Florida, set for the start of training camp and ready to lead a team that — even after missing the playoffs last season — has been set by most sportsbooks as the favorite to win what would be its third Stanley Cup in a four-year span.“Don't take anything for granted,” Barkov said, when asked what he learned from not being able to play for Florida last season. “You just have to enjoy every single chance you get to play hockey, to be with your teammates, to go to every single practice, every single game. You’ve got to be excited about that.”The Panthers — who were holding media day on Wednesday in advance of Thursday's first practice of camp — have plenty of reasons to be excited. Many core players from the runs to the Cup titles in 2024 and 2025 are back, names like Barkov, Matthew Tkachuk, Sam Reinhart, Sam Bennett, Aaron Ekblad, Carter Verhaeghe, Gustav Forsling, Brad Marchand, Anton Lundell, Dmitry Kulikov and Niko Mikkola.Brady Tkachuk, Matthew Tkachuk's brother, has been added to the mix and Florida even brought Radko Gudas — a fan favorite from his first stint with the Panthers — back to help shore up the defense. And in net, with Sergei Bobrovsky gone to Toronto, Florida is turning the goaltender job over to Jacob Markstrom.“Every single guy who has come in, they look so determined to be their best and to show their best," Barkov said. “But they also know that we’re all in this together. Every single person is important, and every single has their own abilities to lead in their own way. We have many of those guys, so that’s the best part of this. No one’s here by themselves. Everyone can be just whatever they are.”That didn't happen last season. Injuries gutted the Panthers, starting with Barkov.He got hurt about 20 minutes into the first practice of training camp, tearing the ACL and MCL in his right knee on Sept. He had surgery a day later and was skating within a few months, but by the time he was ready to seriously consider returning to game action Florida — which dealt with injuries all year — was out of playoff contention and didn't get a chance at trying to win a third consecutive Stanley Cup.It wasn't entirely a lost season for Barkov. He missed the chance to serve as Finland's captain at the Milan Cortina Olympics, but played for his country at the IIHF world championships this past spring — and got to hoist the trophy when Finland beat host Switzerland 1-0 in the gold medal game.And now, Florida's career leader in goals and assists is raring to go with the Panthers once again.“We all know camp is always going to be hard, no matter what. It's going to be hard physically and mentally," Barkov said. "We're all kind of ready for that test.”
