hero.headline: Palm City man surrenders after hours-long SWAT standoff on SW Bessey Creek Trail
hero.body:
A 38-year-old Palm City man surrendered peacefully Saturday evening after an hours-long standoff with Martin County Sheriff's Office SWAT officers and hostage negotiators at a home on SW Bessey Creek Trail near Murphy Road. Darrel Abbey was booked into the Martin County Jail on three charges, including felony aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, and is being held on a $12,500 bond.

Deputies were initially called to the home for a domestic-related incident. The situation escalated when Abbey, who deputies say was armed and dangerous and under the influence of alcohol, barricaded himself inside a guest house on the property.

Neighbors reported hearing several gunshots. Gavin Ryan, an 11-year-old who lives next door, said he was scared because such incidents do not usually happen in the neighborhood. Ryan's mother said deputies asked her to evacuate after she heard the gunshots coming from her neighbor's yard. SWAT officers later positioned themselves near her home as the standoff unfolded.

Hostage negotiators worked throughout the afternoon to convince Abbey to come out peacefully. He eventually surrendered without incident and no injuries were reported. Another neighbor, Julian Tracy, said he was shocked to learn what was happening. Tracy said he had never heard about a shooting in the neighborhood.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce commissioners vote to explore hiring outside counsel to challenge Causeway Cove development
hero.body:
Fort Pierce city commissioners approved a motion to explore hiring an outside land-use attorney to determine whether the city has any legal grounds to challenge the proposed Causeway Cove development under Florida's Live Local Act. The vote escalates a fight over the 913-unit waterfront project on South Hutchinson Island as construction could begin before the end of the year.

The proposed redevelopment would transform the Causeway Cove property along Seaway Drive with five towers ranging from 11 to 17 stories, 913 residential units, two hotels totaling 407 rooms, more than 72,000 square feet of retail and commercial space, and 218 marina slips, according to city records. The city is also monitoring lawsuits filed elsewhere in Florida that seek to restore greater local control over development decisions.

City officials have repeatedly said the proposed Causeway Cove project qualifies under the Live Local Act and therefore moves through an administrative review process rather than a traditional public hearing and commission vote. The law allows qualifying projects to bypass certain local zoning, density and height restrictions if affordability requirements are met. Qualifying developments must reserve at least 40% of units as affordable rental housing for at least 30 years.

Commissioner Michael Broderick said residents' concerns extend beyond the size of the development. "The concern is density, traffic flow," Broderick said, pointing to longstanding concerns about capacity on Seaway Drive. Resident Edie Harrison said the project would alter an area known for its waterfront views, boating access and small-town character. "Everything is still very quaint," Harrison said. "It's one of those gems."

Another major debate centers on affordability. Under Live Local, affordable housing calculations are based on regional income levels rather than income levels specific to Fort Pierce. According to city officials, some qualifying units could rent for more than $2,300 per month, while Fort Pierce's median rent is substantially lower. Broderick said many residents question whether those figures reflect true affordability within the city.

Land-use attorney Keith Poliakoff, who has represented clients in Live Local disputes across the state, said local governments generally have limited discretion once a project satisfies state requirements. Poliakoff said the law effectively requires municipalities to administratively approve qualifying projects, even when residents or local leaders oppose the density, height or scale of a development. State data show more than 200 Live Local projects have been proposed or approved across Florida. The most recent changes to the law, known as Live Local 4.0, took effect July 1, 2026, expanding eligible development sites and further clarifying protections for qualifying projects that include affordable housing.

Qualifying developments must continue to reserve at least 40% of units as affordable rental housing for at least 30 years. Now, Fort Pierce finds itself at the center of a broader statewide debate over growth, affordable housing and home rule. The proposed redevelopment would dramatically transform the Causeway Cove property along Seaway Drive. According to city records, plans call for five towers ranging from 11 to 17 stories, 913 residential units, two hotels totaling 407 rooms, more than 72,000 square feet of retail and commercial space, and 218 marina slips. For residents like Edie Harrison, the project would the area known for its waterfront views, boating access and small-town character. "Everything is still very quaint," Harrison said. "It's one of those gems." Harrison and hundreds of other residents have raised concerns about the size of the development, traffic impacts and what they view as a lack of public input. At the center of the fight is Florida's Live Local Act, a law passed in 2023 to encourage the construction of affordable and workforce housing across the state. The law allows qualifying projects to bypass certain local zoning, density and height restrictions if affordability requirements are met. City officials have repeatedly said the proposed Causeway Cove project qualifies under the law and therefore moves through an administrative review process rather than a traditional public hearing and commission vote. For critics, that process has become one of the most controversial aspects of the proposal. Fort Pierce Commissioner Michael Broderick said residents' concerns extend beyond the size of the development. "The concern is density, traffic flow," Broderick said, pointing to longstanding concerns about capacity on Seaway Drive. Another major debate centers on affordability. Under Live Local, affordable housing calculations are based on regional income levels rather than income levels specific to Fort Pierce. Critics argue the formula can produce rents that technically qualify as affordable under state guidelines but remain difficult for many local residents to afford. According to city officials, some qualifying units could rent for more than $2,300 per month, while Fort Pierce's median rent is substantially lower. Broderick said many residents question whether those figures reflect true affordability within the city. Even some lawmakers who supported the legislation have raised concerns about how it is being applied. Dana Trabulsy, whose district includes parts of the Treasure Coast, has recently questioned whether developments of this scale reflect what legislators intended when they approved the measure. The Fort Pierce dispute is also part of a much larger battle unfolding across Florida. Several lawsuits challenging aspects of the Live Local Act are moving through the courts as cities seek to regain greater authority over local development decisions. Supporters of the law argue it is helping address Florida's housing shortage, while critics contend it has weakened local home-rule powers and limited communities' ability to shape growth. Land-use attorney Keith Poliakoff, who has represented clients in Live Local disputes across the state, said local governments generally have limited discretion once a project satisfies state requirements. Poliakoff said the law effectively requires municipalities to administratively approve qualifying projects, even when residents or local leaders oppose the density, height or scale of a development. State data show more than 200 Live Local projects have been proposed or approved across Florida , making the law one of the most significant growth and housing measures enacted in recent years. Related 2024 article: $100M Kanner Hwy development in Stuart: Affordable housing powered by Live Local Act If things move forward as anticipated, construction on the Causeway Cove development could begin before the end of the year. The property's owner, Palm Beach developer Ashton DePeyster, did not respond to requests for comment. This report is part of an ongoing CBS12 News I-Team investigation examining the impact of Florida's Live Local Act, the legal challenges surrounding the law, and how communities across the Treasure Coast are responding to large-scale development projects.

hero.headline: Palm City SWAT standoff ends with arrest after man barricades in guest house
hero.body:
A 38-year-old man is facing felony charges after barricading himself inside a guest house on SW Bessey Creek Trail near Murphy Road in Palm City during an hours-long standoff with law enforcement Saturday. Darrel Abbey surrendered to SWAT officers and hostage negotiators after firing shots and prompting neighbor evacuations. He is being held on a $12,500 bond.

Deputies were initially called to the home for a domestic-related incident. The situation escalated when Abbey, who was armed and under the influence of alcohol, barricaded himself inside a guest house on the property, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office.

Neighbors were evacuated after gunshots were heard. The mother of 11-year-old Gavin Ryan, who lives next door, said deputies asked her to evacuate after she heard several gunshots coming from her neighbor's yard. SWAT officers positioned themselves near her home as the standoff unfolded. Hostage negotiators worked throughout the afternoon to get Abbey to come out peacefully. He eventually surrendered without incident and no injuries were reported.

Julian Tracy, another neighbor, said he was shocked to learn what was happening. Gavin Ryan said he was scared because it does not usually happen in the neighborhood.

Abbey was booked into the Martin County Jail and is facing three charges, including felony aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. Jail records show he is being held on a $12,500 bond.

cards.headline: Vandrell Jacobs sentenced to 10 years for Vero Beach Orangewood Apartments shooting
cards.teaser: A Vero Beach man received a 10-year prison sentence for his role in a January 2024 shooting at the Orangewood Apartments that sent bullets into a family's home and triggered a high-speed police chase.
cards.body:
Vandrell Jacobs, 25, has been sentenced to 10 years in prison for a January 2024 shooting at the Orangewood Apartments in Vero Beach that sent bullets into a family's home and triggered a high-speed chase. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office announced the sentencing this week, closing out a case that began with a January 28, 2024 shooting.

Deputies responded to reports of gunfire at the Orangewood Apartments on January 28. Five bullets struck an apartment occupied by a family. Witnesses reported seeing people inside a red Mercedes firing shots toward an intended victim before fleeing the scene.

Surveillance footage showed the Mercedes stopping in the area of the shooting before driving away. Flock cameras recorded the car for about two minutes before the shooting occurred. A deputy who responded to the shooting pursued the Mercedes, but the car fled at high speed and ran red lights.

The Mercedes was located the following day, January 29, 2024, and Jacobs was arrested. Jacobs admitted to the allegations at the time of his arrest. He was charged with shooting into a dwelling, vehicle, or building and fleeing police with disregard for safety.

hero.headline: Kukielka charged with attempted homicide, Plotts with burglary after SW Brevity Terrace road rage shooting
hero.teaser: Two Port St. Lucie men are facing felony charges after a road rage confrontation near Southwest California Boulevard and Southwest Brevity Terrace escalated into a shooting Thursday.
hero.body:
Two Port St. Lucie men are facing felony charges after a road rage confrontation near Southwest California Boulevard and Southwest Brevity Terrace escalated into a shooting Thursday. Tylon Kukielka, 57, was charged with attempted homicide, and Dean Plotts, 41, was charged with burglary with assault or battery.

According to the Port St. Lucie Police Department, the incident happened at about 6:30 p.m. The vehicles had passed each other, and one driver believed the other had cut him off. One driver believed he was being followed after merging onto Southwest Crosstown Parkway. Investigators determined there was no intentional following.

Kukielka was driving with his girlfriend to her home after leaving a local restaurant. Plotts was traveling in the same direction. The situation escalated into a physical fight near Southwest Brevity Terrace. During the fight, Kukielka allegedly fired his gun, striking Plotts twice in the left wrist and legs.

A St. Lucie County sheriff's deputy traveling in the area witnessed the incident and detained Kukielka. Plotts was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital for treatment. Kukielka was also taken to a hospital for a medical evaluation. Investigators recovered surveillance video and shell casings during the investigation. Both men were taken into custody. The incident remains under investigation.

cards.body:
Martin County Fire Rescue extinguished a golf cart fire in Hobe Sound that spread to a nearby home on Saturday night. The fire started just after 7 p.m. near the 8100 block of Southeast Eagle Avenue, just off Jimmy Buffett Memorial Highway (Southeast Dixie Highway).

Firefighters quickly put out the flames and confined the fire to the garage, porch, and side of the home. One patient reported minor injuries and smoke inhalation but refused transport. The State Fire Marshal has been notified and will investigate the cause of the fire. The agency credited C-Shift crews including Ladder 33, Engine 30 32, Tender 44, EMS 3, Battalion 3, and Rescue 301, 302, and 331.

hero.headline: Indian River County's Operation Late Checkout nets over 50 arrests in human trafficking sting
hero.body:
Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers announced Thursday that law enforcement made more than 50 arrests during a four-day operation called Operation Late Checkout that targeted human trafficking and illegal sexual activity in the county. The operation ran from Sept. 13 and netted over 60 contacts, more than 50 arrests, and three ICE detainers.

Flowers announced the results during a press conference alongside a representative from the Florida Department of Law Enforcement. Agencies involved in the operation included the Indian River County Sheriff's Office, Florida Department of Law Enforcement, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Seminole County Sheriff's Office, Altamonte Springs Police Department, Vero Beach Police Department, Homeland Security Investigations, Florida Office of Statewide Prosecutor and the U.S. Attorney's Office.

During the operation, several victims were identified and ongoing investigations are underway. Flowers said there are no specific arrests on human trafficking charges at this time. One case involved a man who traveled to Indian River County to meet a minor. Flowers said the arrest was the result of the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force working across agencies to apprehend individuals attempting to lure children online.

Undercover teams were deployed in a variety of capacities during the operation. Victims' advocates trained to work with trafficking victims were on hand to speak with women involved in prostitution to determine whether they were being trafficked. Flowers called the operation unprecedented for Indian River County. "We've never had an investigation like this, to my knowledge, in Indian River County with this many agencies involved, with this many arrests in one shot," he said.

FDLE Assistant Special Agent in Charge Alfonso Williams said Operation Late Checkout was initiated by FDLE in coordination with the Indian River County Sheriff's Office and is the first operation of this magnitude conducted in the county. Williams said the operation focused on identifying human trafficking victims, reducing the demand for prostitution, and apprehending individuals seeking sexual contact with minors. FDLE houses the Florida Trafficking Hotline. Anyone who suspects someone is a victim of trafficking can contact the hotline at 1-855-352-7233.

cards.headline: Indian River County's Operation Late Checkout nets over 50 arrests in human trafficking sting
cards.teaser: Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers announced Thursday that law enforcement made more than 50 arrests during a four-day operation called Operation Late Checkout that targeted human trafficking and illegal sexual activity in the county.
cards.body:
Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers announced Thursday that law enforcement made more than 50 arrests during a four-day operation called Operation Late Checkout that targeted human trafficking and illegal sexual activity in the county.

The operation ran from Sept. 13 and netted over 60 contacts, more than 50 arrests, and three ICE detainers. Flowers called the operation unprecedented for Indian River County. "We've never had an investigation like this, to my knowledge, in Indian River County with this many agencies involved, with this many arrests in one shot," he said during a press conference.

Agencies involved in the operation included the Indian River County Sheriff's Office, Florida Department of Law Enforcement, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Seminole County Sheriff's Office, Altamonte Springs Police Department, Vero Beach Police Department, Homeland Security Investigations, Florida Office of Statewide Prosecutor and the U.S. Attorney's Office. FDLE Assistant Special Agent in Charge Alfonso Williams said Operation Late Checkout was the first operation of this magnitude conducted in the county.

During the operation, several victims were identified. Undercover teams were deployed in a variety of capacities, and victims' advocates trained to work with trafficking victims were on hand to speak with women involved in prostitution to determine whether they were being trafficked. Flowers said there are no specific arrests on human trafficking charges at this time, but many ongoing investigations are underway as a result of the operation.

One case involved a man who traveled to Indian River County to meet a minor. Flowers said the arrest was the result of the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force working across agencies to apprehend individuals attempting to lure children online. "Our team did a great job of getting him off the street," Flowers said.

Williams said the operation focused on identifying human trafficking victims, reducing the demand for prostitution, and apprehending individuals seeking sexual contact with minors. "This operation shows that within our communities there are dangerous individuals committing heinous crimes who think they can get away with it," Williams said. "Our work is far from done."

FDLE houses the Florida Trafficking Hotline. Anyone who suspects someone is a victim of trafficking can contact the hotline at 1-855-352-7233.

hero.headline: Execution date set for man who killed Indian River County deputy in 1986
hero.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis has signed a death warrant setting an Oct. 27 execution date for William Reaves, who murdered Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkoski nearly 40 years ago. The governor signed the warrant Friday morning, ending decades of appeals and a retrial that all resulted in the same outcome: a death sentence.

Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said Friday was a great day for the county. Flowers never met Raczkoski, who was killed in September 1986 when Flowers was only 6 years old. Reaves shot Raczkoski four times at a convenience store near Vero Beach.

Flowers said people still talk all the time about the man everybody knew as Raz. Flowers added a 1986 patrol car, Raczkoski's car, to the department a few years ago to ensure the deputy's legacy lives on. Flowers said he has been vocal for years about wanting the death penalty for Reaves, and the governor's office called him Friday morning to inform him the death warrant had been signed.

The execution is scheduled one week after the 40th anniversary of Raczkoski's death. Flowers said he made calls to retirees and to Raczkoski's son, who was born shortly after his father was killed and never met him. Flowers said Reaves has been wasting taxpayer dollars for the last 40 years and it is time to get this over with. Flowers plans to attend the execution, ensuring the last thing Reaves sees is an Indian River County sheriff's uniform as a reminder of what he did.

hero.headline: Attempted murder, burglary charges filed after Sept. 17 road rage shooting on SW Brevity Terrace
hero.teaser: Port St. Lucie police have charged driver Tylon Kukielka with attempted murder and victim Dean Plotts with burglary with assault following a road rage shooting near Southwest California Boulevard and Southwest Brevity Terrace on Sept. 17.
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie police have charged driver Tylon Kukielka with attempted murder and victim Dean Plotts with burglary with assault following a road rage shooting near Southwest California Boulevard and Southwest Brevity Terrace on Sept. 17. The investigation into the incident remains ongoing.

The shooting occurred at approximately 6:30 p.m. after what investigators determined began as a misunderstanding between two drivers. Kukielka, 57, was traveling with his girlfriend to her home after visiting a local restaurant. Plotts, 41, happened to be traveling in the same direction and onto the same streets. One driver believed he was being followed after changing lanes and merging from Southwest Crosstown Parkway, and one driver thought the other had cut him off. Police said the investigation revealed there was no intentional following.

The situation escalated into a physical confrontation near Southwest Brevity Terrace. During the altercation, Kukielka fired a handgun, striking Plotts twice. A Port St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputy who was in the area traveling on Southwest California Boulevard observed the incident and detained Kukielka. Plotts sustained gunshot wounds to his left wrist and legs and was transported to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital for treatment. Kukielka was also transported for medical evaluation.

Detectives collected evidence including shell casings, surveillance video, dash cam footage, and other physical evidence. Based on the evidence collected, witness information, video footage, and statements obtained during the investigation, detectives determined there was probable cause to charge Kukielka with attempted homicide – murder, dangerous depraved without premeditation, a first-degree felony under Florida Statute 782.04(2). Detectives also determined there was probable cause to charge Plotts with burglary with assault or battery, a felony under Florida Statute 810.02(2)(a). Both men were taken into custody in connection with the investigation. All defendants are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty in a court of law.

cards.headline: Martin County High School evacuated again after third bomb threat in eight days
cards.teaser: Martin County High School received another bomb threat Friday afternoon through the state's FortifyFL reporting system, the third threat involving the campus this week. Principal Lori Vogel warned families that students who make false threats will face severe disciplinary and criminal consequences.
cards.body:
Martin County High School received another bomb threat Friday afternoon through the state's FortifyFL reporting system, the third threat involving the campus this week. The latest threat referenced two specific buildings, requiring students and staff to be evacuated while law enforcement conducted a thorough search.

Students and staff were relocated to other areas of campus during the response. On Monday, students and staff were evacuated after a bomb threat prompted a response from the Martin County Sheriff's Office. Eight days ago, students and staff were evacuated in the afternoon after a bomb threat was received via email.

Principal Lori Vogel addressed families about the repeated disruptions. "Every threat must be taken seriously," Vogel said. "Each report generates a significant law enforcement response, disrupts instruction, displaces students and staff, and creates understandable concern throughout our school community. Unlike many situations that may require an emergency response, the behavior prompting these repeated disruptions is entirely avoidable. We need our families as partners in addressing this behavior. Please speak directly with your children about the seriousness and far-reaching impact of making or participating in a false threat."

The principal warned that false threats carry serious consequences. "What a student may view as a joke or a temporary way to avoid class can have widespread consequences for an entire campus and community," Vogel said. "However, FortifyFL must never be used to submit information that someone knows to be false. The District has zero tolerance for anyone who knowingly misuses the platform or participates in making a false threat. Any individual found responsible will face severe school disciplinary consequences and potential criminal charges."

School officials emphasized that FortifyFL remains an important safety resource for reporting credible threats or questionable, dangerous or criminal activity. Information about submitting a report is available on the school's and the School District's websites.

hero.headline: Indian River County Sheriff announces 50+ arrests in Operation Late Checkout
hero.body:
Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers announced Thursday that law enforcement made more than 50 arrests during a four-day operation called Operation Late Checkout that targeted human trafficking and illegal sexual activity in the county. The operation ran from Sept. 13 and netted over 60 contacts, more than 50 arrests, and three ICE detainers.

Flowers called the operation unprecedented for Indian River County. "We've never had an investigation like this, to my knowledge, in Indian River County with this many agencies involved, with this many arrests in one shot," he said during a press conference.

Agencies involved included the Indian River County Sheriff's Office, Florida Department of Law Enforcement, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Seminole County Sheriff's Office, Altamonte Springs Police Department, Vero Beach Police Department, Homeland Security Investigations, Florida Office of Statewide Prosecutor and the U.S. Attorney's Office.

FDLE Assistant Special Agent in Charge Alfonso Williams said Operation Late Checkout was initiated by FDLE in coordination with the Indian River County Sheriff's Office and is the first operation of this magnitude conducted in the county. The operation focused on identifying human trafficking victims, reducing the demand for prostitution, and apprehending individuals seeking sexual contact with minors.

During the operation, several victims were identified, and ongoing investigations are underway. Flowers said there are no specific arrests on human trafficking charges at this time. One case involved a man who traveled to Indian River County to meet a minor. Flowers said the arrest was the result of the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force working across agencies to apprehend individuals attempting to lure children online.

Undercover teams were deployed in a variety of capacities during the operation. Victims' advocates trained to work with trafficking victims were on hand to speak with women involved in prostitution to determine whether they were being trafficked. "We have many ongoing investigations as a result of this," Flowers said.

FDLE houses the Florida Trafficking Hotline. Anyone who suspects someone is a victim of trafficking can contact the hotline at 1-855-352-7233.

Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies and Martin County Fire Rescue responded to the scene. No injuries were reported, but several bicycles were damaged and believed to be a total loss, the sheriff's office said.

The cause of the crash is under investigation. By Saturday night, the white SUV was moved to a flatbed tow truck. The store owner and manager declined to talk to WPBF News 25.

cards.headline: Armed Palm City suspect Darrel Abbey in custody after SWAT ends standoff
cards.teaser: Darrel Abbey was taken into custody Saturday after barricading himself in a Palm City home following allegations he chased his girlfriend with a gun and fired shots.
cards.body:
Darrel Abbey was taken into custody Saturday after barricading himself with a weapon inside a Palm City residence, ending an armed standoff that began when he allegedly chased his girlfriend down the street with a gun and fired multiple shots, the Martin County Sheriff's Office said.

The Martin County Sheriff's Office SWAT Team safely resolved the armed barricaded subject situation on Southwest Bessey Creek Trail near Murphy Road, the agency posted on Facebook. Abbey was taken to the Martin County Jail.

Sheriff John Budensiek said the sheriff's office received a call from a frantic woman shortly after 3 p.m. who said a man chased her down the street, then went into the backyard and fired multiple shots. The man threatened to kill her, Budensiek said. Multiple people around the neighborhood called 911 after hearing the shots.

Callers indicated the incident was domestic-related and involved an aggravated assault with a deadly weapon inside the residence, the sheriff's office said. Abbey was described as armed and dangerous inside the home. Sheriff's office road patrol, detectives, SWAT and the hostage negotiation team responded to the scene.

Budensiek said Abbey refused to talk to negotiators. The SWAT team used a loudspeaker to order him out. When he refused, the sheriff's office pumped gas into the house. Abbey then left the home and was apprehended.

hero.headline: Indian River County human trafficking operation yields 60+ contacts, 50+ arrests
hero.body:
Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers announced Thursday that Operation Late Checkout yielded more than 60 contacts, more than 50 arrests, and three ICE detainers during a multi-agency operation targeting human trafficking and illegal sexual activity in the county. The four-day operation ran from Sept. 13 in Indian River County. Several victims were identified during the operation, and investigators said ongoing investigations are underway. Flowers said there are no specific arrests on human trafficking charges at this time.

Flowers called the operation unprecedented for Indian River County during a press conference alongside a representative from the Florida Department of Law Enforcement. He said it is the largest trafficking operation in county history. "We've never had an investigation like this, to my knowledge, in Indian River County with this many agencies involved, with this many arrests in one shot," Flowers said.

One case involved a man who traveled to Indian River County to meet a minor. Flowers said the arrest was the result of the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force working across agencies to apprehend individuals attempting to lure children online. "Our team did a great job of getting him off the street," Flowers said.

Agencies involved in the operation included the Indian River County Sheriff's Office, Florida Department of Law Enforcement, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Seminole County Sheriff's Office, Altamonte Springs Police Department, Vero Beach Police Department, Homeland Security Investigations, Florida Office of Statewide Prosecutor and the U.S. Attorney's Office. Undercover teams were deployed in a variety of capacities during the operation. Victims' advocates trained to work with trafficking victims were also on hand to speak with women involved in prostitution to determine whether they were being trafficked.

FDLE Assistant Special Agent in Charge Alfonso Williams said Operation Late Checkout was initiated by FDLE in coordination with the Indian River County Sheriff's Office and is the first operation of this magnitude conducted in the county. Williams said the operation focused on identifying human trafficking victims, reducing the demand for prostitution, and apprehending individuals seeking sexual contact with minors. "Our work is far from done," Williams said. "This operation requires a lot of resources and time. We cannot do this work alone, and our success depends on the great partnership and collaboration that you see today."

FDLE said it houses the Florida Trafficking Hotline. Anyone who suspects someone is a victim of trafficking can contact the hotline at 1-855-352-7233.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie woman arrested for draining $100K from 85-year-old's accounts
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie police arrested Barbara Baumgarten, 60, on Thursday following a months-long investigation into alleged elder exploitation and neglect. Investigators say Baumgarten drained approximately $100,000 from an 85-year-old man's bank accounts and fraudulently listed herself as a co-borrower on a $616,550 mortgage tied to the victim. Baumgarten was booked at the St. Lucie County Jail on $310,000 bond and faces felony charges of grand theft from a person 65 years of age or older, exploitation of an elderly person or disabled adult, and neglect of an elderly person or disabled adult.

The investigation began March 18 when Baumgarten, working as the victim's caregiver, found the elderly man injured on the floor of his Port St. Lucie home. The victim initially claimed four men had entered his home and assaulted him, but surveillance footage showed no one entering or leaving the property and no signs of forced entry or theft. The victim provided inconsistent accounts of what occurred, and detectives determined he was experiencing significant cognitive issues. Detectives continued looking into the victim's overall well-being and circumstances, eventually shifting the investigation toward concerns of elder exploitation and neglect.

The investigation, documented in a 45-page report, found that as the victim's physical and cognitive health declined, he became increasingly dependent on Baumgarten. Detectives determined Baumgarten had assumed significant control over the victim's finances and legal affairs, including power of attorney and healthcare surrogate. Investigators learned the victim had been isolated from family and friends and that changes had been made to his estate documents that benefited Baumgarten. Records reviewed by detectives showed a decline in his financial accounts from $105,971 in March 2023 to approximately $4,897 by April 2026.

Investigators also uncovered a $616,550 mortgage on Baumgarten's residence in which the victim was listed as a co-borrower, despite the property being solely in Baumgarten's name. Evidence indicated the victim was reportedly unaware his signature appeared on the mortgage. Detectives worked with healthcare providers, caregivers, family members, financial institutions and other agencies to establish the full extent of the circumstances. The Florida Department of Children and Families substantiated allegations of exploitation and determined the victim lacked the capacity to independently make his own decisions. The victim was removed from Baumgarten's care, placed under a temporary guardianship, and reunited with his family. Baumgarten had her first appearance in court Friday.

hero.headline: Vandrell Jacobs sentenced to 10 years for Vero Beach Orangewood Apartments shooting
hero.body:
Vandrell Jacobs has been sentenced to 10 years in prison for a January 2024 shooting at the Orangewood Apartments in Vero Beach that sent bullets into a family's home and triggered a high-speed chase. Jacobs, 25, was arrested on Jan. 29, 2024, one day after the shooting.

According to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office, deputies responded to reports of gunfire at the Orangewood Apartments in Vero Beach on Jan. 28, 2024. Investigators said five bullets struck an apartment occupied by a family. Witnesses reported seeing people inside a red Mercedes firing shots toward an intended victim before fleeing.

Surveillance footage shows the Mercedes stopping in the area of the shooting before driving away. Flock cameras recorded the car for about two minutes before the shooting, the sheriff's office said. A deputy who responded to the shooting pursued the Mercedes, but the car fled at a high speed and ran red lights.

The following day, the Mercedes was located and Jacobs was arrested. At the time, he admitted to the allegations. He was charged with shooting into a dwelling, vehicle or building and fleeing police with disregard for safety. Jacobs now begins his decade-long prison sentence.

hero.headline: DeSantis sets Oct. 27 execution for man who killed Indian River County deputy in 1986
hero.body:
Governor Ron DeSantis signed a death warrant Friday for William Reaves, setting an Oct. 27 execution date for the 1986 murder of Indian River County Sheriff's Deputy Richard Raczkoski. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said he received the call from the governor's office Friday morning, less than a week before the 40th anniversary of the killing. Flowers said it has been a great Friday in Indian River County and that he spent the day sharing the news with others.

Reaves shot Deputy Raczkoski four times at a convenience store near Vero Beach in September 1986. The case has gone through 40 years of appeals and a retrial, with each proceeding resulting in a death sentence. Flowers said Reaves has been wasting taxpayer dollars for the last 40 years and that it is time to get this over with.

Flowers, who was 6 years old when Raczkoski was killed and never met him, said the deputy was known as Raz and remembered as one of the best members of the department. According to Flowers, people still talk about Raczkoski all the time, recalling he was known for having his hairbrush in his car. To preserve his legacy, Flowers added a 1986 patrol car that belonged to Raczkoski to the department a few years ago. Flowers said the department wants people to remember that Raczkoski made the ultimate sacrifice and that current members serve the community in his memory.

Flowers said he called retirees and Raczkoski's son after receiving word of the warrant signing. Raczkoski's son was born shortly after his father was killed and never met him. The sheriff said he has been vocal for years about wanting the death penalty for Reaves, which is why the call from the governor's office meant so much to him. Flowers said he plans to attend the execution to ensure the last thing Reaves sees is an Indian River County sheriff's uniform as a reminder of what he did. hero.headline: Two men charged after road rage shooting on SW Brevity Terrace in Port St. Lucie
hero.body:
Two Port St. Lucie men are facing felony charges after a road rage confrontation near Southwest California Boulevard and Southwest Brevity Terrace escalated into a shooting Thursday evening. Tylon Kukielka, 57, was charged with attempted homicide – murder, dangerous depraved without premeditation, a first-degree felony. Dean Plotts, 41, was charged with burglary with assault or battery, a felony.

The incident began as a misunderstanding between the two drivers following a lane change and merging near Southwest Crosstown Parkway. One driver believed he was being followed after the vehicles crossed paths, but investigators found no intentional following. Kukielka was traveling with his girlfriend to her home after visiting a local restaurant. Plotts happened to be traveling in the same direction and onto the same streets.

As the vehicles continued, the situation escalated into a physical confrontation near SW Brevity Terrace. During the altercation, Kukielka fired a handgun, striking Plotts twice. A St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputy traveling on SW California Boulevard observed the incident and detained Kukielka. Neighbors reported hearing gunfire at approximately 6:30 p.m. "OK, last night we were trying to put the kids down, and we just heard like two big pop pops," resident Ripley Crawford said. "All we saw was the cars were kind of already pulled to the side, and you could see there was like a crash of sorts."

Plotts sustained gunshot wounds to his left wrist and legs and was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital for treatment. Kukielka was also transported for medical evaluation. Traffic was rerouted as investigators gathered evidence at the scene. "The traffic was just nonstop because they closed California. My neighbor got a call from her daughter in Tennessee that said there was a shooting down here," resident Ernie Lampreda said. Port St. Lucie Police Department detectives collected evidence, including shell casings, surveillance video, and dash cam footage that captured portions of the incident. Both men were taken into custody. The investigation remains ongoing.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce man arrested after raid seizes fentanyl, cocaine worth millions
cards.teaser: A Fort Pierce man faces multiple drug trafficking charges after authorities seized 4.5 kilograms of fentanyl and other drugs worth several million dollars from a residence on S. 24th Street.
cards.body:
A Fort Pierce man was arrested Friday after a raid by the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office and U.S. Marshals Service found a massive amount of illicit drugs worth several million dollars at a residence in the 3100 block of S. 24th Street in Fort Pierce.

Tony Saunders, 48, was taken into custody during the execution of a narcotics-related search warrant. Saunders is a three-time convicted felon who is on federal probation and had two active warrants related to the sale and delivery of controlled substances. He faces additional charges of trafficking in fentanyl, trafficking in cocaine, trafficking in MDPV, manufacturing cocaine, tampering with evidence and possession of marijuana with intent to sell.

The sheriff's office Special Investigations Division, with assistance from the SWAT Team and the U.S. Marshals Service, seized approximately 4.5 kilograms of fentanyl, 303 grams of cocaine, 97 grams of marijuana laced with MDPV, and 60 oxycodone pills totaling approximately 6.2 grams. Detectives also seized assorted ammunition, drug paraphernalia and materials consistent with the preparation and distribution of narcotics. The street value of 4.5 kilograms of fentanyl can range from $150,000 to nearly $1.8 million, according to U.S. Customs and Border Protection. The estimated street value of 303 grams of cocaine ranges between roughly $18,180 and $60,600.

A single kilogram of fentanyl has the potential to kill 500,000 people, making 4.5 kilograms a lethal volume capable of millions of fatal doses, according to the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration. Sheriff Richard Del Toro said the seizure prevented the drugs from reaching local streets. "Fentanyl is a deadly poison, and those who traffic in it are putting lives at risk for profit," Del Toro said. "I commend our detectives, SWAT Team, and the U.S. Marshals Service for their commitment to this mission. We will continue to pursue those who traffic dangerous narcotics and do everything within our authority to make St. Lucie County the safest county in Florida."

hero.headline: Martin County approves limited-industrial zoning for Hobe Sound site despite data center concerns
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners approved limited-industrial zoning for property along Southeast Powerline Avenue in Hobe Sound on Tuesday in a 3-2 vote that stepped back from a general-industrial designation but left at least one commissioner with concerns about future data center development. The property owner accepted the less-intensive classification after nearby residents pushed back against the broader zoning proposal.

Commissioner Blake Capps voted against the rezoning, citing concerns about the potential for a data center on the site. "Who knows where this is really going in the future and to approve a zoning for this property that allows a data center. I'm not into that," Capps said. The county said there are no plans for a data center at the site. Any proposal exceeding 100,000 square feet would require board approval.

Residents who spoke at the Tuesday commission meeting said their primary concern was protecting the character of the community. "Our biggest concern was preserving our quality of life. We don't have a lot of industry and a lot of noise," said Steve Addison, who has lived in the area since 1969. Kim Call, a resident, said growth needs to be compatible with the existing community. Patrick McDonough, a Hobe Sound resident and Eaglewood Community HOA president, said residents were concerned about the permanence of a general-industrial classification. "We believe is too broad and too open-ended," McDonough said.

Bob Reins, a land-use attorney with Gunster law firm representing the property owner, told commissioners his client was willing to accept the limited-industrial classification. "To cooperate and show if that's what the neighbors feel is more appropriate and that would be a better use then we are willing to accept the light industrial," Reins said. The property has long been slated for some form of industrial use, but the county said the existing zoning was outdated and due for an update. Addison said he felt the compromise was a win for both sides. "I don't want to see over development, but I also don't want to be that guy that doesn't understand land-use and doesn't understand property rights," Addison said.

hero.headline: Vandrell Jacobs sentenced to 10 years for Vero Beach apartment shooting, high-speed chase
hero.teaser: A 25-year-old man will spend a decade in prison for firing bullets into a Vero Beach apartment occupied by a family and leading deputies on a dangerous high-speed pursuit.
hero.body:
Vandrell Jacobs, 25, has been sentenced to 10 years in prison for his role in a January 2024 shooting at the Orangewood Apartments in Vero Beach and the high-speed chase that followed, according to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office.

Deputies responded to reports of gunfire at the Orangewood Apartments on Jan. 28, 2024. Investigators said five bullets struck an apartment occupied by a family. Witnesses reported seeing people inside a red Mercedes firing shots toward an intended victim before fleeing the scene.

Surveillance footage shows the Mercedes stopping in the area of the shooting before driving away. Flock cameras recorded the car for about two minutes before the shooting occurred, according to the sheriff's office. A deputy who responded to the shooting pursued the Mercedes, but the car fled at a high speed and ran red lights.

The Mercedes was located the following day, and Jacobs was arrested on Jan. 29, 2024. At the time, he admitted to the allegations. Jacobs was charged with shooting into a dwelling, vehicle, or building and fleeing police with disregard for safety. He now begins his decade-long prison sentence.

hero.headline: Amendment 3 support at 45% in new poll, below threshold needed to pass
hero.body:
A new St. Pete Polls survey shows support for Amendment 3 at about 45%, well below the 60% threshold required for Florida constitutional amendments to pass, with roughly 30% opposed and nearly a quarter of voters undecided. The property tax measure would increase the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, and lower the annual assessment-growth cap for non-homestead properties from 10% to 5%.

Gov. Ron DeSantis is urging voters to approve the amendment despite acknowledging it falls short of the property-tax changes he wanted. DeSantis said voters should pass the measure or risk getting no relief on property tax. The proposal has the Florida Republican Party's endorsement, and Florida Realtors has committed $10 million to the campaign supporting it.

The Florida Sheriffs Association has launched an advertising campaign opposing the amendment, warning of consequences for public safety. Police and firefighter groups have joined the opposition, questioning how communities would replace revenue supporting emergency services. Jennifer Cook Pritt of the Florida Police Chiefs Association said at a press event this week that the measure provides no clear path to fund core public safety services. Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd described the situation as a train wreck.

A legislative analysis estimates the amendment would reduce local non-school property-tax revenue by approximately $4.95 billion in the 2027-28 fiscal year and $8.78 billion in 2028-29. Supporters argue the changes would help homeowners manage costs and that local governments can reduce spending without sacrificing essential services. The St. Pete Polls survey contacted 913 likely voters Sept. 15-17 and reported a margin of error of 3.2 percentage points. Voters will decide the amendment in November.

hero.headline: Vandrell Jacobs sentenced to 10 years for Vero Beach Orangewood Apartments shooting
hero.body:
Vandrell Jacobs, 25, has been sentenced to 10 years in prison for a January 2024 shooting at the Orangewood Apartments in Vero Beach that sent bullets into a family's home and triggered a high-speed flight from deputies.

The Indian River County Sheriff's Office arrested Jacobs on Jan. 29, 2024, one day after deputies responded to reports of gunfire at the Orangewood Apartments. Five bullets struck an apartment occupied by a family. Witnesses reported seeing people inside a red Mercedes firing shots toward an intended victim before fleeing the scene.

Surveillance footage captured the Mercedes stopping in the area of the shooting before driving away. Flock cameras recorded the car for about two minutes before the shooting occurred. A deputy who responded to the scene pursued the Mercedes, but the car fled at high speed and ran red lights.

The Mercedes was located the following day and Jacobs was arrested. At the time, he admitted to the allegations. He was charged with shooting into a dwelling/vehicle/building and fleeing police with disregard for safety. He now begins his decade-long prison sentence.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie road rage shooting suspect charged with attempted homicide
hero.body:
A road rage confrontation on Southwest Brevity Terrace in Port St. Lucie that escalated into a shooting Thursday evening has resulted in attempted homicide charges for the suspected shooter and burglary with assault or battery charges for the other man involved. Tylon Kukielka, 57, faces the attempted homicide charge after allegedly firing his gun and striking Dean Plotts, 41, twice in the left wrist and legs during a physical fight. Plotts was charged with burglary with assault or battery.

The incident happened at about 6:30 p.m. near Southwest California Boulevard and Southwest Brevity Terrace, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department. Before the shooting, one driver believed he was being followed after merging onto Southwest Crosstown Parkway. The vehicles had passed each other, and one driver believed the other had cut him off. Investigators determined there was no intentional following.

Kukielka was driving with his girlfriend to her home after leaving a local restaurant. Plotts was traveling in the same direction. The situation escalated into a physical fight near Southwest Brevity Terrace. During the fight, Kukielka allegedly fired his gun.

A St. Lucie County sheriff's deputy traveling in the area witnessed the incident and detained Kukielka. Plotts was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital for treatment. Kukielka was also taken to a hospital for a medical evaluation. Investigators recovered surveillance video and shell casings during the investigation. Both men were taken into custody. The incident remains under investigation.

hero.headline: Martin County issues blue-green algae alert for Lake Okeechobee at J&S Fish Camp after toxins detected
hero.body:
The Florida Department of Health in Martin County issued a blue-green algae health alert for the Lake Okeechobee NES135 area after water samples collected in September detected harmful toxins. The area is located on the north shore of the lake at J&S Fish Camp in Martin County.

Residents and visitors should not drink, swim, wade, use personal watercraft or otherwise come into contact with water where a visible algae bloom is present. Health officials advised people to keep pets and livestock away from affected water. Anyone who comes into contact with algae, discolored water or water with an unpleasant odor should wash their skin and clothing with soap and water.

Contaminated water should not be used for cooking or washing dishes because boiling does not remove algae toxins. Blue-green algae are bacteria commonly found in Florida freshwater. Blooms can discolor water and create floating mats, scum, foam or paint-like material on the surface, sometimes with an unpleasant odor. The blooms can produce toxins that may harm people, pets and aquatic life.

Children, older adults and people with weakened immune systems may be at risk even at low toxin concentrations and should avoid exposure. Health officials said it is safe to eat fillets from healthy freshwater fish caught in lakes experiencing blooms if the fillets are rinsed with tap or bottled water, the guts are discarded and the fish is thoroughly cooked. People should not eat shellfish from waters with algae blooms.

The Florida Department of Environmental Protection monitors reported blooms and collects samples for analysis. The public can report an algae bloom online at ReportAlgalBloom.com or call 1-855-305-3903. Anyone who develops symptoms after exposure to a harmful algae bloom can call the Florida Poison Information Center at 800-222-1222. Pet owners who believe an animal became ill after exposure should contact a veterinarian. For health questions about blue-green algae, call DOH-Martin at 772-221-4090.

hero.headline: DeSantis signs death warrant for man who killed Indian River County deputy in 1986
hero.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis signed a death warrant Friday for William Reaves, convicted of killing Indian River County Deputy Sheriff Richard Raczkowski in 1986. Reaves is scheduled for execution by lethal injection at Florida State Prison in Starke on Oct. 20.

Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers has been pushing DeSantis to sign the warrant for Reaves, calling it a priority case. Flowers told WPEC last July that he was frustrated by the delay. "Ultimately it was decided a long time ago that he would face the death penalty, and it's time for him to actually face the consequences," Flowers said. "He's exhausted all of his appeals. Many other cases just like his have resulted in execution, and for some reason, he continues to cost us taxpayer dollars every single day."

According to court records, Reaves shot Raczkowski four times in the back outside a Zippy Mart convenience store near Vero Beach on Sept. 23, 1986. Reaves had called 911 from a pay phone because he didn't have money for a cab. Raczkowski, who was dispatched to the call, phoned the 911 dispatcher to order a cab for Reaves and to inquire about outstanding warrants. During this time, Reaves said a gun fell out of his pants. After Raczkowski attempted to block Reaves from retrieving the gun, a struggle ensued and Reaves wrestled the weapon away. The deputy asked Reaves not to kill him and turned to run away. Reaves then fired four times into Raczkowski's back. The deputy died a short time later.

Reaves went to the home of a friend, who later told police Reaves confessed to shooting the deputy, saying he was high on cocaine and panicked. Police arrested Reaves three days later at a bus stop and charged him with first-degree murder, possession of a firearm by a convicted felon and trafficking in cocaine. A jury found Reaves guilty of first-degree murder in September 1987 and unanimously recommended the death penalty. The Florida Supreme Court reversed the conviction and sentence in 1991, finding the trial court erred by allowing a prosecutor who had previously defended Reaves in a criminal matter. A second jury found Reaves guilty of first-degree murder in February 1992, voting 10-2 to recommend a death sentence.

Counsel for Reaves filed a motion Friday for a stay until pending motions regarding another condemned prisoner, William Lee Thompson, are resolved. Brittney Lacy, Reaves' attorney, stated both clients are due the best representation, particularly when both are facing scheduled execution dates. The warrant is DeSantis' 18th death warrant of the year. Florida has carried out 15 executions this year and 43 under DeSantis.

cards.headline: Sebastian police fatally shoot Keaton Daucher holding shotgun on Joy Haven Drive
cards.teaser: Interim Sebastian police Chief Tim Wood confirmed Friday that two officers fatally shot 41-year-old Keaton Daucher after he emerged from his home with a shotgun during a noise-complaint call Thursday night. The Florida Department of Law Enforcement is now investigating.
cards.body:
Two Sebastian police officers fatally shot 41-year-old Keaton Daucher after he came out of his home with a shotgun Thursday night in the 500 block of Joy Haven Drive, interim police Chief Tim Wood confirmed Friday morning. The officers arrived at about 9:25 p.m. for a noise complaint and have been placed on paid administrative leave.

Wood said officers made contact with Daucher's mother and could hear Daucher yelling inside the home while they were speaking with her. Daucher then came out of the home with a shotgun, prompting the two officers to discharge their weapons, killing him.

Police said it was unclear if Daucher, who lived at the home, pointed the shotgun at the officers or if he fired any shots. Neither of the officers were hurt.

The investigation has been turned over to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, which is standard practice for the Sebastian Police Department. Police said law enforcement had previously been at the house before Thursday but did not specify how many times.

cards.headline: Indian River County sex sting nets 50 arrests, child-luring case highlighted
cards.teaser: Sheriff Eric Flowers announced more than 50 arrests from Operation Late Checkout, a four-day multi-agency operation that targeted human trafficking and illegal sexual activity in Indian River County. The operation also resulted in three ICE detainers and one arrest involving a man who traveled to meet a minor.
cards.body:
Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers announced Thursday that law enforcement made more than 50 arrests during a four-day operation called Operation Late Checkout that targeted human trafficking and illegal sexual activity in the county.

The operation ran from Sept. 13 and netted over 60 contacts, more than 50 arrests, and three ICE detainers, Flowers said during a press conference. Agencies involved included the Indian River County Sheriff's Office, Florida Department of Law Enforcement, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Seminole County Sheriff's Office, Altamonte Springs Police Department, Vero Beach Police Department, Homeland Security Investigations, Florida Office of Statewide Prosecutor and the U.S. Attorney's Office.

One case involved a man who traveled to Indian River County to meet a minor. Flowers said the arrest was the result of the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force working across agencies to apprehend individuals attempting to lure children online. Several victims were identified during the operation, and ongoing investigations are underway. Flowers said there are no specific arrests on human trafficking charges at this time.

Undercover teams were deployed in a variety of capacities during the operation. Victims' advocates trained to work with trafficking victims were on hand to speak with women involved in prostitution to determine whether they were being trafficked. Flowers called the operation unprecedented for Indian River County. FDLE Assistant Special Agent in Charge Alfonso Williams said Operation Late Checkout was initiated by FDLE in coordination with the Indian River County Sheriff's Office and is the first operation of this magnitude conducted in the county. Williams said the operation focused on identifying human trafficking victims, reducing the demand for prostitution, and apprehending individuals seeking sexual contact with minors. FDLE houses the Florida Trafficking Hotline at 1-855-352-7233 for anyone who suspects someone is a victim of trafficking.

The operation’s targeted goal was stopping human trafficking in the Indian River County area, the sheriff’s office said. hero.headline: Martin County High School receives third bomb threat in eight days
hero.body:
Martin County High School received another bomb threat Friday afternoon through the state's FortifyFL reporting system, the third threat involving the campus this week, the school district said.

The latest threat referenced two specific buildings, requiring students and staff to be evacuated while law enforcement conducted a thorough search. Students and staff were relocated to other areas of campus during the response.

Principal Lori Vogel warned families that the district has zero tolerance for false threats and that any individual found responsible will face severe school disciplinary consequences and potential criminal charges.

"Every threat must be taken seriously," Vogel said in a message to families. "Each report generates a significant law enforcement response, disrupts instruction, displaces students and staff, and creates understandable concern throughout our school community."

On Monday, students and staff were evacuated after a bomb threat prompted a response from the Martin County Sheriff's Office. Eight days ago, students and staff were evacuated in the afternoon after a bomb threat was received via email, according to school officials.

cards.headline: Martin County issues blue-green algae alert for Lake Okeechobee area at J&S Fish Camp
cards.teaser: The Florida Department of Health in Martin County issued a health alert after water samples detected harmful toxins in blue-green algae at the Lake Okeechobee NES135 area.
cards.body:
The Florida Department of Health in Martin County issued a blue-green algae health alert for the Lake Okeechobee NES135 area after water samples detected harmful toxins. The alert covers an area on the north shore of the lake at J&S Fish Camp in Martin County and was issued in response to samples collected in September.

Residents and visitors should not drink, swim, wade, use personal watercraft or otherwise come into contact with water where a visible algae bloom is present. Health officials advised people to keep pets and livestock away from affected water. Anyone who comes into contact with algae, discolored water or water with an unpleasant odor should wash their skin and clothing with soap and water. Contaminated water should not be used for cooking or washing dishes because boiling does not remove algae toxins.

Blue-green algae are bacteria commonly found in Florida freshwater. Blooms can discolor water and create floating mats, scum, foam or paint-like material on the surface, sometimes with an unpleasant odor. The blooms can produce toxins that may harm people, pets and aquatic life. Children, older adults and people with weakened immune systems may be at risk even at low toxin concentrations and should avoid exposure.

It is safe to eat fillets from healthy freshwater fish caught in lakes experiencing blooms if the fillets are rinsed with tap or bottled water, the guts are discarded and the fish is thoroughly cooked. People should not eat shellfish from waters with algae blooms. The Florida Department of Environmental Protection monitors reported blooms and collects samples for analysis. The public can report an algae bloom online at ReportAlgalBloom.com or call 1-855-305-3903. Anyone who develops symptoms after exposure can call the Florida Poison Information Center at 800-222-1222. Pet owners who believe an animal became ill after exposure should contact a veterinarian. For health questions about blue-green algae, call DOH-Martin at 772-221-4090.

hero.headline: DeSantis sets Oct. 20 execution for William Reaves Jr. in 1986 Indian River County deputy murder
hero.body:
Governor Ron DeSantis has signed a death warrant for William Reaves Jr., setting an execution date of Oct. 20 for the 77-year-old man convicted of murdering Indian River County Sheriff's Deputy Richard Raczkoski in 1986. The execution is scheduled for 6 p.m. at Florida State Prison in Raiford, 40 years after the deputy's death.

Deputy Raczkoski was killed on Sept. 23, 1986, after responding to a 911 call at a convenience store. During a conversation with Reaves, a gun fell from Reaves's shorts. Deputy Raczkoski placed his knee on the weapon. Reaves then pushed the deputy away, grabbed the gun and pointed it at Deputy Raczkoski's face. As Deputy Raczkoski attempted to draw his own weapon, Reaves said, "I wouldn't do that if I were you." The deputy backed away, turned, and ran. Reaves fired seven rounds, striking Deputy Raczkoski four times.

Reaves was tried in the 19th Judicial Circuit in Indian River County. The Florida Supreme Court reversed the initial conviction and remanded the case for a new trial. On remand, Reaves was again convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death on March 6, 1992, in Vero Beach. The Florida Supreme Court affirmed the conviction and death sentence on April 7, 1994. The United States Supreme Court denied Reaves's petition for a writ of certiorari on Nov. 7, 1994.

Reaves pursued numerous postconviction challenges in both state and federal courts over the following decades. In 2015, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida granted Reaves's federal petition for a writ of habeas corpus. The Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit overturned that ruling and ordered that the petition be denied. Additional postconviction motions and petitions were subsequently denied, and those denials were affirmed on appeal. Executive clemency was also considered and denied.

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, in his letter recommending the warrant, wrote that "the record is legally sufficient to support the issuance of a death warrant," and confirmed that "there are no stays of execution issued by any court of competent jurisdiction in this cause."

cards.headline: Two Sebastian officers confirmed to have fatally shot armed man on Joy Haven Drive
cards.teaser: Two Sebastian police officers are on administrative leave after fatally shooting Keaton Daucher, 41, who emerged from a home with a shotgun during a noise complaint call Thursday night. The Florida Department of Law Enforcement is investigating.
cards.body:
Two Sebastian police officers have been placed on paid administrative leave after fatally shooting a 41-year-old man who emerged from a home with a shotgun Thursday night in the 500 block of Joy Haven Drive.

Interim police Chief Tim Wood said at a Friday morning news conference that officers arrived at the home at about 9:25 p.m. for a noise complaint. While officers spoke with the suspect's mother, they could hear a man, later identified as Keaton Daucher, 41, yelling inside the home.

Daucher then came out of the home with a shotgun, prompting the two officers to discharge their weapons, killing him. Police said it was unclear if Daucher, who lived at the home, pointed the shotgun at the officers or if he fired any shots.

Law enforcement had previously been at the house before Thursday. The investigation has been turned over to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, which is standard practice for the Sebastian Police Department.

Neither of the officers were hurt. Both remain on paid administrative leave pending the investigation.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie MRI technician arrested on felony sexual battery charge
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie Police arrested Gabriel Cruz, a 42-year-old MRI technician, on charges of felony sexual battery after a 64-year-old female patient reported being assaulted during an MRI procedure at HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital. Cruz was working at the hospital as a travel MRI technician hired through a third-party agency when the alleged assault occurred.

Detectives responded to the hospital at 1800 SE Tiffany Ave. on Sept. 14, 2026, after staff reported that the patient disclosed she was sexually assaulted while undergoing an MRI the previous day. The victim had been administered medication that caused her to become significantly drowsy prior to the procedure.

Video evidence obtained with the hospital's assistance showed Cruz exiting the MRI room after the victim and disposing of materials that were later secured by law enforcement. Testing of the materials returned presumptive positive results for the presence of male semen. Detectives confirmed Cruz had been working at the hospital since Aug. 24, 2026.

Detectives determined there was probable cause to charge Cruz with sexual battery, a first-degree felony under Florida Statute 794.011(4)(b), involving a victim who was physically helpless or incapacitated. Cruz was arrested in Brevard County on the evening of Sept. 16, 2026.

HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital said it cooperated fully with law enforcement throughout the investigation. In a statement, the hospital said it does not tolerate behavior that jeopardizes the safety or security of patients. The hospital contacted law enforcement when the allegation was reported and ended Cruz's assignment. The hospital said it remains focused on supporting the patient.

The Port St. Lucie Police Department reminded the community to report incidents of sexual assault immediately to law enforcement or trusted resources, emphasizing that such reports can ensure victims receive support and allow law enforcement to investigate. The investigation remains active and ongoing.

cards.headline: Free Responsible Dog Ownership Day in Fort Pierce Saturday aims to ease shelter overcrowding
cards.teaser: The Treasure Coast Kennel Club and Dogs and Cats Forever Animal Sanctuary are hosting a free event Saturday at 9 a.m. to educate families about responsible pet ownership and support overcrowded local shelters.
cards.body:
The Treasure Coast Kennel Club and Dogs and Cats Forever Animal Sanctuary are hosting a free Responsible Dog Ownership Day on Saturday at 9 a.m. at Dogs and Cats Forever Animal Sanctuary, located at 4600 Selvitz Road in Fort Pierce. The event aims to educate pet owners about training and care while raising support for shelter animals as local rescues deal with overcrowding and supply shortages.

Susan Lyons with the Treasure Coast Kennel Club said the event is designed to help reduce shelter returns. "It's a free event so that people can come out and get information about how to be responsible dog owners so that we don't see dogs being returned to the shelter," Lyons said.

The event will feature dog training demonstrations, agility showcases, therapy and service dog education, raffles, food trucks and activities for children including bounce houses and a scavenger hunt. The Fort Pierce canine unit will conduct a demonstration. Families who participate in the scavenger hunt can collect vouchers from vendors to receive a free raffle ticket. Raffle prizes include gift baskets, gift cards, and a television.

Dogs available for future adoption through Dogs and Cats Forever Animal Sanctuary will be featured during the event, including Libby, a 9-year-old terrier. Nancy Dunn of Dogs and Cats Forever Animal Sanctuary said the first 50 people who bring a donation will receive swag bags. "Things that we need are dog food, cat food, flat sheets right now for puppies, blankets, towels — those kinds of things we're always in need of," Dunn said. Organizers encourage attendees to bring unopened pet food, towels, blankets, or other donation items to support the shelter.

hero.headline: Sebastian police officer-involved shooting Thursday night under FDLE investigation
hero.body:

The Sebastian Police Department said the shooting occurred at about 9:34 p.m. Thursday. The agency announced the incident in a Facebook post at 5:55 a.m. Friday.

cards.headline: MRI technician arrested for felony sexual battery of sedated patient at HCA Florida St. Lucie
cards.teaser: Gabriel Cruz, a 42-year-old travel MRI technician, was arrested on charges of first-degree felony sexual battery after a 64-year-old patient reported being assaulted during an MRI procedure at the Port St. Lucie hospital.
cards.body:
Gabriel Cruz, a 42-year-old MRI technician, was arrested on charges of felony sexual battery after a 64-year-old female patient reported being assaulted during an MRI procedure at HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital. The Port St. Lucie Police Department arrested Cruz in Brevard County on the evening of Sept. 16, 2026, in connection with the investigation.

On Sept. 14, 2026, detectives responded to the hospital, located at 1800 SE Tiffany Ave., after staff reported that the patient disclosed she was sexually assaulted while undergoing an MRI the previous day. Detectives learned the victim had been admitted for medical treatment and was administered medication that caused her to become significantly drowsy prior to the procedure. Cruz was identified as the MRI technician assigned to the procedure.

Video evidence obtained with the hospital's assistance showed Cruz exiting the MRI room after the victim and disposing of materials that were later secured by law enforcement. Testing of the materials returned presumptive positive results for the presence of male semen. Detectives confirmed Cruz had been working at the hospital as a travel MRI technician since Aug. 24, 2026, and was hired through a third-party agency.

Following the review of evidence, detectives determined there was probable cause to charge Cruz with sexual battery, a first-degree felony under Florida Statute 794.011(4)(b), involving a victim who was physically helpless or incapacitated. HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital has cooperated fully with law enforcement throughout the investigation. In a statement, the hospital said, "We do not tolerate behavior that jeopardizes the safety or security of our patients. When this serious allegation was reported to us, we contacted law enforcement and ended the individual's assignment. We have assisted law enforcement throughout its investigation and remain focused on supporting our patient." The investigation remains active and ongoing. The Port St. Lucie Police Department reminded the community to report incidents of sexual assault immediately to law enforcement or trusted resources. Defendants are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty in a court of law.

hero.headline: Indian River County sex sting nets 50 arrests, child-luring case highlighted
hero.body:
Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers announced Thursday that law enforcement made 50 arrests during a four-day operation called Operation Late Checkout that targeted human trafficking. Nearly all the arrests were for prostitution. Investigators also identified multiple individuals they believe are victims of human trafficking, and those investigations are ongoing.

Flowers said the operation specifically targeted the trafficking of children and worked to capture people trying to lure children on the internet and meet up with them. Authorities pointed to the case of Carlos Reyes-Ayala, who is accused of traveling to Indian River County to meet with a child for sex.

Flowers said investigators connected with many others seeking to exploit children during the operation. "We had a whole roomful of detectives that were chatting undercover with people who wanted to meet up with children. Our team was busy for days," Flowers said.

Operation Late Checkout involved local, state, and federal law enforcement agencies. "This operation shows that within our communities, there are dangerous individuals committing heinous crimes who think they can get away with it," said Special Agent Alphonso Williams of the Florida Department of Law Enforcement.

Flowers said he expects more arrests to happen as a result of Operation Late Checkout. "It hurts our hearts when we see these cases and we see these kids. So, that's why we do these things," Flowers said.

hero.headline: Trail camera captures Florida panther mother with three cubs near Fort Myers
hero.body:
A trail camera at a nature reserve in Fort Myers has captured new footage of a Florida panther mother with three young cubs, offering a promising sign for the endangered species' recovery. The sighting is significant because it occurred farther north than where the endangered cats are usually seen in the state.

Experts say the footage indicates the panthers are expanding their breeding range, which could help the population recover. Florida panthers are an isolated population of the North American cougar, a species of large, solitary wild cats that range mostly in western North America and most of South America. There are thought to be some 200 individuals living in southern Florida.

Florida has spent decades trying to protect its panthers, primarily from encounters with cars and from a shrinking natural habitat. The cats' natural habitat has been reduced by about 95 percent from its original expanse.

The trail camera video shows the mother and three young cubs moving through the Fort Myers nature reserve. The expansion of the breeding range north of their typical territory represents a potential turning point for a species that has faced severe population pressures from both vehicle collisions and habitat loss throughout southern Florida.
