hero.headline: Indian River County sex sting nets 50+ arrests, child-luring case
hero.body:
More than 50 people were arrested in a multi-agency operation targeting human trafficking and illegal sexual activity in Indian River County, including a man who traveled to meet a minor. Sheriff Eric Flowers announced the results of Operation Late Checkout during a press conference Thursday alongside a representative from the Florida Department of Law Enforcement.

The operation ran from Sept. 13 and netted over 60 contacts, more than 50 arrests, and three ICE detainers, Flowers said. One case involved a man who traveled to Indian River County to meet a minor. Flowers said the arrest was the result of the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force working across agencies to apprehend individuals attempting to lure children online.

Agencies involved in the operation included the Indian River County Sheriff's Office, Florida Department of Law Enforcement, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Seminole County Sheriff's Office, Altamonte Springs Police Department, Vero Beach Police Department, Homeland Security Investigations, Florida Office of Statewide Prosecutor and the U.S. Attorney's Office. During the operation, several victims were identified, and ongoing investigations are underway. Flowers said there are no specific arrests on human trafficking charges at this time.

Flowers called the operation unprecedented for Indian River County. "We've never had an investigation like this, to my knowledge, in Indian River County with this many agencies involved, with this many arrests in one shot," he said. FDLE Assistant Special Agent in Charge Alfonso Williams said Operation Late Checkout was initiated by FDLE in coordination with the Indian River County Sheriff's Office and is the first operation of this magnitude conducted in the county.

Undercover teams were deployed in a variety of capacities during the operation. Victims' advocates trained to work with trafficking victims were also on hand to speak with women involved in prostitution to determine whether they were being trafficked. "We have many ongoing investigations as a result of this," Flowers said. Williams said the operation focused on identifying human trafficking victims, reducing the demand for prostitution, and apprehending individuals seeking sexual contact with minors. Anyone who suspects someone is a victim of trafficking can contact the Florida Trafficking Hotline at 1-855-352-7233.

cards.teaser: The Vero Beach Police Department has placed an officer on administrative leave with pay amid an investigation into alleged misuse of the Flock Safety license plate reader system.
cards.body:

cards.headline: Vero Beach Regional Airport approves 500-space paid parking lot, ending free parking
cards.teaser: Vero Beach City Council approved construction of a new long-term parking lot that will expand capacity from 80 spaces to over 500 at Vero Beach Regional Airport, ending free parking as officials cite rising flight demand.
cards.body:
Vero Beach City Council approved construction of a new long-term parking lot that will expand capacity from 80 spaces to over 500 at Vero Beach Regional Airport, ending free parking as officials cite rising flight demand and the airport's self-funding model.

Brandon Dambeck, interim airport director, said the expansion is driven by new flights coming to the airport. The current parking situation is not keeping up, Dambeck said, and the grass parking area looks disorganized. The airport operates without taxpayer dollars and must use the funds to cover the costs of any upgrades to the airport, Dambeck said.

Envision Parking Partners will build and pay for the lot. The airport will be responsible for maintaining it. John Mostoller with Envision said travelers will be able to pay through a prepaid option using license plate readers or at the lot gate. The new lot will also add cameras and lighting for security. No parking spot will be more than two to four minutes from the terminal, Mostoller said.

Some travelers said they will miss the free parking. Traveler Reana Tejada said that sucks and that free parking was a nice plus. Sydney Banak, who was able to park for free during her visit, said she understands the reasoning behind the change. Free parking is nice, Sydney said, but maybe they need to expand the airport or provide more services.

Construction is expected to begin in March and be completed by next summer. The airport previously announced upgrades including new covered walkways and baggage claim, and a new patio.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie MRI technician arrested on sexual battery charge after patient assault
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie Police arrested Gabriel Cruz, a 42-year-old MRI technician, on charges of felony sexual battery after a 64-year-old female patient reported being assaulted during an MRI procedure at HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital. Cruz faces a first-degree felony charge under Florida Statute 794.011(4)(b), involving a victim who was physically helpless or incapacitated.

Detectives responded to the hospital at 1800 SE Tiffany Ave. on Sept. 14, 2026, after staff reported the patient disclosed she was sexually assaulted while undergoing an MRI the previous day. The victim had been admitted for medical treatment and was administered medication that caused her to become significantly drowsy prior to the procedure.

Video evidence obtained with the hospital's assistance showed Cruz exiting the MRI room after the victim and disposing of materials that were later secured by law enforcement. Testing of the materials returned presumptive positive results for the presence of male semen. Detectives confirmed Cruz had been working at the hospital as a travel MRI technician since Aug. 24, 2026, and was hired through a third-party agency.

Cruz was arrested in Brevard County on the evening of Sept. 16, 2026. The investigation remains active and ongoing.

HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital has cooperated fully with law enforcement throughout the investigation. In a statement, the hospital said the facility does not tolerate behavior that jeopardizes the safety or security of patients. When the allegation was reported, the hospital contacted law enforcement and ended Cruz's assignment.

The Port St. Lucie Police Department reminded the community to report incidents of sexual assault immediately to law enforcement or trusted resources, emphasizing that such reports can ensure victims receive support and allow law enforcement to investigate. Defendants are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty in a court of law.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce planning board delays decision on Willow Lakes data center rezoning
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce's planning board delayed a decision on rezoning 200 acres near Interstate 95 and Midway Road for a data center after residents expressed divided opinions on environmental impact and job creation.
cards.body:
Fort Pierce's planning board delayed a decision on a proposal to rezone 200 acres near Interstate 95 and Midway Road for a data center and commercial development after residents expressed mixed reactions. The board requested the planning department conduct further research and asked the city to discuss the item at the next commission meeting.

The property, currently zoned for a mixed-use development called Willow Lakes, would be partially rezoned under the proposal. About 174 acres would be designated for light industrial use limited to data center operations, while the remaining 26 acres along Midway Road would be rezoned for general commercial use, potentially allowing for a hotel, gas station, restaurants or retail businesses.

The planning board did not decide whether a data center qualifies as a permitted use within the light industrial zoning category. The applicant, Willow Lakes LLC, tabled the rezoning application as a result. W. Lee Dobbins, the attorney representing Willow Lakes LLC, said there is no point in moving forward with rezoning to light industrial until the city makes a decision on the code. Willow Lakes LLC emphasized the site's access to significant electrical infrastructure, including Florida Power Light transmission lines and a nearby substation. A large man-made lake on the property could serve as a water source for the data center's cooling system.

Residents expressed divided opinions about the proposal. Sarah Quinette said residents are not OK with a data center built next to their homes. She said keeping the area as agricultural land has a great impact in the form of pollinating insects that will return season after season. Felix Rodriguez said he thinks the project is cool because it brings in more jobs, construction and trade work, and the freight brings in more business. Shirley McHellon voiced opposition, saying the city needs to stop taking away the trees, woods and animals.

Before the data center can move forward with approval, the city must first decide whether to approve the rezoning request. Further research is required before the planning board revisits the proposal.

hero.headline: Martin County approves limited-industrial zoning for Hobe Sound property in 3-2 vote
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners voted 3-2 Tuesday to rezone a property along Southeast Powerline Avenue in Hobe Sound to limited-industrial, a compromise that stepped back from a general industrial designation that drew pushback from nearby residents. Commissioner Blake Capps voted against the rezoning, citing concerns about the potential for a data center on the site.

The property has long been slated for some form of industrial use, but the county said the existing zoning was outdated and due for an update. After hearing from residents who opposed the general industrial classification, the property owner offered to accept the less-intensive limited-industrial designation.

Bob Reins, a land-use attorney with Gunster law firm representing the property owner, told commissioners his client was willing to accept the light industrial classification if that was what neighbors felt was more appropriate. Capps said he remained opposed even to the compromise. "Who knows where this is really going in the future and to approve a zoning for this property that allows a data center. I'm not into that," Capps said.

Residents who spoke at the commission meeting said their primary concern was protecting the character of the community. Steve Addison, who has lived in the area since 1969, said his biggest concern was preserving quality of life. "We don't have a lot of industry and a lot of noise," Addison said. Kim Call, a resident, said growth needs to be compatible with the community that already exists. Patrick McDonough, a Hobe Sound resident and Eaglewood Community HOA president, said residents were concerned about the permanence of a general industrial classification which they believed was too broad and too open-ended.

The county said there are no plans for a data center at the site. Any proposal exceeding 100,000 square feet would require board approval. Addison said after the vote he felt the compromise was the right move. "I don't want to see over development, but I also don't want to be that guy that doesn't understand land-use and doesn't understand property rights," Addison said. "I feel like it was a win win for the both of us."

hero.headline: Florida requires parental opt-in for AI classroom tools by July 1, 2027
hero.body:
Parents will have to give permission before public and charter school students in Florida use artificial intelligence instructional tools under rules approved Wednesday by the State Board of Education.

Public school districts and charter schools have until July 1, 2027, to adopt and implement policies requiring parental opt-in. Students whose families decline must receive a comparable alternative without AI. The rules prohibit instructional chatbots designed to simulate friendship or emotional relationships with students, undisclosed psychological profiling and vendors selling student data.

Schools must notify parents when an AI instructional tool is approved, including which tool students would use, the courses involved and how students would interact with it. Tools used with children in pre-kindergarten through fifth grade face additional review for age and developmental appropriateness.

Gov. Ron DeSantis promoted the requirements during a Thursday appearance in Melbourne, saying technology should supplement classroom instruction. "We are not going to be displacing a classroom teacher with machines," DeSantis said. "We're going to continue to value the human experience in education, and not sacrifice that at the altar of technology."

Education Commissioner Henry Mack said the concern is whether students are developing their own understanding when they turn to AI for answers. "So if a course is designed to cultivate critical thinking, we do not want AI doing that on behalf of the learner," Mack said.

The board also approved rules for Florida College System institutions. Their policies must prohibit students from using AI on graded assignments or tests unless an instructor explicitly authorizes it.

Florida Education Association Vice President Carole Gauronskas expressed support for the policies overall while questioning how much additional work implementation could create for school districts. "We encourage this board to convene a panel of experts, including parents, guardians, and come up with more guidance and guardrails just to make sure that that human touch is there," she said.

Teachers and administrators will also need training on AI's risks, limitations, safety and compliance requirements. Many districts already have AI policies but will need to align them with the new statewide requirements. Mack said the Department of Education would organize work groups, coordinate with superintendents and provide resources to help carry out the rules.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce planning board delays data center rezoning at I-95 and Midway Road
hero.body:
The Fort Pierce planning board delayed a decision on a proposal to rezone 200 acres near Interstate 95 and Midway Road for a data center and commercial development, requesting further research before the matter moves to the city commission.

The board made two motions at its meeting. The first requested the planning department to conduct further research on the data center proposal and report back. The second motion called for the city to discuss the item at the next commission meeting. The board did not decide whether a data center qualifies as a permitted use within the light industrial zoning category, prompting the applicant to table the rezoning application.

The property, currently zoned for a mixed-use development called Willow Lakes, would be partially rezoned under the proposal submitted by Willow Lakes LLC. About 174 acres would be designated for light industrial use, limited to data center operations, while the remaining 26 acres along Midway Road would be rezoned for general commercial use, potentially allowing for a hotel, gas station, restaurants or retail businesses.

W. Lee Dobbins, the attorney representing Willow Lakes LLC, said the applicant would wait for the city to resolve the code definition question. "Therefore, there is no point in us moving forward with rezoning to light industrial," Dobbins said. "We would need to wait until that decision is over and make a decision at that time based upon what they changed the code to say."

The applicant emphasized the site's access to significant electrical infrastructure, including Florida Power Light transmission lines and a nearby substation. A large man-made lake on the property could also serve as a water source for the data center's cooling system.

Residents expressed divided opinions about the proposal. "We're not OK with them building a data center right next to our homes," said resident Sarah Quinette. "An area like that, if we keep it as agricultural land, it has a great impact in the form of pollinating insects that will return season after season."

Felix Rodriguez offered a different perspective. "I think it's pretty cool personally, just because it brings in more jobs, construction, that trade. All the freight just brings in more business," he said.

Shirley McHellon voiced opposition to the project. "I think they need to stop. They're taking away the trees, the woods and the animals ... they're just killing the animals," she said.

Before the data center can move forward with approval, the city must first decide whether to approve the rezoning request.

cards.headline: Vero Beach City Council approves 500-space paid parking lot at Regional Airport
cards.teaser: Vero Beach Regional Airport will replace free parking with a paid 500-space lot as the airport funds upgrades ahead of new flight service. Construction begins in March.
cards.body:
Vero Beach City Council approved construction of a new long-term parking lot at Vero Beach Regional Airport that will expand capacity from 80 spaces to over 500 spaces and end free parking at the facility.

Brandon Dambeck, interim airport director, said the expansion is driven by new flights coming to the airport. The current parking situation is not keeping up, Dambeck said, noting the grass parking area looks disorganized. The airport operates without taxpayer dollars and must use the funds to cover the costs of upgrades to the airport.

"The airport is responsible for maintaining its self-sustainability, meaning we don't take any taxpayer dollars," Dambeck said. "We have to make sure that our charges will help to to maintain the operations that happen at the airport."

Envision Parking Partners will build and pay for the lot. The airport will be responsible for maintaining it. John Mostoller with Envision said travelers will be able to pay through a prepaid option using license plate readers or at the lot gate. The new lot will also add cameras and lighting for security. No parking spot will be more than two to four minutes from the terminal, Mostoller said.

Traveler Reana Tejada said she will miss the free parking. "That sucks. I mean, that's — it's a nice plus to be able to park, especially if it was already free," Tejada said.

Sydney Banak, who was able to park for free during her visit, said she understands the reasoning behind the change. "Free parking is nice," Sydney said. "But maybe they need to expand the airport or provide more services, so I do understand where they're coming from with that."

Construction is expected to begin in March and be completed by next summer. The airport is also adding new covered walkways and baggage claim, and a new patio.

cards.body:
Gabriel Cruz, a 42-year-old travel MRI technician, was arrested on a first-degree felony sexual battery charge after a sedated patient reported an assault at HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital in Port St. Lucie. Port St. Lucie police arrested Cruz in Brevard County on the evening of Sept. 16.

The investigation began Sept. 14 after hospital staff reported that a 64-year-old female patient said she had been sexually assaulted during an MRI the day before at the hospital at 1800 SE Tiffany Ave. The woman had been admitted for medical treatment and was given medication before the MRI that left her significantly drowsy, police said.

Detectives identified Cruz as the technician assigned to the procedure. With the hospital's assistance, investigators obtained video that police said showed Cruz leaving the MRI room after the patient and disposing of materials. Those materials were recovered and tested, returning presumptive positive results for male semen, according to police.

Cruz had worked at the hospital as a travel MRI technician since Aug. 24 and was hired through a third-party agency, police said. The charge is sexual battery involving a physically helpless or incapacitated victim. The investigation remains active.

HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital cooperated with investigators, police said. In a statement, the hospital said it does not tolerate behavior that jeopardizes the safety or security of patients. The hospital said it contacted law enforcement when the allegation was reported and ended Cruz's assignment. The hospital said it has assisted law enforcement throughout the investigation and remains focused on supporting the patient.

hero.headline: Indian River County sheriff announces 50+ arrests in multi-agency human trafficking operation
hero.body:
Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers announced more than 50 arrests following a multi-agency, multi-day operation targeting human trafficking and illegal sexual activity in the county. Operation Late Checkout ran from Sept. 13 and netted over 60 contacts, more than 50 arrests, and three ICE detainers. The operation also resulted in a child-luring case in which a man traveled to Indian River County to meet a minor.

Flowers said during a Thursday press conference that several victims were identified during the operation, and ongoing investigations are underway. Victims' advocates trained to work with trafficking victims were on hand to speak with women involved in prostitution to determine whether they were being trafficked. There are no specific arrests on human trafficking charges at this time, Flowers said.

Flowers called the operation unprecedented for Indian River County. "We've never had an investigation like this, to my knowledge, in Indian River County with this many agencies involved, with this many arrests in one shot," he said. FDLE Assistant Special Agent in Charge Alfonso Williams said Operation Late Checkout was initiated by FDLE in coordination with the Indian River County Sheriff's Office and is the first operation of this magnitude conducted in the county.

Agencies involved in the operation included the Indian River County Sheriff's Office, Florida Department of Law Enforcement, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Seminole County Sheriff's Office, Altamonte Springs Police Department, Vero Beach Police Department, Homeland Security Investigations, Florida Office of Statewide Prosecutor and the U.S. Attorney's Office. Undercover teams were deployed in a variety of capacities during the operation. The child-luring arrest was the result of the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force working across agencies to apprehend individuals attempting to lure children online. "Our team did a great job of getting him off the street," Flowers said.

Williams said the operation focused on identifying human trafficking victims, reducing the demand for prostitution, and apprehending individuals seeking sexual contact with minors. "Our work is far from done," Williams said. "This operation requires a lot of resources and time. We cannot do this work alone, and our success depends on the great partnership and collaboration that you see today." FDLE houses the Florida Trafficking Hotline. Anyone who suspects someone is a victim of trafficking can contact the hotline at 1-855-352-7233.

cards.headline: Vero Beach animal hospital manager arrested for abandoning cats after reclaiming them from Humane Society
cards.teaser: Deanna Rae Wesley, 43, a manager at Dr. Dan's Animal Hospital in Vero Beach, faces two counts of animal abandonment after investigators said she picked up two cats from the Humane Society and left them outside without care.
cards.body:
Deanna Rae Wesley, 43, a manager at Dr. Dan's Animal Hospital in Vero Beach, was arrested Sept. 15 on two counts of animal abandonment after investigators said she reclaimed two cats from the Humane Society of Vero Beach and Indian River County and then abandoned them outdoors without care. A judge set bond at $250 per count, for a total of $500, according to Indian River County court records.

Animal Control investigators said Wesley picked up two white-and-brown tabby cats from the Humane Society on Sept. 8. Wesley told staff the cats were being returned to a caregiver but would not identify that person, the affidavit said.

The next day, Animal Control received a complaint about a white-and-brown tabby cat crying at a resident's front door. The cat was taken to Animal Control, where its microchip and Humane Society staff confirmed it was one of the cats Wesley had picked up. Wesley initially denied it was the same cat but acknowledged the matching microchip number, according to investigators. She declined to explain how the cat ended up loose at the home, the affidavit said.

The resident told investigators that a woman matching Wesley's description, wearing a Dr. Dan's T-shirt, spoke with her mother and warned her to watch out for Animal Control in the area. The woman allegedly called the cats colony cats, the affidavit said.

Animal Control recovered the second cat at the same residence Sept. 10. Both cats were described as extremely friendly, with debris on their faces and chins. Investigators said the cats were not capable of surviving outdoors on their own and that no one was known to be caring for them. The warrant alleges Wesley abandoned the cats on a public street without providing care, food, protection or shelter.

cards.headline: Amazon shuts Port St. Lucie fulfillment center for $200 million robotics overhaul
cards.teaser: Amazon closed its Port St. Lucie fulfillment center Thursday for a renovation expected to last until 2028, with roughly 300 workers taking severance. The company plans to invest $200 million to add advanced robotics, artificial intelligence, and 870,000 square feet to the facility.
cards.body:
Amazon closed its Port St. Lucie fulfillment center Thursday for a major renovation expected to last until at least 2028, with the company investing about $200 million to add advanced robotics and artificial intelligence capabilities along with an additional 870,000 square feet. Around 300 employees are expected to take severance as the facility shuts down.

Amazon filed a layoff notice in July listing 494 affected employees. Workers who were employed at the facility before the closure will be eligible for rehire when it reopens, according to the Economic Development Council of St. Lucie County.

Local workforce organizations, including CareerSource Research Coast and the Economic Development Council of St. Lucie County, have spent recent months holding job fairs and helping affected workers connect with other employers. St. Lucie County Commissioner Cathy Townsend said the closure highlights the importance of attracting a wider range of businesses to the county.

"I think we need to be more strategic on the companies we want coming here," Townsend said. "My focus would be more on small businesses."

Amazon plans to reopen the facility in the second half of 2028 and hire more than 1,000 employees, according to the St. Lucie EDC. The closure is not expected to impact customers because operations will be handled by other facilities during the renovation, Amazon has said.

Amazon closed its Port St. Lucie fulfillment center Thursday for a major renovation, with around 300 employees taking severance as the facility shuts down. The company plans to invest about $200 million to renovate and expand the warehouse, which will remain closed until at least late 2028.

When Amazon filed its layoff notice in July, 494 employees were listed as affected. More than 200 workers have since transferred to other Amazon locations. The renovation will add 870,000 square feet and include advanced robotics and artificial intelligence capabilities.

CareerSource Research Coast and the Economic Development Council of St. Lucie County spent recent months holding job fairs and helping affected workers connect with other employers. St. Lucie County Commissioner Cathy Townsend said the closure highlights the importance of attracting a wider range of businesses to the county.

"I think we need to be more strategic on the companies we want coming here," Townsend said. "My focus would be more on small businesses."

Amazon plans to reopen the facility in the second half of 2028 and hire more than 1,000 employees. Workers who were employed at the facility before the closure will be eligible for rehire when it reopens, according to the St. Lucie EDC. Amazon said the closure is not expected to impact customers because operations will be handled by other facilities during the renovation.

hero.headline: Indian River County sheriff announces 50+ arrests in multi-agency human trafficking operation
hero.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff's Office announced more than 50 arrests following a multi-agency, multi-day operation targeting human trafficking and illegal sexual activity in the county. Operation Late Checkout ran from Sept. 13 in Indian River County and netted over 60 contacts, more than 50 arrests, and three ICE detainers, Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a press conference on Thursday. Flowers said there are no specific arrests on human trafficking charges at this time.

Agencies involved in the operation included the Indian River County Sheriff's Office, Florida Department of Law Enforcement, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Seminole County Sheriff's Office, Altamonte Springs Police Department, Vero Beach Police Department, Homeland Security Investigations, Florida Office of Statewide Prosecutor and the U.S. Attorney's Office, Flowers said. During the operation, several victims were identified, and investigators said ongoing investigations are underway.

One case involved a man who traveled to Indian River County to meet a minor. Flowers said the arrest was the result of the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force working across agencies to apprehend individuals attempting to lure children online. Undercover teams were deployed in a variety of capacities during the operation. Victims' advocates trained to work with trafficking victims were also on hand to speak with women involved in prostitution to determine whether they were being trafficked.

Flowers called the operation unprecedented for Indian River County. He said he has no knowledge of an investigation in Indian River County with this many agencies involved and this many arrests in one shot. FDLE Assistant Special Agent in Charge Alfonso Williams said Operation Late Checkout was initiated by FDLE in coordination with the Indian River County Sheriff's Office and is the first operation of this magnitude conducted in the county. Williams said the operation focused on identifying human trafficking victims, reducing the demand for prostitution, and apprehending individuals seeking sexual contact with minors. FDLE houses the Florida Trafficking Hotline. Anyone who suspects someone is a victim of trafficking can contact the hotline at 1-855-352-7233.

cards.headline: Liquor theft at Martin County Publix leads to high-speed chase into Palm Beach County
cards.teaser: A 24-year-old man faces theft and fleeing charges after stealing liquor bottles from a Publix and leading deputies on a pursuit that crossed county lines.
cards.body:
A 24-year-old man faces theft and fleeing charges after stealing liquor bottles from a Publix in Martin County and leading deputies on a pursuit that crossed into Palm Beach County. Derwyn Edwards stole several bottles of liquor from a Publix before deputies attempted to stop him, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office.

Edwards refused to pull over when a deputy caught up with his vehicle, investigators said. Video from the pursuit shows him speeding, running red lights and coming dangerously close to other drivers on the road, authorities said.

Sheriff's office air crews tracked Edwards as he continued driving into Palm Beach County, deputies said. The chase ended when Edwards was taken into custody.

Edwards is now charged with theft and fleeing police.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce grants King's Landing developers six-month extension after failed termination motion
hero.body:
Fort Pierce city commissioners voted 3-2 Monday night to grant developers of the King's Landing project a six-month extension to raise $15 million for the long-delayed mixed-use development near the downtown marina.

The vote came after Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky made a motion to terminate the development agreement, which failed. Dzadovsky expressed frustration with the seven-year timeline. "Well, it's been seven years. We should be well past this process. I was disappointed in the outcome for sure," Dzadovsky said.

The multi-million-dollar project is expected to include a Marriott hotel, restaurant, residential units, retail space, and a parking garage. Current developer Bill Ware with Live Oak Holdings attended the meeting and requested commissioners not hold his company accountable for delays prior to Live Oak being approved in the April 2025 third amendment. "I respectfully request that we not be held captive or accountable for this ten-year-plus period of time and prior to Live Oak being approved in the April of 2025 third amendment," Ware said. Ware committed to continuing monthly and quarterly email updates.

Commissioners agreed to move forward but instructed developers to formally document their default. "Our concerns need to be addressed in that document, or it's not going to get approved," Michael Broderick said. Dzadovsky expressed skepticism about the extension leading to progress. "Given the seven years' experience, I think six months from now we'll be back to where we started today, last night," Dzadovsky said. Developers now have 180 days to secure the funding and move the project forward.

cards.body:
The U.S. Navy confirmed on Tuesday, Sept. 15, that an underwater explosion seen off the Fort Pierce coast earlier that day was a controlled detonation. The blast was recorded around 12:30 p.m. and captured on video showing the explosion in the water.

The Navy has not released further details about the purpose of the detonation or the specific location off the coast where it occurred. Efforts to obtain more information from the Navy are ongoing.

The explosion was visible from the shore and drew attention from residents along the Fort Pierce coast. Video footage showed a plume of water erupting from the ocean surface during the midday blast.

The Navy's confirmation came the same day as the explosion, though officials did not immediately provide additional context about the controlled detonation or whether similar operations are planned in the area.

hero.headline: Martin County approves limited-industrial zoning in Hobe Sound 3-2 despite data center concerns
hero.body:
The Martin County Commission approved rezoning a property along Southeast Powerline Avenue in Hobe Sound to limited-industrial in a 3-2 vote Tuesday, stepping back from a general industrial designation that drew pushback from nearby residents. Commissioner Blake Capps voted against the rezoning, citing concerns about the potential for a data center on the site, while residents remain divided over whether the compromise adequately protects the community.

The property has long been slated for some form of industrial use, but the county said the existing zoning was outdated and due for an update. After residents voiced concerns at the Tuesday commission meeting, the property owner offered to accept the less-intensive limited-industrial classification.

Steve Addison, who has lived in the area since 1969, said residents were focused on preserving quality of life. Kim Call, a resident, said she believes growth needs to be compatible with the community that already exists. Patrick McDonough, a Hobe Sound resident and Eaglewood Community HOA president, said residents were concerned about the permanence of a general industrial classification which they believe is too broad and too open-ended.

Bob Reins, a land-use attorney with Gunster law firm representing the property owner, said they were willing to accept the light industrial classification to cooperate with neighbors. Capps said he was not willing to approve zoning for the property that allows a data center. The county said there are no plans for a data center at the site. Any proposal exceeding 100,000 square feet would require board approval. Addison said he felt the compromise was a win for both sides.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce approves $10.1 million contract for police body cameras and AI tools
hero.body:
The Fort Pierce city commission on Monday voted unanimously 5-0 to approve a $10.1 million, decade-long contract with Axon Enterprise, Inc. for body cameras, Tasers, and artificial intelligence technology tools for the police department.

The contract runs for five years with an optional automatic renewal for another five years. The 10-year contract will cost Fort Pierce $10,139,037.87. The city will make annual payments of $999,000 during the first five years. If the renewal option is exercised, the city will pay Axon Enterprise $1,028,807.57 annually for the final five years.

Fort Pierce Police Department Chief David M. Smith described the package as Axon Enterprise's top-tier offering. The equipment includes Tasers, also known as stun guns, and body cameras that translate languages immediately for officers. An officer would speak in their language, and the body camera will relay the message to the subject in their language. Smith said prior to the vote that the technology "will absolutely be a force multiplier for us."

The Axon technology will also help officers with redaction of police reports. Redactions are used to prevent personal information, like Social Security numbers, from being made public. According to the commission agenda, the current Axon body cameras owned by the police department were at the end of their life and needed to be replaced. Axon Enterprise is in Scottsdale, Arizona.

hero.headline: Diver finds suspected WWII torpedo off Fort Pierce beach during lobster hunt
hero.body:
A diver searching for lobster off Fort Pierce beach last month discovered a suspected World War II-era torpedo, prompting a controlled detonation by the U.S. Navy on Tuesday.

Luke Neiman was diving with his father and a friend just south of the jetty when he spotted the unusual object. Neiman said he was near a large condominium building when he came across something on the seafloor that did not look like a reef.

"I couldn't really make out what it was, but I just knew it wasn't a reef, and I was kind of inspecting it, looking at it," Neiman said. "I'm like, this just looks different, you know, and then before I knew it, I'm like, this is a torpedo, because I could make out the end of it and it had a cone nose."

Neiman returned to the boat, told his father to mark the spot, and contacted the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission. The FWC alerted the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office bomb squad, and the U.S. Navy was then notified.

Navy Explosive Ordnance Disposal personnel conducted a controlled underwater detonation at the site on Tuesday afternoon, Sept. 15, 2026. Navy officials confirmed the operation in a statement, saying the personnel conducted a routine underwater ordnance disposal operation in the waters off St. Lucie County. The Navy identified the object as a suspected World War II-era munition.

Neiman reflected on the discovery with surprise. "Yeah, it just really blew my mind literally that I found a torpedo down here right where I catch a bunch of lobster and stuff!" he said.

hero.headline: Martin County approves limited-industrial zoning for Powerline Avenue site in Hobe Sound
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners voted 3-2 Tuesday to rezone property along Southeast Powerline Avenue in Hobe Sound to limited-industrial, stepping back from a general industrial designation that drew pushback from nearby residents. Commissioner Blake Capps voted against the rezoning, citing concerns about the potential for a data center on the site, and the county confirmed any proposal exceeding 100,000 square feet would require board approval.

The property has long been slated for some form of industrial use, but the county said the existing zoning was outdated and due for an update. Residents who spoke at the commission meeting said their primary concern was protecting the character of the community.

Steve Addison said he has lived in the area since 1969. "Our biggest concern was preserving our quality of life. We don't have a lot of industry and a lot of noise," Addison said. Kim Call said she believes growth needs to be compatible with the community that already exists. Patrick McDonough, a Hobe Sound resident and Eaglewood Community HOA president, said residents were concerned about the permanence of a general industrial classification which they believe is too broad and too open-ended.

After hearing from residents, the property owner offered to accept the less-intensive classification. "To cooperate and show if that's what the neighbors feel is more appropriate and that would be a better use then we are willing to accept the light industrial," Bob Reins, a land-use attorney with Gunster law firm, said.

Capps said he was not comfortable approving zoning for the property that allows a data center. "Who knows where this is really going in the future and to approve a zoning for this property that allows a data center. I'm not into that," Capps said. The county said there are no plans for a data center at the site.

Addison said he felt the outcome was the right move. "I don't want to see over development, but I also don't want to be that guy that doesn't understand land-use and doesn't understand property rights," Addison said. "I feel like it was a win win for the both of us."

hero.headline: Jolly proposes AI data center moratorium; Donalds warns freeze would drive investment from Florida
hero.body:
Florida's gubernatorial candidates have drawn a sharp line over artificial intelligence infrastructure, with Democrat David Jolly proposing a one-year moratorium on new data centers and Republican Byron Donalds warning that a statewide freeze could drive investment elsewhere.

Jolly, in a Sept. 13 interview with CBS Miami, said Florida needs more time to assess the effects on communities and natural resources. During a Tallahassee stop, he framed the proposal as a response to residents' concerns about water use, electricity costs and local control as communities weigh new facilities ahead of November's gubernatorial vote.

"We don't need data centers in the state of Florida at all, at all, at all," Jolly told CBS Miami. His campaign announced Sept. 14 that he would visit Northern Virginia's Data Center Alley this week to meet residents who say nearby facilities have disrupted their lives with persistent noise, air quality issues and other effects. Democrats launched a "Data Center Donalds" tour Tuesday in Pinellas County, with agriculture commissioner nominee Joey Mendoza Atkins and state House candidate Bryan Beckman joining residents at the site of a previously proposed data center.

Donalds argues Florida can protect communities while remaining open to infrastructure businesses need. "Capital goes where it's valued," he said in an August interview, warning that talk of bans and moratoriums could signal Florida is not the place to invest. "But you can't build for your life if you don't have a high-paying job. And you're not going to have a high-paying job if you don't have companies who invest in your state," Donalds said. Last week, Donalds described AI as a force multiplier, comparing its potential to the internet and personal computers. He supports keeping facilities away from homes and using cooling technology that conserves water, and said local governments should retain control over whether projects are built.

A July survey from the University of North Florida's Public Opinion Research Lab found 68% of likely Florida midterm voters opposed an AI data center in their local area, while 28% supported one. The poll surveyed 848 likely voters July 8–17. Voters were evenly divided on the general increase in AI use, with 49% supporting it and 49% opposing it.

Florida adopted new rules for large data centers when Ron DeSantis signed SB 484 in May. The law requires electricity rate structures designed to ensure large customers pay their own service costs, preserves local planning and land-use authority, and establishes water-permitting requirements for large data centers. It also calls for an independent study of their economic, environmental and public-health effects. Jolly argues paying for utilities does not resolve broader concerns. "He's basically saying you can come plunder our natural resources as long as you pay your own way," Jolly said of Donalds' position.

cards.headline: Florida ranks 8th most expensive in US for grocery essentials
cards.teaser: Florida shoppers pay $134.35 for a basket of 30 essential grocery items, about $2 more than the national average, according to a new study by Self Financial. Local shoppers say they cope with rising prices through couponing, bulk buying, and adjusting family meals.
cards.body:
Florida shoppers pay $134.35 for a basket of 30 essential grocery items, about $2 more than the national average, according to a new study by Self Financial. The analysis compared 30 essential grocery items, including meat, milk, eggs and produce, and found Florida ranks eighth most expensive in the country for the cost of essentials.

Local shoppers say they feel the impact every time they head to the store. Elaine Capute said looking for deals at the grocery store is a full-time job. "I go online for the Publix ad. I clip all the digital coupons because you never know what you're going to buy," Capute said. "I don't know what people do that work full time, because it really takes up a lot of my time, but we're retired, and I do what I have to do."

Retired chef Monte Schrier said his go-to strategy is shopping at a wholesaler, where he gets deals as a member. He showed his last receipt, where 40 pounds of bulk chicken breasts cost just $1.39 a pound. "Clean it, cut it, cryo-vac it and freeze it. A lot of people don't like to do that. They don't like to freeze stuff, but if you want to pay $6 a pound every time," Schrier said. Schrier said he also shops around, hitting two or three stores and getting the best deals at each.

Shopper Betty Magar said the strategy is planning ahead. "I eat for that week, what's on sale or what's a BOGO," Magar said. Shopper Bryce Hipp said with a fourth child on the way, the priority is making sure his kids have plenty. "Take a look at what we eat versus what our kids eat. We want our kids to not go without anything. Sometimes we might dial back what we might want," Hipp said.

Food prices continue to fluctuate. Uncooked turkey and other poultry are up 11.5% in the past year, and instant coffee is up 11%. Egg prices are down 23% over the past year.

hero.headline: Martin County approves limited-industrial zoning for Hobe Sound Powerline Avenue property in 3-2 vote
hero.body:
The Martin County Commission voted 3-2 Tuesday to approve limited-industrial zoning for a property along Southeast Powerline Avenue in Hobe Sound, stepping back from a general industrial designation that drew opposition from nearby residents. The approval leaves lingering concerns among some residents and Commissioner Blake Capps about the potential for a data center at the site, though the county requires board approval for any future project exceeding 100,000 square feet.

The property owner offered to accept the less-intensive limited-industrial classification after hearing from residents at the meeting. Bob Reins, a land-use attorney with Gunster law firm, said the property owner agreed to cooperate with neighbors who felt the designation would be more appropriate.

Capps voted against the rezoning despite the compromise, citing concerns about what could be built on the site. "Who knows where this is really going in the future and to approve a zoning for this property that allows a data center. I'm not into that," Capps said. The county said there are no plans for a data center at the site.

Residents who spoke at the commission meeting said their primary concern was protecting the character of the community. Steve Addison, who has lived in the area since 1969, said the biggest concern was preserving quality of life in an area without much industry and noise. Kim Call, a resident, said growth needs to be compatible with the community that already exists. Patrick McDonough, a Hobe Sound resident and Eaglewood Community HOA president, said residents were concerned about the permanence of a general industrial classification which would be too broad and open-ended.

The property has long been slated for some form of industrial use, but the county said the existing zoning was outdated and due for an update. Addison said he felt the outcome was a win for both sides. "I don't want to see over development, but I also don't want to be that guy that doesn't understand land-use and doesn't understand property rights," Addison said.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce commissioners grant King's Landing developers six-month extension
hero.body:
Fort Pierce city commissioners voted 3-2 Monday night to grant developers of the King's Landing project a six-month extension to raise $15 million for the long-delayed development near the downtown marina.

The extension gives Live Oak Holdings 180 days to secure funding for a hotel that is part of the mixed-use development. The multi-million-dollar project is expected to include a Marriott hotel, restaurant, residential units, retail space, and a parking garage.

Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky expressed frustration with the project's history and made a motion to terminate the development agreement, but that motion failed. Dzadovsky said the project has faced delays for seven years.

"Well, it's been seven years. We should be well past this process. I was disappointed in the outcome for sure," Dzadovsky said.

Current developer Bill Ware with Live Oak Holdings attended the meeting and told commissioners he should not be held accountable for delays that occurred before his company was approved in a third amendment in April 2025.

"I respectfully request that we not be held captive or accountable for this ten-year-plus period of time and prior to Live Oak being approved in the April of 2025 third amendment," Ware said.

Ware said he will continue monthly email updates and quarterly updates.

Officials agreed to move forward but instructed the developers to formally document their default. Michael Broderick said the document must address the city's concerns or it will not be approved.

Dzadovsky said he is not optimistic the deadline will be met.

"Given the seven years' experience, I think six months from now we'll be back to where we started today, last night," Dzadovsky said.

hero.headline: Jolly proposes data center moratorium; Donalds warns freeze could drive investment from Florida
hero.body:
Florida's gubernatorial candidates have turned artificial intelligence infrastructure into a campaign battleground, with Democrat David Jolly proposing a one-year moratorium on new data centers and Republican Byron Donalds warning that a statewide freeze could drive investment elsewhere. The clash puts water consumption, electricity costs and local land-use control at the center of debate as voters prepare to choose the state's next governor in November.

Jolly told CBS Miami in a Sept. 13 interview that Florida does not need data centers at all and should pause new development to assess effects on communities and natural resources. His campaign announced Sept. 14 that he would visit Northern Virginia's Data Center Alley this week to meet residents who say nearby facilities have disrupted their lives with persistent noise, air quality problems and other development impacts. During a Tallahassee stop, Jolly framed the proposal as a response to residents' concerns, saying leaders need to listen and follow public opinion.

Donalds argues Florida can protect communities while remaining open to infrastructure businesses need. He said in an August interview that capital goes where it is valued and that talk of bans and moratoriums could signal Florida is not the place to invest. He supports keeping facilities away from homes and using cooling technology that conserves water, including systems that recirculate water or use air cooling. Last week, Donalds described AI as a force multiplier comparable to the internet and personal computers. He said local governments should retain control over whether projects are built, stating that if a local government does not want to build it, they will not build it.

Democrats launched their Data Center Donalds tour Tuesday in Pinellas County, accusing Donalds of putting industry donors ahead of communities. Agriculture commissioner nominee Joey Mendoza Atkins and state House candidate Bryan Beckman joined residents at the site of a previously proposed data center. A July survey from the University of North Florida's Public Opinion Research Lab found 68% of likely Florida midterm voters opposed an AI data center in their local area, while 28% supported one. The same survey found voters evenly divided on the general increase in AI use, with 49% supporting it and 49% opposing it. The poll surveyed 848 likely voters July 8-17.

Ron DeSantis signed SB 484 in May establishing new rules for large data centers. The law requires electricity rate structures designed to ensure large customers pay their own service costs, preserves local planning and land-use authority, establishes water-permitting requirements for large data centers, and calls for an independent study of their economic, environmental and public-health effects. Jolly argues paying for utilities does not resolve broader concerns, saying Donalds is basically saying companies can plunder natural resources as long as they pay their own way. Donalds countered in August that leadership requires more than following public opinion, saying it is easy to listen to what everybody is saying and follow the polling, but that is not leadership.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce grants King's Landing developers fifth extension despite motion to terminate deal
hero.body:
Fort Pierce city commissioners voted 3-2 Monday night to grant developers of the King's Landing project a six-month extension to raise $15 million for the long-delayed mixed-use development near the downtown marina. The vote came after Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky made a motion to terminate the development agreement, which failed. Dzadovsky expressed frustration with the project's timeline, saying he was disappointed in the outcome. "Well, it's been seven years. We should be well past this process. I was disappointed in the outcome for sure," he said.

The extension gives Live Oak Holdings 180 days to secure funding for a hotel that is part of the project. Current developer Bill Ware attended the commission meeting and said he would continue providing updates. "I will continue my monthly email updates, but I'll also continue my monthly quarterly updates," Ware said. The multi-million-dollar project is expected to include a Marriott hotel, restaurant, residential units, retail space, and a parking garage. However, the project has faced several delays over the years.

Ware asked commissioners not to hold Live Oak accountable for delays that occurred before the company was approved in an April 2025 third amendment to the development agreement. "I respectfully request that we not be held captive or accountable for this ten-year-plus period of time and prior to Live Oak being approved in the April of 2025 third amendment," Ware said. The commissioners agreed to move forward but instructed the developers to formally document their default.

Commissioner Michael Broderick said the city's concerns must be addressed in that document or it will not be approved. "Our concerns need to be addressed in that document, or it's not going to get approved," Broderick said. Dzadovsky said he is not optimistic the extension will change the outcome. "Given the seven years' experience, I think six months from now we'll be back to where we started today, last night," he said. The developers now have 180 days to secure the funding and move the project forward.
